📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When residents of a state are born can be an key factor in determining several pieces of information. How old people are can contribute to things like healthcare or retirement benefits for the older residents, as well as schooling and workforce opportunities for the younger population.

Sources indicate that but which states have more older populations and which have younger? And what are the most common birth dates? See how your state fares when it comes to the most popular birth months and years, based on CDC data reviewed by Kremp Florists.

According to recent reports, it's easy to find residents with earlier birth years on the West Coast, with Hawaii and Oregon leading the way. The most common birth year in the two states is 1953, with the most residents around 72 years old.

Two more Western states also make the top five list for the oldest most common birth years. Montana and New Mexico claim 1954 as the most common birth year along with New England state Vermont. Nearby Maine is only a year behind at 1955, making 70 years old the most common age in the state.

Three states are a year younger than Maine. Louisiana, South Dakota, and West Virginia have the most residents who are 69-70 years old, with the most common birth year being 1956 in those states.

On the other end of the spectrum, there are five states where the most common birth year is in the 21st century.

According to recent reports, alaska leads the list with the most common birth year of 2010, making 16 the most common birthday being celebrated this year. That's quite a lot of latest provisional driver's licenses for residents of the state compared to other years.

Alaska is also the only state where the most common birth year results in teenagers. Second-place Idaho claims 2005 as the most common birth year, with those residents turning 21 in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that third-place Utah is a year behind at 2004, while two Latest England states round out the top five states with most common birth years in the 21st century. Both Massachusetts and Rhode Island count 2002 as the most common birth year among its population.

Higher education could be a factor in different ways among these states. In Rhode Island and Massachusetts, for example, more than 50% of 18-24-year-olds in each state are enrolled in college, boosting the number of residents born in the early 2000s.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, the state with the least number of 18-24-year-olds in college is Alaska, with 20.5% of that age group enrolled. A youth outmigration trend in Alaska could be contributing to people leaving the state when they can.

It has been revealed that birth years vary widely from state to state, with an almost 60-year gap between the oldest and youngest most common birth years. Birth month, according to Kremp Floristsâ findings, however, is pretty consistent.

Almost every state has the same month as the most common in this reporting: August. Only five states have a different month, with July leading the way in Maine, Montana, Fresh Hampshire, and South Dakota. Wyoming is the only state where the most common birth month is May.

These stats may be a bit surprising, considering September 9 is the most common birthday in America.

#316. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • According to recent reports, in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • In a recent development, to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

According to recent reports, in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

In a recent development, to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

Sources indicate that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

According to recent reports, be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

According to recent reports, but there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

In a recent development, if you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Sources indicate that most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

Industry observers note that but we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

Sources indicate that in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

According to recent reports, secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

According to recent reports, need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

It has been revealed that for something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

Industry observers note that this is probably a temperature concern. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Recent findings suggest that another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that J.R.R. Tolkien created an entire universe of creatures, monsters, races, languages, and cultures in his Lord of the Rings stories and their supporting mythologies. Many of them were his own invention, with monstrous Balrogs, sentient tree-like Ents, half-bred Uruk-Hai, andâperhaps most famously of allâhobbits all being products of Tolkienâs unending imagination.

But alongside his numerous original creations, Tolkien utilized a number of creatures from existing real-world folklore, and borrowed considerably from Norse, Celtic and Anglo-Saxon mythology, as well as several other sources, in filling Middle-earth with its array of legendary creatures.

Recent findings suggest that tolkienâs elves are portrayed as wise, graceful, and nigh-on immortal beings (killable only in battle or by sorrow), and the fairest of all the inhabitants of Tolkienâs world. Outside of his stories, however, elves originated in tales from ancient Germanic mythology, with some of their earliest detailed descriptions coming from old Icelandic legends and Old English mythology.

Recent findings suggest that how the elves of Germanic folklore were portrayed varied enormously. It is the elves of northern and Scandinavian folklore who most resemble those of Tolkienâs writing, and as such were generally seen as being graceful and rather indifferent creatures, who would largely leave humans alone and live in peace and quiet in pastoral settings. Other Germanic elves were typically portrayed as diminutive beings that could either be a help or a hindrance to people, depending on their notoriously volatile moods. The Anglo-Saxons, for instance, blamed various medical issues on the malevolent or tricky behavior of elves, labelling hiccups or some other mysterious complaint as âÃ¦lfsogoÃ°a,â or âelf-chokes.â Later, tangles in a personâs hair on waking up in the morning were nicknamed âelf-locks,â and blamed on the mischievousness of elves overnight.

In a recent development, popular etymology links goblins to malevolent creatures from Germanic folklore known as kobolds or kobolts. Among miners and earth workers, these creatures were stated to dwell in caves far below ground and were blamed for spoiling ores, ruining seams of valuable material, noxious gases and vapors, and all the mysterious ailments that many mine workers would succumb to. In fact, the workersâ ills were due to the rocks with which they were working being laced with arsenic; the more valuable metal they obtained from them, however, became known as cobalt.

Industry observers note that that particular bit of folklore is true, but the connection between goblins and kobolts is not. Instead, goblins appear to be a more Western rather than Germanic invention, with the word borrowed into English from French in medieval times. Its roots ultimately lie in Latin and Greek, and the word can at length be traced back to an ancient Greek word for a rogue or vagabond.

According to recent reports, unlike Tolkienâs monstrous goblins, the goblins of European folklore were typically portrayed as diminutive, mischievous, and often rather mysterious gnome-like creatures that would attach themselves to a household and cause mischief around the homeâpulling bedclothes of sleeping people, banging doors and pots and pans, and moving furniture under cover of darkness. Far from being the vicious, âcruel, wicked, and bad-heartedâ creatures that Tolkien writes about in The Hobbit, these folkloric goblins were more malevolent nuisances that could easily be done away with by rapping noisily on walls or furniture.

Orcs are one of those creatures that many Lord of the Rings fans will popularly claim Tolkien himself made upâbut thatâs not strictly true. As far back as the 10th century, the Old English word orc was being used as an early translation of the far older Latin word orcus (which was in turn the byname of a kind of underworld deity in Roman mythology), while the compound form âorcneas,â likewise interpreted as the name of some kind of monster, is used in the legendary poem Beowulf. Itâs been , but is by no means certain, that this word may be a distant relative of ogre, perhaps via an old Italian word for a man-eating monster, orco.

Confusing things slightly here is the existence of another Old English word, orc or ork, which was used for a kind of sea creature (and shares its roots with the orca killer whale). Despite both terms being used for monstrous creatures in early English folklore, they were ultimately separate wordsâand only one, it seems, was resurrected by Tolkien around 1,000 years later.

Rather than inventing orcs himself, therefore, Tolkien appears to have picked up and revived an established Anglo-Saxon term for a monsterâbut with no actual folklore to go on, created an entirely latest creature, which he henceforth referred to as an orc in his writings. The success of his stories led to the term becoming popularized and finally reestablished in our language in the late 1900s, a millennium or so after it was first used in print.

Sources indicate that tolkien lifted the trolls that appear in his stories almost directly from Nordic and later Scandinavian folklore. In the original myths and legends of northern Europe, trolls were portrayed as giant, powerful, man-eating monsters that lived in remote or dark placesâand, just as happens in The Hobbit, can be turned to stone when exposed to sunlight.

In later talesâespecially those introduced to the far north of Scotland by Scandinavian settlers in later medieval timesâtrolls became smaller and more human-like creatures, but were still portrayed as malevolent, nasty, or dim-witted.

Industry observers note that dwarves are another being Tolkien borrowed from Germanic and Scandinavian folklore. Norse mythology in particular includes a number of characters who are identified as dwarves, including the brothers Brokkr and Sindri (also known as Eitri), who forged Thorâs hammer, MjÃ¶lnir.

Myths and folkloric tales about dwarves were varied and numerous across ancient northern Europe, with many stories creating different kinds, kingdoms, or races of dwarves. Almost always, though, dwarves were portrayed just as Tolkien went on to do too, and were considered industrious workers, miners, metalworkers, and craftsmen, who dwelled in immense halls full of gold and precious stones deep in remote mountains.

Largely excluded from Peter Jacksonâs film series, Tolkien wrote extensively of âbarrow-wightsââwraith-like beings that were essentially animated bones, possessed by evil spirits and sent back to walk the earth.

Recent findings suggest that in early Old English, the word wight (or wiht as it was originally spelled) meant simply a being or living thing, but by later medieval times the word had picked up a secondary meaning and come to be used more specifically of supernatural or spiritual beingsâjust like those described by Tolkien. It has been revealed that heracles (more commonly known by his Roman name, Hercules) is one of the most famous figures in mythology, often seen as the paragon of Greek heroism. However, many people in the modern day know little about the demigod. Heracles was the son of Perseusâs granddaughter Alcmene and Zeus, a fact which caused him no small amount of trouble. According to recent reports, the Iliad began in the tenth year of the Trojan War, prioritizing a conflict between Achilles and Agamemnon over the conflict between the Trojans and the Greeks. Feeling this was a slight against him, Achilles declared that his troops would leave the war.

While Achilles eventually allowed his men to fight, he refused to join the battle personally, depriving the Greeks of their greatest warrior. Gods and men alike fought for their respective sides, but Troy was destined to win unless Achilles stepped in. This caused waves of hopelessness to go through the ranks, prompting Agamemnon to offer to return Briseis, marry his daughter to Achilles, and even give the man several cities to rule. Achilles refused, too consumed by pride to accept any offer.

It has been revealed that after many Greeks were killed and injured in battle, the remaining leaders asked Achilles's best friend (and rumored lover) Patroclus to appeal to him on their behalf. Patroclus asked Achilles to either join the fight or loan him his armor so they could bluff the Trojans. Achilles agreed to let Patroclus use his armor, a strategy which worked well until the Trojans killed Patroclus. Fueled by grief, rage, and divine power, Achilles entered the field in armor crafted by Hephaestus himself, killing every Trojan he saw until he found and killed the man who killed Patroclus. Recent findings suggest that in the Croatian village of Čigoč, some of the most conspicuous residents live above the rooftops. White storks build bulky nests on traditional wooden houses, sharing the settlement with the people below.

Industry observers note that situated in Lonjsko Polje Nature Park beside the Tišina oxbow of the Sava River, the village is surrounded by wet meadows, pastures, and pools. These habitats provide feeding grounds close to the nests, allowing adult birds to gather frogs, insects, and other small animals for their young.

It has been revealed that in 1994, the conservation foundation EuroNatur named Čigoč the first European Stork Village. The designation recognised the village’s importance for white storks and its long-standing relationship between people, traditional farming, and wildlife. It also launched an initiative that would connect stork villages across Europe.

Industry observers note that the wooden houses are part of this story. Their rooftops provide nesting places, while the surrounding agricultural landscape helps sustain the birds. During the breeding season, a walk through the village offers a chance to watch adults tending their nests and travelling between the rooftops and nearby feeding grounds.

Recent findings suggest that plan a spring or summer visit to see storks occupying their nests. April through June coincides with the nature park’s scheduled white-stork educational programmes. Bring binoculars for viewing the rooftops from the village road.

Industry observers note that start at the Čigoč Visitor Centre in the restored Oberhofer–Hangi manor at Čigoč 4. The park asks visitors to park in the manor courtyard because the village road is narrow.

The village is a residential community. Observe nests from a respectful distance and ask permission before entering private yards.

Check the park’s website for visitor-centre opening hours, admission arrangements, and guided programmes.

Visitor-centre telephone: +385 44 715 115.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In June 2024, when Scholastic announced a fifth Hunger Games novel set on the morning of Haymitch Abernathyâs reaping, the statement from Suzanne Collins started with philosophy: âWith âSunrise on the Reaping,â I was inspired by David Humeâs idea of implicit submission and, in his words, âthe easiness with which the many are governed by the few.ââ Hume, who lived from 1711 to 1776, was a leading figure of the Scottish Enlightenment. Collinsâs earlier books leaned on Greek myth and Roman gladiators, but this time she opened the novel with two passages by him, and his influence runs through the story.

Collins didnât find Hume in grad school: her father was a historian and a doctor of political science, a career Air Force officer who taught at West Point before he left for Vietnam, and he treated his kids as never too young to learn. âMy dad introduced me to David Hume when I was a child, along with many other philosophers,â she told her editor, David Levithan, in Scholasticâs interview for the book. âHe talked about them while using more kid-friendly examples. Like, in Humeâs case, sunrises and billiard balls.â.

Those are Humeâs own examples: in his 1748 Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, he used billiard balls to argue that you canât know one thing will move the other until youâve watched it happen. He used the sunrise to make the bigger point: âThat the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.â Nothing guarantees the future will behave like the past, no matter how many mornings in a row it has.

According to recent reports, thatâs the argument Haymitch loses to Lenore Dove in the first chapter. Heâs certain the reaping will always fall on his birthday because it always has, and she points out that itâs only been around for 50 years. âShe makes Haymitch promise that he will fight to make sure there is never another sunrise on the reaping,â Collins said, and thatâs where the title came from.

It has been revealed that the second passage is the one Collins most wanted readers to sit with. It comes from Humeâs essay âOf the First Principles of Government,â and it asks why a handful of rulers can control a population that vastly outnumbers them: âWhen we enquire by what means this wonder is effected, we shall find, that, as Force is always on the side of the governed, the governors have nothing to support them but opinion.â.

Sources indicate that âIf all people do is read this Hume quote and discuss it, this book has been a win for me,â Collins remarked. She went around asking people whether Hume was right that the few end up governing the many, even in a democracy (âevery single person I asked about this said yes. No one seemed happy about itâ), and she built the book so that implicit submission plays out on three levels: âindividual, Hunger Games, and national.â Haymitch has to decide whether heâll keep submitting to the Capitol as an alliance of tributes in the arena tries to upend the Careersâ usual run, and meanwhile, the whole country has handed its power to Snow. The opinions that prop it all up are manufactured by propaganda, which the Capitol wields in various ways, from Plutarchâs altered District 12 reaping to âthat endlessly waving flag.â.

Hume wasnât the first philosopher sheâd borrowed from. For the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, she handed out aspects of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau to her characters, with Coriolanus inheriting Hobbesâs view of human nature from Volumnia Gaul.

Hume never sold anything nearly as successful as The Hunger Games in his own day. His first book, A Treatise of Human Nature, fell âdeadborn from the press,â as he later put it, and the reputation it earned him as a skeptic and an atheist led to public opposition to his 1745 application for a philosophy chair at the University of Edinburgh. He never held an academic job. His essays did much better with ordinary readers, which is part of where the line about the many and the few comes from.

Meanwhile, Sunrise on the Reaping sold more than 1.5 million copies in English in its first week, and Lionsgateâs film adaptation hits theaters on November 20, 2026, putting an 18th-century argument about whether the sun has to come up into multiplexes.

We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it.

The bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it.

Sources indicate that if you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun fresh seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Industry observers note that testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

According to recent reports, the next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

Industry observers note that the bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

It has been revealed that if you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes.

Sources indicate that tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service.

Industry observers note that the beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds.

The bottom line: I love to try upcoming coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you.

If you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water currently only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out.

Industry observers note that tester: Alaina Chou I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Organization, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be said for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley.

The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you.

Recent findings suggest that of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different.

Tester: Noah Kaufman Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States.

The ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The organization only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be.

I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month.

The bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees.

According to recent reports, we are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving.

It has been revealed that if you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees.

According to recent reports, tester: Alaina Chou What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme.

Folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny.

There is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America.

It has been revealed that tester: Noah Kaufman As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process.

It has been revealed that for people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something new. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee.

Contemporary Coffee Subscription.

Recent findings suggest that the Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans.

In a recent development, I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black).

It has been revealed that our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee.

Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying fresh coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we enhancement it often.

There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test:.

Industry observers note that A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping.

It has been revealed that the other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a big advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options.

Intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally.

This is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind.

Industry observers note that I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee.

Sources indicate that just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia. I don’t think it has changed the quality of the coffee at all, but it is something worth being transparent about.

Tester: Carly Westerfield, associate manager of audience strategy Best for: Someone who likes high-quality beans and doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for, but might get overwhelmed by some of the multi-roaster options on this list.

Counter Culture is a longtime favorite roaster of many a BA staffer (food director Chris Morocco included). It has storefronts in several major cities, and you can find Counter Culture’s coffee in stores across the country, but they also offer several subscription options online.

In a recent development, I had a really easy time ordering the coffee. There aren’t endless options to choose from, which is nice because subscriptions like these can sometimes be a lot to manage. Because I wanted to see a variety of beans, there were only two: the Single-Origin Subscription and the Blend Box. I opted for the latter. As someone who’s often overwhelmed by choices, I always appreciate a curated shopping experience where there are fewer things to choose from and therefore fewer things to compare, contrast, and potentially have buyer’s remorse over. I did struggle a little to figure out how to end the subscription; Counter Culture makes that part a little trickier than everything else.

It has been revealed that this subscription sends two different blends (12-oz. bags) at a time at a frequency of your choosing. Options there ranged from every week to every eight weeks, and the ability to change this post-purchase was clear. The Blend Box subscription pulls from six blend options ranging from light to dark roast, plus any “seasonal blend’ they have available, so you will end up seeing the same beans after about four deliveries. Shipping was fast and the email communication from CC made it so I always knew when I was being charged and when the box would be shipped and delivered.

While trying out this subscription, I received four different coffee blends: Iridescent Winter Blend, Significant Trouble, Fast Forward, and Forty-Six. At home, I use a Moccamaster Thermal Carafe Coffee Brewer and a Baratza Encore Coffee Grinder. With each of the blends I received, I was able to use the same measurements that I always use (9 g of coffee per 6 oz. of water) and found the coffee to be the right strength for me. Each blend has spot-on tasting notes provided as well. Overall, while the flavor profiles were totally different, none were overwhelmingly bitter or acidic—a big no-no in my book. These coffees all had a really well-rounded, almost creamy quality to them that actually resulted in me using way less half-and-half than I normally take in my coffee. By far my favorite blend is, sadly, the limited edition Iridescent Winter Blend. Big Trouble came in a close second.

Industry observers note that this subscription is great for someone who likes high-quality beans but doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for—perhaps, for instance, a recent college grad who’s been drinking coffee for years but hasn’t had to buy it for their own home yet. The ability to pause or change how often the deliveries come also makes it nice for someone who might travel often or need to have more coffee on hand at random times (maybe they have frequent house guests?).

Tester: Maria Paz Mendez Hodes, director of creative development Best for: Eager-to-learn beginners.

Stumptown is a Portland, OR–based roaster that’s been around since 1999. It offers three subscription options: Roaster’s Choice, Blend Shuffle, and Favorite on Repeat. As a novice coffee brewer, I wished there were a little more elaboration on the differences between Roaster’s Choice and Blend Shuffle. In the end I opted for the Roaster’s Choice, which promised to be a tour of seasonal, single-origin, and occasionally rare coffees, changing every two weeks.

In a recent development, I wasn’t 100% sure until the bag showed up at my door that I was ordering whole beans versus ground coffee. To some that may be glaringly obvious, but just another reminder that the site did not seem aimed at rank beginners like me. From what I can tell, Stumptown subscriptions are all whole-bean-only. Beyond that, the ordering process was clear and easy! My first bag arrived three days after ordering, and the next one almost exactly on schedule.

Recent findings suggest that A guilty confession: We keep breaking the Hario V60 carafe that I use to make pour-over, and I’ve gotten hooked on the extravagant convenience of bottled cold brew. The arrival of the Stumptown beans was exciting enough that we couldn’t wait for a replacement to arrive from Amazon, so we improvised by setting the dripper over a mason jar. Unglamorous setup aside, the first brew was an immediate reminder of the sense pleasures of the morning coffee ritual, dramatically amplified by using the fanciest beans I’d ever purchased. The freshness of the seasonal beans was obvious upon opening the package—they were lustrous and almost oily, with juicy notes that I’ve rarely detected in the supermarket brands near me. I don’t have a highly attuned coffee nose, but I could certainly taste distinct differences between the bags I received: light, bright fruit in the Montes de Oro from Costa Rica and deep caramel and spice in the Duramina from Ethiopia.

There were blurbs on the back of each bag sketching details about the coffee producers (e.g., how long they’d partnered with Stumptown and some unique features of their agricultural operations). It’s a good initiation for an interested newbie, but I think a coffee enthusiast could still glean quite a bit from these brief details. The one addition I would have loved would have been a card in the box with some deeper insights connecting the tasting notes and flavors to the processes and places mentioned. While there were tasting notes on the website for “Pick of the Week,” the coffee described wasn’t one I had received—another argument for a card in the box.

Tester: Travis Rainey, staff photographer/visuals editor Best for: People who like a little personality in their morning coffee.

Recent findings suggest that I was tempted to choose a curveball and select the espresso subscription, but opted for a more American coffee experience this time. I chose to test the Curated Single Origin subscription, which sends you a different single-origin coffee bean each week. The first bag of beans I received was from Concepción Huista, just north of Huehuetenango in western Guatemala. It was a very light, almost delicate kind of coffee. I had to adjust the grinder setting to a finer coffee ground to make the coffee a little more bold. For the most part, I make coffee with a pour-over method. A latest coffee arrives each week, so the next selection was from Abana Estate near Jimma in southwestern Ethiopia. This has been my favorite coffee to make so far. It's distinctive, spiced, but still goes down smooth. The third variety is Panangan Mata from Aceh on the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. I’ve only had one cup yet, but it’s fruity, which is a fun surprise.

In general, I’ve found that each Equator coffee has had a distinct personality, making this subscription ideal for people who want to have opinions about coffee—the beans here are the kind that sort of demand one of you. I also appreciate that the containers the coffee beans come in feature detailed, but succinct information on where the coffee is coming from.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director Best for: Both novice and experienced coffee drinkers alike who want their coffee selections handled for them.

My ordering experience was straightforward. I chose the Roaster’s Choice Subscription, so I didn’t know what I’d be getting first. My first bag (Honduras San Francisco whole beans) had a roast date just three days before it arrived at my house, so you can’t get much fresher than that. I appreciated this first blind bean as I’m not sure I would have chosen it for myself based on my personal preferences. I used a medium grind on the whole beans for my drip coffee maker. I’m curious to see how I’ll enjoy it pulled in the big boy coffee maker as an Americano.

Recent findings suggest that the bag touts tasting notes of strawberry, raspberry, and dark chocolate, which are spot-on. The first whiff gave me a fruit-and-nut chocolate bar, and the taste matches in a delicate way with a touch some floral undertones.

Tester: Carina Finn Best for: Best for someone with a high-end caffeine routine.

You can find a Blue Bottle café in most major cities—the brand makes a reliably great cup of coffee, whether you’re into fruity pour-overs or sophisticated seasonal lattes. Blue Bottle’s coffee subscription makes it easy to recreate that experience at home. It has around 10 different subscription options for things like instant espresso and matcha powders to rotating single-origin offerings and subscriptions tailored to specific roast level preferences.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: Someone looking for seasonality in their coffee.

Sources indicate that sightglass is a coffee-shop-slash-roaster based in San Francisco. They offer subscriptions for all of the coffees in their regular lineup if you find a fave you want to stick to, but we’d recommend trying out one of their rotating options to get a taste for all the brand has to offer. That leaves you with either the Blend Shuffle or the Seasonal Variety subscription. The ordering process is simple: Just select which subscription you want, how much coffee you want in each shipment (12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds), what kind of grind you want, and how often you’d like to receive deliveries.

Sources indicate that one of the things I like about Sightglass, as opposed to some other coffee shop-roaster hybrids, is that they regularly introduce latest single-origin coffees, which might feature in that seasonal subscription. You can also opt in to get notified about any new drops through the Sightglass Batches text-to-order service.

According to recent reports, I'm partial to Sightglass’s Blueboon blend. It's a medium roast with notes of milk chocolate, mandarin, and honeysuckle that I quite enjoy brewed as espresso and used in my morning iced latte. It’s beautifully balanced, and the components get changed seasonally to retain the right ratio of sweetness, body, and acidity.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: People who want to hone their coffee-tasting skills.

Sources indicate that if you dream of being able to approach the coffee world with sommelier-like expertise but you aren’t quite there yet, a Driftaway coffee subscription will help. Driftaway is an immigrant-owned, woman-led roastery based in Brooklyn, NY, and it’s the only service we’ve tried that starts out with a blind tasting. When you go to place your first order, you’ll have the option to choose between light roast, medium, and dark roasts, or espresso (which each include two or three different 4-oz. bags of coffee to blind taste test), or opt for the Explorer Box, which includes five different coffees spanning all roast levels.

If the tasting aspect of this service appeals to you, I’d recommend going with the Explorer Box option. Each initial Explorer Box comes with five mystery coffees, a wheel with flavor notes, a tasting form, and an envelope revealing the identities of your coffees. Driftaway offers weekly virtual tasting classes free of charge, but if you’d rather taste on your own time, they also have prerecorded tasting tutorials available on their website. Regardless of whether you opt for the Explorer Box or a roast-specific subscription, after your initial order, you’ll give feedback on which coffee you preferred in order to inform your future shipments. Many coffee companies even give you the option to send the farmer feedback, which I appreciated.

It has been revealed that along with the Explorer Box, I also tried out the espresso subscription. I was partial to the Burundi Turihamwe and Guatemala Ella blend, which was wonderfully nutty and had notes of milk chocolate and stone fruits. I loved being able to read more about the women farmers behind this blend and trace the story of the coffee from harvest to brewing, a feature that’s in keeping with Driftaway’s overall ethos.

Sources indicate that founded in 2015 in NYC's East Village, Coffee Project NY has grown from a single café into a full operation spanning retail, roasting, wholesale, and education. Owner Chi Sum Ngai is a certified Q grader and roasting championship competitor who personally oversees the roasting program, sourcing from small-scale cooperatives and family farms committed to improving conditions for workers.

Sources indicate that tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior commerce editor The subscription is straightforward: select the Roaster's Choice Single Origin Subscription and receive one to three 10-oz. bags one to two times a month. Coffee Project New York is not shy about its credentials; each bag arrives with tasting notes, farm sourcing, processing methods, and MASL (metres above sea level, which indicates the altitude at which beans were grown and profoundly impacts flavor). My standout was the Cabra Noir Wush Wush from the Competition Series, a runner-up at Mexico's prestigious AMCCE competition. Produced through anaerobic fermentation, I hand-ground the beans for a Hario pour-over and was met with such vivid guava notes that I double-checked the bag to make sure it wasn't a cofermentation. It wasn't. It was just that good.

Bottom line: Any coffee drinker will appreciate the expertly sourced beans, but this is a subscription where nerds can truly geek out, sampling rare cultivars and competition-level coffees from around the world.

Wonderstate Coffee (Single Origin).

Wonderstate Coffee Blend Shuffle).

Wonderstate Coffee (Roaster's Choice).

A certified B-Corporation with a fully solar-powered roastery, a transparent farmer payment model, and a novel profit-sharing model, Viroqua-based Wonderstate has gained a lot of goodwill for its business practices, but it also makes really good coffee.

According to recent reports, tester: Noah Kaufman Admittedly, this is a bit of a homer pick, as I have long thought Wonderstate to be the preeminent coffee roaster from my beloved home state of Wisconsin. But for those of you not lucky enough to be from Wisconsin, you should get to know them too. Twice named roaster of the year by Roast magazine (which is probably how it ended up as part of the Podium Coffee subscription), Wonderstate regularly has delicious, clean limited edition single origins—I like to get them as part of the single origin flight subscription. The subscriptions themselves come in a few varieties. The single-origin flight delivers three 100-gram packages of Wonderstate’s rarer coffees every two weeks. Roaster’s choice delivers a different single-origin coffee at an interval of your choosing. And the single coffee subscription gives you a regular delivery of the Wonderstate blend of your choosing, if you’re the type who wants more consistency of flavor in your morning cup.

According to recent reports, the bottom line: Wonderstate makes excellent coffee and runs an ethical business, which is a combination that's rarer than it should be. If you care about where your money goes as much as what's in your cup, this is the subscription for you.

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Specialty Subscription).

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Year Round Subscription).

If you find most black coffee off-putting, you might still love an unadulterated cup from Raleigh, North Carolina’s Black and White Coffee Roasters. Started by two American barista champions, Black and White are masters of the funky and fruity, with lots of experiments in co-fermented coffee (a process that uses actual fruit) and anaerobic fermented coffee (which produces very pronounced fruit notes).

Recent findings suggest that tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor It can be a very hands-off subscription. The only required information is whether you want one or two bags at a time and the frequency you need your coffee (anywhere between one and six weeks). Black and White will take care of the rest. If you do see a bag on their website you like, you can add it to your queue; otherwise, the team in North Carolina will select for you.

Every bag I received was of a funky variety, using ingredients like passion fruit, but they produce a number of more classic flavor profiles, which are available as part of their “year-round” subscription; the year-round is also about 20% cheaper than a subscription with the specialty bags.

According to recent reports, the bottom line: If you're drawn to funky, fruit-forward coffee but don't want to think too hard about what to order next, Black and White is the subscription for you. Just set your frequency and let the barista champions decide.

Bean Box is focused on the “curation” experience. The service’s tasting team offers what they claim is the largest selection of specialty coffee online, with over 600 different brews in its rolodex. The selection is sourced from dozens of small-batch, sustainably focused roasters from around the country—meaning you could likely go years without tasting coffee from the same roaster twice.

Tester: Dan Siegel, head of video Starting my subscription was exceptionally easy and clear. I appreciated the option to tailor the subscription to my own tastes: Bean Box asked me to choose among Light & Bright, Medium & Cozy, Dark & Toasty, Espresso, or Decaf. For this run, I selected the Curators' Choice option, marketed as the curation team’s seasonal favorites and a mix of upcoming and old coffees. There is an app available to manage subscriptions and read lengthy details on each roaster or track the origin of your beans.

This subscription was not designed to save me money on coffee; this is for enthusiasts. My first bag from “Gimme! Coffee,” out of Ithaca, NY, hit hard on the Bean Box mission: The roaster is employee-owned, shipping fair trade beans from Coopfam, Brazil’s first certified fair trade coffee grower. This was a standout for any time of day as a medium-bodied brew, subtly sweet with virtually no bitterness or acidity via my automatic OXO 8-cup machine or my Hario V60 pour-over. My second bag, La Cumbre from Little City in Austin, was a bit too bright and fruity for my taste, advertising caramel, mango, and green apple tasting notes—but this was the path I chose with the Curator’s Choice option.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: If you have the means, get the beans. I would keep this going for years if money were no object. The money seems to be going toward roasters that align with my values. One of my values is delicious coffee. But also treating workers at every stop along the way like human beings.

In a recent development, if receiving personalized coffee picks from a catalogue of nearly 600 coffees from 60 different roasters sounds like your cup of tea (or, rather, joe), then I will point you toward MistoBox. I found a lot to love about this service after testing it for several months, particularly the way Misto tailored its selections to me and my taste.

Sources indicate that tester: Alaina Chou, commerce writer The ordering process starts with a quiz covering your preferences: how you take your coffee, roast level, whole or ground beans, and frequency. But what sets MistoBox apart is what comes after: a second, more detailed quiz where you share how you brew, how you grind, and any other specifics to help the team dial in your order. The whole process feels genuinely personal, and that expert-curated aspect is, to me, the other major perk that makes a subscription worth it in the first place.

I’ve loved every coffee MistoBox has sent me so far. The first shipment was the Roma Espresso Blend from Parisi Artisan Coffee, which was aptly described as having notes of milk chocolate, almond, and honeysuckle. I tend to drink espresso, most often with milk in a cappuccino made using my Breville Oracle Jet. The Roma blend, which MistoBox sent me based on that information, worked beautifully for this.

After you receive each coffee, you’ll have the chance to rate it out of five and leave any tasting notes, which you can share with your curators if you’d like. Coffees you’ve tried show up in a customer dashboard, as will your “Brew Queue,” a.k.a. the lineup of the next coffees coming to your door. These will appear as “MistoBox’s choice” by default, but if you loved a coffee you tried and want it again, or spy a coffee in their collection that you’d like to request, you can opt to add specific coffees to your queue as well. Anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering new coffees from roasters all over the country will enjoy MistoBox.

The bottom line: MistoBox’s user-friendly interface and extensive feedback options make it a great choice for anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering upcoming coffees from roasters all over the country.

Are coffee subscriptions worth it?

Industry observers note that if you’re a frequent coffee drinker, the answer is probably yes. Whether you have a favorite blend you find yourself buying on repeat or you’re eager to try new beans and hone your tasting skills, a coffee subscription will make your life easier and may even save you some money. If you’re presently buying a bag of beans every few weeks at your local coffee shop or grocery store, that bag could potentially be cheaper when bought on subscription—and you’ll get the added convenience of never needing to worry about restocking your stash.

How do coffee subscriptions work?

It has been revealed that at the most basic level, a coffee subscription works much like any other subscription service: You select a quantity and frequency, and lo and behold, a bag of freshly roasted coffee shows up at your doorstep every one to four weeks, depending what you chose. But no one wants to come home from vacation to a pile of beans that are past their prime, only to receive another package the following day. So these coffee subscriptions make it easy to put your coffee deliveries on hold, or cancel them altogether. Some also offer personalization in the form of quizzes or feedback forms, so you can know you're getting a curated selection that’s tailored specifically to your tastes.

How much coffee should you order?

Sources indicate that many of the subscriptions on this list will let you customize your delivery frequency and bag quantity to best accommodate your household size and coffee drinking habits. Ideally, you’ll want to hit a sweet spot where you're using up nearly all of your beans by the time the next shipment comes. According to recent reports, if instant coffee is more your speed, we don’t blame you—it’s hard to beat the convenience. And while instant coffee has historically gotten a bad wrap from third-wave coffee nerds and espresso heads everywhere, you’d be surprised what innovations have been made in the space in recent years. After tasting a whopping 40, we found a range of great-tasting options that would impress even the most seasoned coffee pro. Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is fast approaching, and if youâre in the midst of preparations, you know costs can add up swiftly. From the all-important turkey to stuffing, mashed potatoes, and pumpkin pie, Thanksgiving meals can take a lot of time and a lot of cashâthough exactly how much cash depends on what you purchase and where you live.

The American Farm Bureau released its 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner price report on November 18, 2026, using data from its yearly survey of Americans in all 50 states and Puerto Rico. It found the average Thanksgiving meal for 10 people will cost $58.63, a 6% increase from 2025. This is the first time that Thanksgiving dinner prices have increased year-to-year since 2022.

Industry observers note that the region serving up the most expensive Thanksgiving in the United States is the Northeast, where the meal will cost around 5% more than anywhere else in the U.S, at $61.57 for 10 people. The South saw the lowest cost for Thanksgiving for 10, at $54.33 on average.

The Midwest and West, meanwhile, saw prices closer to the national average, with the West spending an average of $58.74 and the Midwest spending $56.89.

Recent findings suggest that turkeys cost an average of $23.68 in 2026, an increase of 10% from 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau. Boneless ham, dinner rolls, sweet and russet potatoes, cranberries, frozen peas, and frozen green beans all grew more expensive in the past year as well. About a third of the items tracked in the survey decreased in price, including frozen pie crusts and whipping cream.Â.

It has been revealed that that rise in prices is connected to rising energy costs in part due to the Iran war, which has led to increased diesel prices for farmers who rely on it to power their equipment. Something to celebrate is that prices are still lower than they were in 2022, when the average Thanksgiving cost an average of $64.05 in the U.S. partly due to the Ukraine war.Â.

âHigher prices for these items arenât a complete surprise, as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the food chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers,â Farm Bureau economists Faith Parum and Cameron Castillo wrote. Still, all this doesnât mean that farmers are raking it in. âEven if the farmer does capture some additional revenue, those earnings are needed to cover increased fertilizer, fuel, and other production expenses,â they continued.Â.

How did an organization whose founder followed a philosophy based on doing the greatest amount of good possible for the world end up in prison for misappropriating billions of dollars of customer funds?

Thatâs the central question at the heart of The Altruists, the Netflix series that explores the rise and fall of the cryptocurrency exchange tech giant FTX. Before FTXâs collapse, its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, was a poster child for effective altruism, a philosophy that uses research and evidence to identify the worldâs biggest problems and find strategies to solve them.Â.

Sources indicate that he openly cited effective altruism as the reason he entered the crypto industry, and had vowed to eventually give away most of his wealth to charity. Yet Bankman-Fried is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence. So how did this all play out, and how did effective altruism influence Bankman-Friedâs actions?

Effective altruism is both a philosophy and social movement. It is based on using reason and logic to identify major global problems and solutions, and helping people to figure out how they can do the most good possible with their lives.

According to recent reports, âEffective altruism is about using scientific evidence and careful reasoning to find the best ways to help others, and putting those findings into practice,â reads the programâs website. âIt's both an ongoing research project and a global movement of people working to do good.â.

It has been revealed that the movement draws much of its inspiration from the philosopher Peter Singer, who has long argued that people have a moral obligation to help people in poverty. It has mobilized billions of dollars in donations over the years. The movement generally encourages people to either dedicate their time or careers to improving specific social problems, or to âearn to giveââmaking as much money as possible and donating it to charity.Â.

Bankman-Fried was first introduced to effective altruism after meeting William MacAskill, one of the movementâs founders, when he was an MIT undergraduate. Less than a decade later, he had promised to donate the entirety of his net worthâat one point some $26 billionâto charity. Bankman-Fried also publicly mentioned his desire to help as many people as possible through donations drove his decision to take significant financial risks.Â.

In a recent development, FTXâs collapse was devastating for effective altruism proponents and gleefully celebrated by many of its critics. âBankman-Fried's behavior went against values central to effective altruism, such as honesty, humility, integrity, and concern for other people,â reads a statement on the Centre for Effective Altruismâs website. âIn the years since, leaders in the effective altruism movement have consistently condemned Bankman-Friedâs actions.â.

It would be incorrect to say that effective altruism directly caused Bankman-Friedâs actions. Yet his connection to the movement certainly reveals the potential pitfalls of fixating on a potential future outcomeâno matter how beneficial for the worldâwhile failing to act with integrity in the present.Â.
