According to recent reports, home is where the heart isâand for those who watched 2026's Sense and Sensibility, that likely means the English countryside. In contrast to the clean lines of adaptations past, the latest take on Jane Austen's beloved romance novel leans into the rugged terrainâand messy matters of the heart.

As location manager Ian Hutchinson notes, director Georgia Oakley's vision for the film was to "make it quite raw and quite natural," adding that "you can really get into the rustic side of things." Thankfully, you donât need a Regency inheritanceâor a heartbreak at the hands of John Willoughbyâto experience the extravagant estates and moody moorlands firsthand. Here are five real-life filming locations across England where you can yearn, frolic, and live out your own period-drama fantasies to the fullest.

Industry observers note that the sisters' story begins at Norland Park, which in nonfictional England is brought to life by two separate estates in Dorset. The exterior grounds are played by Parnham Park, a 139-acre historic estate featuring ancient forests, rose gardens, and a spring-fed lakeâa fitting backdrop for fostering a hopeless romantic like Marianne. Itâs easy to see why a landscape so serene would be painful to leave; from skipping stones in the fuchsia flower-framed pond to taking long walks across the manicured lawns, much of the early action unfolds across the pristine grounds.

It has been revealed that roughly 15 miles away, Kingston Russell House stood in for Norland Park's interior shots and main entrance, its baroque-style arched windows and white stone Georgian facade creating an immediate visual contrast against the earthy, modest Barton Cottage that defines the rest of the film. Visitors looking to live out their Jane Austen fantasy can explore the picturesque grounds of Parnham Park or book a stay within the guest wing of the actual Kingston Russell House to fully immerse themselves in the Dorset countryside.

When the Dashwood women are forced to leave their frilly family home, they find refuge in the modest, moorland charm of Barton Cottage. In reality, the production team transformed Ditsworthy Warren Houseâa dilapidated cottage nestled deep within Dartmoor National Park. Like any run-down abode amidst the moors, the stone structure needed some work before it could fully emulate Barton Cottage. For logistical filming reasons as well as the benefit of the once-wealthy fictional family, windows and a new door were added. Otherwise, the stormy skies, rolling hills, and overall secludedness did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the drama of the Dashwoods' new home. Like any National Park in the UK, nature and Willoughby lovers alike can frolic through the tall, oftentimes damp grasses, imagining what could have been (or at least getting their steps in).

Recent findings suggest that for the windswept coastal moments where the drama of the waves mirrors the mental states of the characters, the production headed to Mothecombe Beach on the south Devon coast. The silverâor rather, seafoam greenâlining of the Dashwood sisters' migration to Barton comes in the form of whimsical strolls along the nearby shoreline. While you probably wonât find Willoughby or Marianne at Mothecombe Beach, this privately owned stretch of sand has all the moody views that most likely caught your eye in the 2026 adaptation. A quaint path leading down to the surf is located near the mouth of the Erme Estuary, alongside a cozy teahouse for when the sea breeze gets the best of you.

There's no such thing as a free lunchâor countryside cottage. That's where Barton Parkâin real life, Broughton Castle in Oxfordshireâcomes in. As the price for their humble accommodations, the Dashwoods are frequently summoned to the 14th-century moated manor of their spirited landlord and cousin, Sir John Middleton. With its fortified gatehouse, armor-adorned Great Hall, and Tudor-era upgrades, the castle looks far more suited for fending off medieval sieges than hosting awkward Regency dinner parties. Today, travelers (and fans of The Crown and My Lady Jane, which also filmed at Broughton Castle) can cross the stone bridge over the moat to tour the historic rooms and manicured gardensâminus the obligation of amusing Mrs. Jennings.

Sources indicate that the Dashwood sisters experience all the emotions in Sense and Sensibilityâand seemingly every postcode in southern England while theyâre at it. Eventually, the drama sweeps them to London, brought to life by West Wycombe Park in Buckinghamshire. This 18th-century Palladian villa was constructed for a real-life DashwoodâSir Francisâand its lavishly decorated staterooms, marble walls, and cross-era architectural accents are now owned by the National Trust. Today, the estate opens to the public during the summer months, when hopeless romantics can spend the day staring at painted ceilings and strolling along the swan-shaped lake within its 45 acres of landscaped parkland.

Breaking: Thai Luxury Leads Minor’s Quarter Despite Tourist Slump

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skift

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Minor is earning more in a country drawing fewer tourists because its luxury guests are paying up and because it owns most of its hotels.
  • Thailand’s international visitor numbers are slipping, but Minor Hotels reports that its luxury guests in the country  are each paying more on average.
  • According to recent reports, minor’s Anantara-branded high-end hotels in Thailand reported a 19% like-for-like increase in RevPAR in the third quarter, on a 13% rise in average daily rate, Minor mentioned in its quarterly results statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photo Credit: An Anantara resort. Anantara.

Minor is earning more in a country drawing fewer tourists because its luxury guests are paying up and because it owns most of its hotels. That means rate gains land directly in its results. The same ownership set-up cuts the other way in the Middle East, where demand has turned and four in 10 of its hotels are its own.

Thailand’s international visitor numbers are slipping, but Minor Hotels reports that its luxury guests in the country  are each paying more on average.

According to recent reports, minor’s Anantara-branded high-end hotels in Thailand reported a 19% like-for-like increase in RevPAR in the third quarter, on a 13% rise in average daily rate, Minor mentioned in its quarterly results statement. Across all of Minor’s Thai hotels, RevPAR rose 13%, the strongest growth of any major market in the group, on a 9% rise in ADR and a two-point gain in occupancy to 64%.

The strong numbers landed despite Thailand cutting its 2026 international arrivals forecast to 33 million from 36.7 million, with arrivals through mid-October down 4.1%. Cushman & Wakefield told Skift luxury was holding up better than the rest of the market because guests in that segment are less price sensitive.

Thailand led the way for a quarter in which Minor’s core profit rose 13% year over year to THB 2.1 billion (about $62.9 million), with the Maldives and Europe also contributing growth. Core revenue rose 6% to THB 35.4 billion (about $1.06 billion), and EBITDA rose 4% to THB 7 billion (about $210 million). Company-wide RevPAR rose 5%, mostly on rate.

In a recent development, part of the Thai performance story is the fruit of Minor’s recent investments. It finished a $50 million renovation of Anantara Siam Bangkok in September, refurbishing all 335 rooms along with the hotel’s restaurants and event spaces. The Maldives, where Minor operates nine resorts, also improved: RevPAR rose 10% as occupancy climbed four points to 46%.

RevPAR across Minor’s Middle East & Africa hotels fell 11% in the third quarter, with occupancy down about three points and rates down roughly 5%. Minor cited the regional conflict and associated weaker travel demand. Over nine months, the region’s RevPAR is down 15%.

Recent findings suggest that the softening performance puts Minor in line with its larger peers. Skift reported last week that Marriott’s Middle East RevPAR fell 12% in the third quarter, while Accor’s fell 3% with a roughly 12% decline assumed for the fourth quarter, and Hilton mentioned it expected a low double-digit full-year decline in the Middle East and Africa. In Oman, Minor executives told Skift they were seeing shorter stays, later bookings and fourth-quarter demand down.

Minor said rates in the region held broadly steady over nine months, while occupancy fell around nine points. Its Gulf strategy is to protect price rather than chase volume. The third quarter suggests that is getting harder to hold: rates fell for the first time this year.

Where the losses land matters more for Minor than for many of its rivals. Marriott mostly earns fees in the Middle East, and the region accounts for only about 3% of its global fees. Hilton has said the region’s decline will cost it more than $20 million in earnings this year, mostly in lost management fees. Minor, for its part, owns about 40% of its Middle East & Africa hotels, the firm told Skift, with the other 60% managed or franchised. That’s lighter than Minor’s portfolio as a whole, where almost 70% is owned or leased. But it still means the regional slump hits Minor’s own earnings directly at about four in 10 of its hotels there, which is a heavier exposure than a fee-based chain carries.

Europe & Americas, home to NH Hotels in Minor’s portfolio, grew RevPAR 7% in its seasonally strongest quarter, led by Madrid (up 11%) and Barcelona (up 8%). East Africa also grew, with Kenya and Tanzania up 5%, while Australia & New Zealand both held at 80% occupancy.

It has been revealed that over nine months, Minor’s core profit rose 3% to THB 4.2 billion (about $126 million). The third quarter accounted for half of it, after a first-quarter core loss.

Minor expects mixed trading in the fourth quarter. Forward bookings for Thailand and the Maldives are ahead of last year for both the fourth quarter and early 2027. The tech giant gave no specific outlook for the Middle East.

“Our third-quarter performance demonstrates the value of having a geographically diversified portfolio, particularly when trading conditions vary so widely between markets,” said Dillip Rajakarier, group CEO of parent Minor International, in a statement. He said the company would focus on protecting margins and pricing discipline while accelerating the shift to fee income.

Sources indicate that that shift is visible in Minor’s pipeline. Asset-light arrangements make up more than 90% of Minor’s active development pipeline, and it signed 38 hotels in the first nine months, putting it on track to beat its 2025 record of 40 signings. Until those hotels open, Minor’s results will keep moving with the markets where it owns the buildings.

On November 11, the 2026 World Ski Awards named its winners — and once again, European resorts took nearly every global title. According to the organizers, ballots come from ski-industry professionals such as employees, tour operators, travel agents, and media, as well as the skiing public. The organization notes “hundreds of thousands” of professionals and skiers take part each year, though it does not publish an exact annual total.

Val Thorens was named the World’s Best Ski Resort, a title the French resort has won 11 times, as well as France’s Best Ski Resort. Its village sits at roughly 7,500 feet above sea level, giving it the highest base of any ski resort in Europe and a long, dependable snow season. It also connects to Les Trois Vallées, the largest linked ski area in the world.

In a recent development, switzerland won most of the global hotel categories. W Verbier was named the World’s Best Ski Hotel, while the Grand Hotel Belvedere took Best Newly introduced Ski Hotel. Chalet Zermatt Peak won Best Ski Chalet, and Chez Madeleine was named Best New Chalet. Pashmina Le Refuge, also in Val Thorens, was voted the World’s Best Boutique Ski Hotel, Dutch operator Sunweb won World’s Best Ski Tour Operator, and rocksresort in Switzerland took World’s Best Green Ski Hotel.

The full country-by-country list of award winners is available on the World Ski Awards winners announcement.

As in past years, no North American property won a global category. Every world-level title went to Europe, and US and Canadian winners were recognized only within their national categories. It likely reflects not just the concentration of ski resorts in Europe, but the fact that voters likely favor regions with the largest number of participating resorts. The awards are also based in Europe — though it’s possible the high cost of skiing in the US vs. Europe could also be influencing voting, with some US ski resorts charging $300 or more per person per day for a walk-up window ticket.

The US lodging categories were also in Deer Valley. Stein Eriksen Lodge won US Best Ski Hotel, and the Goldener Hirsch won Best Boutique Ski Hotel.

In Canada, Lake Louise was named the country’s Best Ski Resort. It’s an Ikon Pass resort and part of the SkiBig3 group, alongside Banff Sunshine and Mt. Norquay. The nearby Post Hotel & Spa won Canada’s Best Ski Hotel, and Whistler took two awards: the Pan Pacific Whistler Village Centre for Best Boutique Hotel and Wedge Mountain Lodge & Spa for Best Chalet.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that originally a chapel that served the wealthy vacationers that flocked to the area in the late 1800's and early 1900's, the chapel now serves as an Episcopal Summer Church.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

St Matthews Chapel is an historic, darling, and well maintained church building located in the picturesque White Mountains of New Hampshire. Built in 1893 (1883 by some accounts - but the cornerstone lists 1893), it is mentioned to be one of the most photographed churches in New England. On first sight, the delighted traveler will know why it is so widely photographed. Surrounded by vibrant foliage in the fall, it offers a serene and meditative landscape. It is just as beautiful in the early summer, when it’s surrounded by fields of blooming purple lupine. The church itself is a stunning example of the Gothic Revival style that was popular at the time of its construction. Its pastoral charm is evident from its vibrant yellow door to its detailed stained glass depicting mountain scenes. One notable stained glass piece, located near the baptismal font,  is said to be from Tiffany.

Recent findings suggest that originally a chapel that served the wealthy vacationers that flocked to the area in the late 1800's and early 1900's, the chapel now serves as an Episcopal Summer Church. They do still hold services here on Sundays, but only in July and August, and the first Sunday of September. Their website states that visitors are welcome. You don't have to be religious to appreciate this breathtaking scene where both the church and the surroundings are equally striking.

As a side note, this chapel is available to people of all faiths (or no formal faith) from May til September/October  for weddings, baptisms, memorial services and other such events.

Also nearby, be sure to check out The Frost Place and maybe grab some breakfast at  Polly’s Pancake Parlor.

Because this is a seasonal chapel, they are served by visiting pastors through out the summer, and have no live-in clergy or daily operational staff. Therefore, to view the interior of the chapel, you have a few options:.

Doors are open to the public May-October on Sundays starting at 10am (when services are held). Visitors of all backgrounds are welcome to attend services, or come tour the interior of the chapel following services.

Sources indicate that the chapel is occasionally open outside of Sunday services for weddings, baptisms, or other scheduled community events, and the interior can be viewed during these times (if appropriate to the event taking place). Call ahead to find out what, if any events are scheduled during the time of visiting.

Lastly, you can explore the exterior grounds which are completely open to the public 24/7 and easily accessible and visible from the main road. An exploration of the grounds and landscape make this stop worth the time all by itself.

This Colombia River Cruise Is Putting Local Communities at the Heart of Travel

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1225 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waking up portside on the AmaMagdalena to my first sunrise in Colombia, I wondered if Capitán “Fantástico” Julio had weighed anchor ahead of schedule.
  • Stronger after heavy rainfall, this organic debris flows from the Colombian Andes where the Magdalena River begins its course, before eventually meeting the Caribbean Sea in Barranquilla — the embarkation port for my seven-night sailing to Cartagena.
  • Industry observers note that each year before Lent, Shakira’s home city erupts with street parties, parades, and processions celebrating Colombian folklore, dance, and music; the Carnaval de Barranquilla is one of the world’s largest carnivals with an emphasis on active participation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waking up portside on the AmaMagdalena to my first sunrise in Colombia, I wondered if Capitán “Fantástico” Julio had weighed anchor ahead of schedule. Branches raced past my balcony at such velocity I assumed the stationary ship was already making its way upstream.

Stronger after heavy rainfall, this organic debris flows from the Colombian Andes where the Magdalena River begins its course, before eventually meeting the Caribbean Sea in Barranquilla — the embarkation port for my seven-night sailing to Cartagena. That morning, only the torrent of water and squawk of birds interrupted my peace as I replayed an evening spent with dancers disguised as alligators moving to the beat of the llamador drum.

Industry observers note that each year before Lent, Shakira’s home city erupts with street parties, parades, and processions celebrating Colombian folklore, dance, and music; the Carnaval de Barranquilla is one of the world’s largest carnivals with an emphasis on active participation. AmaWaterways, the firm opearting the ship I was traveling on, sought inspiration from the four-day event when curating an embarkation extravaganza for the Magic of Colombia, a community-focused river cruise that feels like a floating festival.

Clapping along on the riverbank, I was oblivious to the motifs and meanings presented to us. All questions would be answered in the following days: I’d learn how courtship plays out through cumbia’s steps and come to recognize a llamador from a tambora. A mysterious cloaked figure disrupting couples was identified as La Muerte in a representation of the Garabato, a dance of life and death.

An especially puzzling cohort of dancers dressed, to my eye, as elephants was unmasked as El Hombre Caimán, the Alligator Man. This comedic fable tells of a man turned into a caiman after spying on women bathing in the river. Karma.

Recent findings suggest that fishermen at the sunrise birdwatching experience. Photo: Hannah D. Cooper.

Colombia has a river for each of its rhythms. Known interchangeably as the “land of a thousand rhythms” and the “land of a thousand rivers,” there are, go figure, a little over a thousand of each. Although playing a major role in trade and remaining the country’s most key waterway, tourism is new to the Magdalena, and AmaWaterways is its first luxury river cruise line.

Sources indicate that with the exception of AmaMelodia (sailing Cartagena to Barranquilla), I spotted only the occasional tugboat or barge. Tender trips at sunrise and dusk followed artisanal fishers casting nets in placid canals. Some motored alongside to show us their catch of bocachico and catfish. With fish populations in decline, responsible tourism can bring economic relief; my river guide explained how villagers are taking greater care to preserve these wetlands whose winged inhabitants we were tracking through our binoculars.

Days were chockful of rhythm. Cumbia, Colombia’s most well-known style of music, was described by Valerie of Casa Calíbana as a way to express emotion and identity. In El Banco, cumbia’s supposed birthplace, people dance when they’re happy; they dance when they’re sad. Her ensemble navigated four hours of waterways to share their story onboard AmaMagdalena, pinning flowers to our hair and teaching us the steps. We tested out the instruments, hearing how the guache (a metal shaker) mimics ocean waves and the caña de millo reflects the melody of birdsong.

Industry observers note that in Santa Bárbara de Pinto, Magdalena Department (Colombia is made up of 32 separate departments and its capital district), we witnessed how even a snack can inspire a rhythm. Villagers demonstrated the harvest cycle of bollo limpio — husk-wrapped cornmeal rolls, a popular street food during Barranquilla Carnival — in a sequence portraying laborers in the fields.

It has been revealed that amaMagdalena from the stern. The ship has a capacity 60 guests. Photo: Hannah D. Cooper.

It has been revealed that our penultimate day before reaching Cartagena started in Calamar, a riverside town in the Bolívar Department whose significance faded as roads took prominence. A rickety passage by “Paola” (bicycle taxi) jolted us past fishermen unloading their morning catch and vendors receiving early-bird grocery shoppers.

Here we watched a performance of Son de Negro, a dance originating from the colonial era where male dancers painted their bodies black and attached red feathers — symbolic of spilled blood — to their heads. Exaggerated facial expressions mocked Spanish enslavers and reclaimed power in this energetic choreography.

Sources indicate that the afternoon was spent in San Basilio de Palenque, a hub for the high-stamina Afro-Colombian Mapalé dance and host of the annual Palenque Drum Festival. Founded by those who escaped slavery, this is the first “free” Black town in the Americas; a “palenque” refers to a community of self-liberated slaves. The Guardia Cimarrona, a volunteer group of predominantly women and farmers overseeing law and order, greeted us. Poultry theft, we heard, is the dominant crime, punishable by 12 hours in solitary “reflection” or community service.

Palenque is also the home of the palenqueras, women sporting colorful dresses with full skirts (polleras) and balancing bowls laden with fruit on their heads. Many of Palenque’s women commute to Cartagena, where they make a living posing for photos in the walled city and selling candies. It’s respectful to approach the women with “kumo, kusa a tá?” (KOO-moh, KOO-sah ah-TAH), which means “how are you?” before asking for their rate and supporting their work.

Industry observers note that our local guide shepherded us from the home of a traditional healer, schooling us further in palenquero, a Spanish-based creole language. Learning that their name translates to “my friends,” we met with Kombilesa Mí, a folk rap band fusing traditional rhythms with hip-hop. A jamming session in their studio was the parting activity from our musical cruise before Capitán Julio dropped anchor.

Recent findings suggest that guardia Cimarrona in San Basilio de Palenque. Photo: Hannah D. Cooper.

It has been revealed that the Magic of Colombia’s soundtrack is set by musicians and birdsong; the route is determined by the river. Since launching in 2025, the crew has needed to adapt each sailing around variable conditions, El Niño-imposed droughts, and those high-flow currents that continuously tricked me into thinking the boat was underway. Fluctuating river levels mean it isn’t always possible to dock overnight at the postcard-pretty riverside town of Santa Cruz de Mompox; access to El Banco is why cumbia artists are instead brought to the ship.

Industry observers note that before bringing a boost to river communities through tourism, the riverboats generated employment. Arriving in Cartagena as shells, Colombians were hired in construction, and artisans were commissioned to produce soft furnishings for the AmaMagdalena’s 30 staterooms and for the 32 staterooms of its sistership, the AmaMelodia.

In a recent development, the Ama team explored 900 miles of navigable river by canoe, identifying communities interested in welcoming visitors in this overlooked part of Colombia and seeking to understand how the cruise could benefit their people. Our Cruise Manager admitted he had thought the idea of launching a luxury river cruise on the Magdalena ambitious. Residents were equally confused — while wondering what they had to offer tourists, they were clearly taking for granted the region’s natural beauty and its rich cultural heritage. Just as the Barranquilla Carnival is built on active participation, the Magic of Colombia fully immersed me in the sounds, rhythms, and voices of the Magdalena.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PetScreening founder and CEO John Bradford discusses how vacation rental operators can capitalize on growing demand for pet-friendly stays while managing property risks and improving operational consistency.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

This edition of “Industry Insights” features an interview with John Bradford, founder and CEO of PetScreening, a platform that helps property managers screen pets and assistance animals and manage related policies.

Recent findings suggest that bradford sees a growing business opportunity for vacation rental operators willing to accommodate pets. According to AirDNA findings cited by PetScreening, pet-friendly listings generated 14.4% more annual revenue potential and commanded 6% higher average daily rates than non-pet-friendly properties. Bradford shares how operators can capitalize on this demand while addressing concerns about property damage, liability, and policy compliance.

Skift Studio: What are the biggest opportunities for short-term rental operators when it comes to accommodating pets, particularly in terms of revenue growth and guest demand?

John Bradford: The biggest opportunity is the gap between the number of travelers who want to bring their pets and the number of rentals that welcome them.

Approximately 71% of U.S. households own a pet, yet only about 30% of U.S. short-term rental listings are pet-friendly. That creates an opportunity for operators to differentiate their properties and reach a large, underserved audience.

There is also a real revenue opportunity. In a recent 2026 Pet Influence Study by Veridata Insights, 67% of pet owners said they would pay at least $25 more per night for a pet-welcoming vacation rental. AirDNA also found that pet-friendly rentals are being introduced into the market at twice the rate of latest non-pet-friendly rentals.

Sources indicate that that doesn’t mean every property needs to accept every pet. But with the right policies and processes, operators can pursue additional bookings and revenue without giving up operational control.

What are the biggest challenges or risks facing vacation rental operators when it comes to pets, and how can they better manage them?

One of the biggest challenges is that pets and other animals are not always disclosed at the time of booking. In our analysis of reservations from integrated short-term rental clients, PetScreening submissions identified approximately 60% more pets and animals than the booking data originally indicated. We found that nearly 70% of assistance-animal submissions involved an animal not noted on the original booking.

It has been revealed that this doesn’t necessarily mean guests intentionally withheld information. The value is that property managers learned about these animals before check-in, giving them time to clarify details, apply appropriate policies, and prepare the property. That visibility helps prevent undisclosed arrivals and reduces the risk of property damage, compliance problems, fee disputes, and safety incidents. Clear policies and connected documentation further reduce risk.

How is PetScreening helping move the vacation rental industry forward by making it easier for operators to adopt and manage pet-friendly policies?

According to recent reports, we’re helping operators move from an informal, property-by-property approach to a more consistent and repeatable process. PetScreening gives teams a way to understand who is traveling with a pet or assistance animal before arrival, communicate expectations, and apply policies more consistently.

Industry observers note that guest attestations and clear documentation add a layer of protection by creating a record of what was submitted and acknowledged. That means fewer surprises for operators, owners, and guests.

It has been revealed that we often hear from third-party managers that our platform is a business development tool that helps them attract more owners and convince them to become pet-friendly. When there is a way to manage pet policies, owners feel more comfortable accepting pets.

Our larger goal is to help create a hospitality industry that is both more pet-inclusive and more pet-responsible, across vacation rentals, hotels, campgrounds, and timeshares.

As someone who travels frequently, what’s your favorite travel tip or hack?

Whenever I can, I bring my dog Berkeley along when I travel. Before we leave, I make sure her FidoAlert profile is up to date, and her QR code ID tag is attached to her collar. If we ever get separated, I can send an alert to nearby pet finders, and someone who finds her can scan her tag and send a text alert to let me know she’s been found. It gives me a little extra peace of mind while we’re away.

  • Sources indicate that typical ships carrying these guns included Dealey-class destroyer escorts, Claud Jones-class destroyer escorts, and Asheville-class gunboats.

On the east side of State Road 31 near Peru, Indiana, sits a naval gun on the grounds of the Pipe Creek Mercantile Trading House. The shop features a wide selection of items in individual booths. If you go in not knowing what you are looking for, they probably have it.

Sources indicate that the gun sits in the northwest corner of the property, along the fence line near the highway. The gun's information identifies it as a Mark 79 Mod 1 Weather Shield, which was used with the United States Navy's 3-inch/50-caliber dual-purpose anti-aircraft gun mounts. The weather shield was a lightweight combination of fiberglass and aluminum designed to protect the crew from harsh weather and heavy sea spray. The gun would have been used during World War II and afterward.

Sources indicate that typical ships carrying these guns included Dealey-class destroyer escorts, Claud Jones-class destroyer escorts, and Asheville-class gunboats. Naval experts may want to weigh in here and provide a clearer understanding of which ships used this gun.

The former gun owner may have attempted to donate it to the nearby Grissom Air Museum, but it was not accepted and was left here. The Mark 79 does not have a price tag, so perhaps the best offer will be accepted. You will have to supply your own ammunition, however.

What Are Thanksgiving Sides That Don't Need to Go in the Oven?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that on Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are millions of recipes on the internet, but you still don’t know what to cook. Tell us about it! Dear Bon Appétit is an advice column where we answer your culinary conundrums with handpicked recipes and well-seasoned advice. Submit a question here.

Recent findings suggest that on Thanksgiving the oven is always precious real estate for the quintessential spread—stuffing, green bean casserole, sweet potatoes, and, of course, the turkey. In years past, the stress of getting everything in and out of the oven with the right amount of time has been a nuisance that I’d like to avoid this year. Are there any Thanksgiving sides that feel classic but don’t need the oven? —Oven-whelmed.

Industry observers note that if there was a proverbial dartboard of Thanksgiving problems, you have just hit the bull’s-eye. (And as someone who has never hit a real bull’s-eye in her life, I mean this as quite the compliment!) Even if you place oven racks strategically—even if you have one of those fancy double ovens—there’s always a bottleneck of dishes that need to be roasted and baked.

The solution is not to plot out an overwrought schedule of when things go in and out, and in and out, but to ruthlessly reduce the number of recipes that require the oven in the first place.

With that in mind, I would like to point out that turkey can thrive in other settings. And no, I’m not talking about deep-frying it in your yard, which we all know is a rowdy and risky idea, as proven in Gilmore Girls season three, episode nine. You could grill it. You could smoke it. Both delightful.

But you asked about sides specifically, so sides are what we will tackle today. Beyond the classics like mashed potatoes, boxed stuffing, and cranberry sauce, here are 10 recipes that do not need an oven at all—and brazenly, boldly get away with it.

Green Beans and Mushrooms With Crispy Shallots. The same cozy flavors as a classic green bean casserole—earthy mushrooms, frizzled shallots—but it comes together entirely on the stovetop. Now is the time to branch beyond white button or baby bella; opt for shiitake or oyster, the wonkier the shape the better.

According to recent reports, green Beans With Tahini Sbagliato. For something less traditional, from Samin Nosrat’s recent cookbook, this recipe is make-ahead-friendly on multiple fronts. You can blanch the green beans a day ahead and whip up the tahini-miso sauce up to four days ahead. All that’s left on Turkey Day is assembly.

Industry observers note that brussels Sprouts Stir-Fry With Cheddar and Golden Raisins. Thinly sliced and swiftly sautéed, brussels sprouts take on a savory char. The cheddar could be swapped out for Gouda, or any aged cheese you love. Likewise, the golden raisins could be replaced with dried cranberries or chopped dates. It’s flexible!

Air Fryer Crispy Brussels Sprouts With Honey Butter. Or free up the stove and turn to your trusty air fryer instead. In the concentrated and circulating heat, the sprouts’ outer leaves become crackly like potato chips, craveable enough to go back for thirds.

In a recent development, sweet Potatoes With Tahini Butter. Most sweet potatoes in our archive are roasted, so isn’t it ironic that one of our most popular recipes is steamed. Author Carla Lalli puts it perfectly: “Steaming offers extreme speed and high hydration, which means that whatever you cook will be done promptly and always moist. Sweet potatoes in particular benefit from this treatment, which makes their flesh pudding-like and fluffy.”.

In a recent development, glazed Carrots. Li’l retro! These saucy carrots are sweet but not too sweet thanks to a floral mixture of orange juice and honey, plus a welcome zing from fresh ginger. I could see parsnips swapping in happily here.

In a recent development, parsnip Purée. Speaking of parsnips, from the Barefoot Contessa herself, this is a cousin to mashed potatoes that, in my humble opinion, is a whole lot better. Parsnips have a je ne sais quois, needing no more than butter, salt, and pepper, to shine bright.

Adult Mac and Cheese. Despite its title, this dish will be a hit with grown-ups and kids alike. It comes together on the stove with just six ingredients (and that’s including salt!). A few of its rave reviews: “Staple now in my house,” “Super easy and always delicious!” and “Lovelovelove. I’ve made this so many times.” Medium shells catch the sauce like little canoes; or could be a fun moment for radiatori.

It has been revealed that kale Salad With Pecan Vinaigrette. Pecans are good for more than pie. Here they turn into a nutty dressing for ruffled kale and perky radishes. Though salad is not the first (or even second) thing one might think of for Thanksgiving, it has become an absolute must on my family’s table. A refreshing reprieve to all the richness. We have more great options here.

Instant Pot Collard Greens. On a holiday table, when there’s so much going on, sometimes a simple dish is just the thing. Bacon, greens, onion, chile, done. An Instant Pot is like a Thanksgiving cheat code, freeing up the oven and the stove too.

Recent findings suggest that readers, what sides are you making this year for Thanksgiving? Share menu inspiration in the comments!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that photo Credit: Hydrogen fueled prototype by ZeroAvia. ZeroAvia.

According to recent reports, cranfield’s exit leaves one fewer route to zero-emission flights for airlines, and for the island and regional routes where hydrogen was meant to arrive first. The industry’s net-zero prepares still count on aircraft that their developers are walking away from.

Cranfield Aerospace Solutions, which set out to fly one of the first hydrogen-powered passenger aircraft, has abandoned that goal, new accounts show.

According to recent reports, “The directors have, over the past year taken some deliberate steps to improve the company’s long term outlook,” the company remarked in its accounts, filed last week with the UK’s company register, Companies House. “This has resulted in pivoting the strategy away from Project Fresson and the zero emission passenger flight objective.”.

In a recent development, under Fresson, Cranfield had been converting a nine-seat Britten-Norman Islander, a plane used on short island routes, to run on hydrogen fuel cells. It is now developing hydrogen-powered drones, “targeting wider markets and segments than those solely associated with zero emission passenger flight,” the directors wrote.

The organization is also going back to its roots. It “took early steps to restart the aerospace design consultancy services that had been the foundation of the business prior to Fresson,” the accounts say. Its motorsport simulator business “signed an exclusive contract with a premier venue entertainment provider,” which meant setting up a upcoming factory.

It has been revealed that trade publications reported last year that Cranfield had paused work on the Islander. The accounts, for the year to Sept. 29, 2025, are the tech giant’s first formal confirmation that it has moved away from passenger flight altogether, and the first look at the finances behind the decision.

Cranfield lost £4.5 million ($6.1 million) in the year, up from £4.3 million. Revenue rose to £6.9 million ($9.3 million) from £1.9 million, mostly from the simulators, and the company still made a loss on its sales before overheads. Average staff fell to 64 from 82.

It ended the year with £414,000 ($554,000) in the bank and £13.4 million ($18 million) of convertible loan notes, on which it pays 12% interest. The repayment dates have been pushed beyond September 2026, “with no fixed date.” The directors say the firm can keep going because of “expected grant money” and further loans from existing shareholders.

The balance sheet still values the development work on “a hydrogen fuelled prototype aircraft” at £16.3 million ($21.9 million), with no write-down, though the company remarked its drones build on that work. A write-down of that size would far exceed its £937,000 in net assets.

Sources indicate that the accounts were due on June 29 and were filed more than four months late. Last year’s accounts were out by June.

Cranfield is the latest hydrogen and electric aircraft developer to retreat.

Industry observers note that in June, Maeve Aerospace went bankrupt, leaving backers Delta, SkyWest and Japan Airlines without the hybrid-electric regional jet they had supported. ZeroAvia also cut about half its staff this year. “Billions are needed, years before there is any possibility of generating revenue,” aviation decarbonization analyst Adrian Norris told Skift after Maeve’s collapse. “Sadly, Maeve won’t be the last to fail.”.

Cranfield did not respond to a request for comment.

In a recent development, these aren’t your slow-braised, leisurely Sunday-sauce meatballs. They’re let’s-get-this-crew-fed-at-the-end-of-a-busy-workday meatballs. The large amount of breadcrumbs isn’t just a filler; combined with the water, they make the meatballs impossibly tender and springy. You can use any ground meat you’d like; pork, lamb, turkey, or chicken (only dark meat for the poultry, though) all work well. Roasting the meatballs in the oven instead of frying them on the stovetop reduces the active cook time and makes cleanup simple.

More crowd-pleasing meatballs recipes here.

It has been revealed that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 425°. Using a sturdy wooden spoon, vigorously mix 2 large eggs, zest of 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, 1 cup panko, ½ cup finely chopped dill and/or parsley, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 2 tsp. dried oregano, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ cup water in a large bowl until nearly a smooth paste. Add 1 lb. ground beef and mix vigorously until well combined and mixture is slightly tacky. Oil your hands; divide mixture into 16 portions and roll into balls. Arrange on a large rimmed baking sheet.

Industry observers note that toss 1 large red onion, cut through root end into 2"-thick wedges, 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, a large pinch of salt, and a large pinch of pepper in a small bowl. Arrange in a single layer around meatballs. Bake meatballs and onions until meatballs are deeply browned underneath and an instant-read thermometer inserted into centers registers 160°, 25–30 minutes. Let cool slightly.

To serve, generously top with sliced cucumbers, crumbled feta, and more dill and/or parsley if desired. Serve with country-style bread and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Looming over the quiet countryside of An Nhon, Hoang De Citadel represents an extraordinary historical palimpsest where two distinct Vietnamese empires converged upon a single plot of land.
  • Originally built in the eleventh century as Vijaya, the formidable stone-walled capital of the Champa Kingdom, the grounds were transformed in 1776 when Emperor Nguyen Nhac established it as the imperial stronghold of the Tay Son movement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looming over the quiet countryside of An Nhon, Hoang De Citadel represents an extraordinary historical palimpsest where two distinct Vietnamese empires converged upon a single plot of land.

Originally built in the eleventh century as Vijaya, the formidable stone-walled capital of the Champa Kingdom, the grounds were transformed in 1776 when Emperor Nguyen Nhac established it as the imperial stronghold of the Tay Son movement.

Beneath its current overgrown earthen ramparts lie layers of complex history: medieval Cham elephant sculptures and carved stone guardians stand alongside ruined Tay Son palace foundations and later Nguyen Dynasty tombs.

Walking through its weathered stone gates reveals an unsettling, atmospheric blend of ancient spiritual art and military strategy, offering a profound glimpse into a fortress that witnessed the rise and fall of rival dynasties.

Accessible throughout the day, though early morning or late afternoon provides a moody, shadow-filled atmosphere ideal for exploring the scattered ruins and carved stone relics.

Located in An Nhon town, easily reached via national highways heading north from Quy Nhon center.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, no one is entirely sure why an unmarried man is known as a bachelor. The word was borrowed into English from French in medieval times, and was once used as a far more general term for a young man (or, in particular, a novice knight) before coming to be used all but exclusively of an unattached young man in the 14th century. It would take another 500 years or so for the female bachelorette to be invented in the late Victorian era.Â.

Elsewhere in the dictionary, though, there are a handful of words for unattached people that havenât quite stood the same test of time, or else remain too obscure to be much used today.Â.

In a recent development, from the same clutch of words that includes the likes of bigamist and polygamist, an agamist is someone who is not married, or who actively chooses not to marry. All these words (alongside monogamy and monogamist) derived from the Greek word for marriage, gamosâwhich is also the origin of the genetic term gamete.Â.

In a recent development, if you know your Shakespeare, this might be a familiar one. âLeading apes in Hell,â a phrase Shakespeare alluded to in The Taming of the Shrew, was once the supposed proverbial punishment for a woman who had died without having children (and had therefore not done as God commanded in the Book of Genesis and gone forth and multiplied). As a result, ape-leader emerged as a jokey nickname for a single woman in 17th century English.Â.

In a recent development, although not much used in English, a catherinette is a popular term in France referring explicitly to a young woman of 25 years old, who remains unmarried in her 25th year by the time of St. Catherineâs Day, on November 25.

St. Catherine is the patron saint of unwed or engaged young women, having supposedly been romantically pursued by the Roman emperor Maxentius, but always turning down his advances. For her refusal, the emperor had Catherine imprisoned and tortured, but still she stood her ground and was eventually martyred for her refusal to wed.Â.

It has been revealed that the quintessential âdamsel in distressâ is, by definition, an unmarried young woman (often with the implication that she was also of noble birth). Damsel comes from the same root as the French mademoiselle, and was adopted into English in medieval times.Â Â.

Dating back to the 17th century, a pussock is a proverbial âold maid,â or a single woman who is now widely considered too old to be of marriageable age. Itâs one of a handful of feline-derived terms relating to aged or unmarried women that emerged around the same time; in the 1700s, for instance, a tabby was an old woman who lived on her own.Â Â.

In the 17th century, âold bachelorâ specifically became an established phrase for an older gentleman who has explicitly chosen to live a single lifeâespecially if such a man is seen to have grown to have extremely fussy or fastidious habits from such a long time on his own. In the 19th century, âold bachelorâ was cut down to âold bach,â which remained in use until the early 1900s.Â.

Less so someone who is single and more so someone who just wants to be left alone in life, the term solitudinarian was coined in the 17th century and is first recorded as far back as 1691. It has remained in albeit infrequent use ever since, largely in formal or literary contexts.Â.

According to recent reports, although the term spinster dates back to medieval times, by the 1600s a popular image had emerged of unmarried women who were expected to pass their single life by spinning and weaving. Itâs from that rather old-fashioned image that the term spinster came to be attached to unmarried or single women, and itâs spinster that was ultimately cut down to spin in the Victorian era.Â.

According to recent reports, if spinning was once seen as the typical activity of a single or unmarried woman, then tea was seen as their drink of choice. From the notion of an unattached woman ultimately drinking large quantities of tea, tea-bottleâliterally a kind of tea flaskâcame to be used as a nickname for an unmarried older woman in the early 1900s.Â.

According to recent reports, the name thornback has been used since medieval times to refer to any one of a number of creatures with a noticeably prickly or spiny back, including a species of ray or skate, a kind of spider crab, and the stickleback fish. A young stickleback, entirely coincidentally, is called a maidâand as a punning reference to an âold maidâ being an old unmarried woman, in the 1600s thornback came to be joking attached to single women too.Â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gothic architecture was one of the most prominent building styles in Europe from the 12th to the 16th centuries, and a large number of towns can be found in many European countries which feature notable examples of this style, as well as later styles which took inspiration from the Gothic era.

And while Gothic architecture was not originally connected with the supernatural, the revival of interest in the form which began in the late 18th century gradually saw the stories of vampires and other paranormal creatures become visually intertwined with places which contained or evoked the sense of this style.

Here is an alphabetical look at five towns in this veinâincluding one which actually was one of the settings for the most famous vampire novel of all time.

It has been revealed that germany has always been closely associated with the Gothic, as the original Goths were a Germanic people. Germany was also the setting for one of the classic vampire films, F. W. Murnauâs Nosferatu (1922), which used several real German places as locations for the story, including the city of Wismar.

A number of towns embodying a medieval spirit can still be found in the country today, including the town of Bamberg which is stated to be one of the most well-preserved medieval locations in Germany, and is widely celebrated for its beautiful architecture.

France is the country where Gothic architecture originated, so it is natural that many atmospheric towns in the Gothic style can found there. It has also been an crucial location in vampire storytelling, as Carl Theodor Dreyerâs legendary film Vampyr (1932) was entirely shot in the country.

According to recent reports, the town of GuÃ©rande is one of Franceâs most intact examples of Gothic style, located in Loire-Atlantique in the west of the country. Its abundance of towers and fortified walls lend themselves well to the imagery evoked by Gothic literature.

The idea of a mysterious town by the sea has close connections with classic vampire fiction. In Bram Stokerâs Dracula, the titular vampire travels from his home country by sea before arriving at a coastal town. The idea of vampires being intertwined with the ocean illuminates the fictional potential of places like Kotor in Montenegro: the town is surrounded by dramatic stone walls, dating from its time as a part of the Republic of Venice, and contains a number of striking Gothic buildings.

In a recent development, romania is closely connected with vampire-related lore, as the home of the notoriously ruthless medieval ruler Vlad the Impaler, and the historic Transylvania region from where the fictional Dracula originates. One of the towns which is most evocative of this sense of the Gothic (in a dramatic if not literal sense) is the town of Sinaia in the historic Muntenia region.

One of its most sensational buildings is PeleÈ Castle: while not a Gothic building (it was constructed in the late 19th century), it very much evokes the kinds of castles which might be imagined to be occupied by vampires in fiction, with elaborate towers rising up amidst a mysterious hillside forest.

Sources indicate that and now we come to the town which inspired Dracula itself. Whitby is located on the North Yorkshire coast of England and is a town steeped in history and atmosphere, with a ruined abbey amongst its most haunting features. In the novel, Whitby also becomes an important location in the story as this is the town where Draculaâs ship first docks when he arrives in England.

It was also in Whitby that Bram Stoker found a number of inspirations for the novel while he was visiting the town including the name of the title character, which he found through reading a book about Romania in the local library.
