  • Sources indicate that no city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources.
  • Industry observers note that as long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the Upcoming Guinea Highlands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

Sources indicate that no city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

Industry observers note that as long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the Upcoming Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Contemporary live marine traffic map available at marinetraffic.com.

Whoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.

Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation.

‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a upcoming breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.

In a recent development, comanche warriors, photographed in 1892. Courtesy Wikipedia.

The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.

According to recent reports, look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.

The expansion of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century. Courtesy Wikipedia.

Yet the Sinocentric paradigm – the predominant vision of human history and civilisation with China at its centre – structurally erases extrahuman transportation and, with it, pastoralism, steppe empires and charisma from state formation, thereby negating the Eurasian steppe as the prime centre of human history. This framework shapes our current understanding of world history, leaving us with a view defined by entrapment, doom and despair. Becoming aware of this paradigm is essential if we are to break free from this bleak outlook, better comprehend the world we live in, and chart a brighter future.

While scholars critique world history for its Eurocentric bias, its conceptual framework and narrative are profoundly Sinocentric. This is because the origin of the state – and consequently the birth of civilisation – is the question that shapes our vision of world history. The latest authoritative iteration of this view is James C Scott’s Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States (2017), along with his The Art of Not Being Governed (2009). ‘The Origin of the State: Land Productivity or Appropriability’ by Joram Mayshar and colleagues is its economic restatement. Scott, readers might counter, focuses almost exclusively on Mesopotamia and rarely mentions China. Yet his underlying framework actually rearticulates the paradigm established by the American Orientalist Owen Lattimore’s influential work, Inner Asian Frontiers of China (1940). Precisely for this reason, Scott not only frequently mentions ‘the loess soils along the Yellow River’, but also, directly quoting Lattimore, claims that ‘irrigation was spectacularly rewarding in the loess core of ancient China’.

Sources indicate that A 1925 map of China and Mongolia by the George F Cram company, Chicago. Courtesy the David Rumsey Map Collection.

In a recent development, lattimore sought to legitimise the Republic of China’s claims over Mongolia, Manchukuo, Tibet and Eastern Turkestan. To this end, he advanced the grain thesis to locate the origins of statehood and civilisation in the Yellow River Valley, positioning China as the Cradle of the East. By mapping Frederick Jackson Turner’s American frontier thesis onto the region, Lattimore framed China as the civilised centre and reduced the aforementioned territories to ‘Inner Asia’ – a mere geohistorical frontier akin to the American West. In doing so, Lattimore abandoned the traditional conquest theory – a framework he had previously espoused – which held that both China’s early states and most of its subsequent empires were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors rather than indigenous dynamics. The rejection of the conquest theory was a repudiation of extrahuman transportation and pastoralism as forces that led to statehood, and an exaltation of sedentism and grain agriculture instead.

The paradigm owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence.

In a recent development, the theory that entrenched Lattimore’s thesis in academia is Robert Carneiro’s circumscription hypothesis, published in the journal Science as ‘A Theory of the Origin of the State’ (1970). Not just conventional narratives, but a wide array of prominent thinkers – including Michael Mann, Jared Diamond, Francis Fukuyama and Yuval Noah Harari – popularised Carneiro’s theory in different guises. Even David Graeber and David Wengrow ultimately remain within this framework.

Drawing on Carneiro’s concept of circumscribed agricultural land, Mann’s The Sources of Social Power (1986) posits ecological and social cages with no ‘escape route’, while Diamond’s Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997) similarly focuses on regions with ‘nowhere to flee’ to isolate the environmental conditions that generate the population pressure needed for the rise of the state. Fukuyama’s The Origins of Political Order (2011), however, is far more direct in delineating the primary conditions for pristine state formation: ‘that population needs to be physically constrained so that it increases in density’ and ‘that subjects cannot run away when coerced’. When Diamond wrote in Nature in 2002 that agricultural storable food surpluses ‘led to social stratification, political centralisation and standing armies’, he was merely rationalising the Lattimore-Carneiro population-pressure dogma as an ‘autocatalytic’ process. Harari’s Sapiens (2011), with its disease-ridden ‘luxury trap’, Scott’s The Art of Not Being Governed, along with his Against the Grain, and Graeber and Wengrow’s lamentation that ours is a species ‘enslaved to its crops’ all ultimately stem from the same grain thesis.

It has been revealed that indeed, the Lattimore-Carneiro framework relied on a population-pressure model, arguing that agriculture and sedentism triggered overpopulation, forcing the creation of hierarchies and states. However, Carneiro’s circumscription thesis required areas such as Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley and the Peruvian coast to be entirely overcrowded. Instead, empirical settlement surveys revealed that these areas lacked the demographic density to exhaust arable land, with some even experiencing depopulation during early state-formation. Because no population pressure existed to catalyse state formation, archaeological findings invalidated Carneiro’s theory.

According to recent reports, scott’s novelty lies neither in his rhetoric of ‘political crops’, nor in his laser-focused ‘circumscribed ecological niches’ of ‘alluvial or loess soils’, but rather in his theoretical sleight of hand: dynamic climatic circumscription. His fertile alluvial or loess soils mirror Carneiro’s circumscribed agricultural land, though on a minuscule scale, engineered by a millennium-long drought rather than geographic barriers. Ultimately, Scott repurposes Carneiro’s model of resource concentration – a resource-rich habitat that draws people from surrounding regions – yet he supercharges it with the driving force of drought. In sum, drought – simultaneously reconfiguring the physical terrain into a localised cage and driving populations inward – enables Scott to isolate the minuscule, 250-hectare footprint of Uruk as the circumscribed agricultural land. Scott’s model here is a clever manoeuvre to salvage the Sinocentric paradigm. That paradigm, as we shall see, owes its formation to Cold War politics and is at odds with archaeological evidence.

Whether climatic or geographical, the agricultural cage is inherently an anti-mobility framing that structurally erases pastoralism from the formation of the state. This erasure is, however, not just a conceptual flaw; it is written into the paradigm’s DNA, as the framework is fundamentally built against mobility, and actively argues for its exclusion. The erasure takes the form of epistemic theft by way of attributing the authorship of domestication of livestock and pastoralism to farmers, delaying the date of the advent of pastoralism through hyper-restrictive definitions, and relying on exclusionary framing. While the initial framework was a politically motivated, instrumental scheme, subsequent models have resulted from paradigmatic biases.

Industry observers note that the question that led to this erasive framing was not the origin of the state in general, but its emergence in what is now China – specifically, whether it was indigenous or born of nomadic conquest. This issue was linked to a raging political dilemma: did Manchuria, and by extension the Daiching Empire (also known as the Qing dynasty), constitute a Chinese or an Inner Asian empire? This debate was a political question concerning the definition of China and the delineation of its territory. Specifically, should China be defined as ‘China proper’, restricted to the Ming provinces, or as ‘China imperial’, encompassing the domains of the Daiching Empire.

The controversy escalated into a heightened political crisis with the declaration of Manchukuo. Japanese scholarship argued that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian state that had conquered China, and that the Manchus were a distinct people deserving independence. The Chinese nationalist regime and its scholarship countered, arguing that the empire was inherently Chinese, and that Manchuria had been an integral part of China since antiquity. Meanwhile, contemporary critical scholarship essentially agreed with the Japanese view; the dominant framework for the origins of the state in China was the invasion theory, which argued that early Chinese states, as well as many subsequent empires, were forged by Eurasian nomadic conquerors. Crucially, until then, Lattimore himself had been a proponent of this theory.

It has been revealed that monks on White Hill overlooking Urga (now Ulaanbaatar), Mongolia, in 1913. Courtesy the Musée Albert-Kahn, France.

According to recent reports, A rider beside a river near Urga. Courtesy the Musée Albert-Kahn, France.

The Republic of China was a legal fiction enabled by the Open Door policy (authored by US diplomats in 1899). Yet, this very regime claimed sovereignty over Mongolia, Manchuria, Eastern Turkestan and Tibet. By the 1930s, however, the Open Door order was in tatters: Outer Mongolia had declared independence in 1911, Tibet in 1912, and Manchukuo had broken away in 1932, absorbing Eastern Inner Mongolia. The rest of Inner Mongolia was ruled by a Japanese-allied government, while Eastern Turkestan declared independence in 1933.

Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours.

Recognising the Daiching Empire as an Inner Asian state meant forfeiting China’s claim over all of these regions, stripping the regime of what Lattimore estimated at nearly two-thirds of its claimed territory. Worse still for the West, the Soviet Union was poised to become the ultimate beneficiary – an outcome the regime and its primary architect, the US, were determined to prevent. The regime had to ensure that its territory emerged as inherently Chinese, and scholarship was needed to substantiate this claim. This required refuting the invasion theory and reframing China as the Cradle of the East. Lattimore’s book, Inner Asian Frontiers of China, accomplished precisely this.

Recent findings suggest that executing a complete about-face from his earlier position, building on Chinese nationalist scholarship, and drawing on Turner’s American frontier thesis, Lattimore reframed Mongolia, Manchuria, Chinese Turkistan (today’s Xinjiang) and Tibet as the frontiers of China. Reducing these territories to a mere geographic area – Inner Asia – and rebranding them as mere frontiers required rendering the region stateless, tribal and barbarian. Had Mongolia and the others remained states, they could not have been conceptualised as frontiers, but rather as independent neighbours; his framework thus demanded a terra nullius.

Recent findings suggest that refuting the invasion theory required disarming it of its most potent weapon of conquest – mobility – and supplanting it with an alternative framework. Lattimore accomplished this by casting mobility as an anti-state force, substituting the invasion thesis with evolutionary materialism. Inverting his earlier argument that mobility provided a ‘snowball’ effect to Mongol political organisation, Lattimore was the first to equate mobility with dispersal. He thereby transformed what was previously understood as the ultimate mobilising and concentrating mechanism into an inherently dispersive element. This reframing neutralised conquest theory, turning its defining weapon into an anti-state force.

Furthermore, by establishing mobility as the defining feature of pastoralism, and immobility as that of irrigated agriculture, Lattimore posited both a positive correlation between wealth and power and a negative one between mobility and wealth/power, thus advancing his ‘wealth versus mobility’ thesis. And by asserting that ‘grain, accumulated and stored, was beyond question the standard of real wealth in essentials’, he guaranteed ‘the ascendancy of wealth over mobility’. In this manner, Lattimore not only erased mobility as the state-making force but also established grain as that very force. In fact, Lattimore is the author of the grain thesis, and in his framework, the state emerges as a grain store.

Mobility, thus, emerged not merely as dispersal, but as a mechanism of destitution, rather than a driver of state-building. While Lattimore declared that ‘it is the poor nomad who is pure nomad,’ intellectual successors like the cultural anthropologist Marshall Sahlins observed that a nomad’s wealth ‘is a burden’ that ‘soon poses a contradiction to his mobility.’ Anatoly Khazanov pushed this thesis further, arguing that pastoralism is inherently non-self-sufficient (non-autarkic) or even anti-autarkic, thereby rendering it fundamentally incapable of producing a state.

At the same time, by mapping environmentally determined societies – specifically, forest-hunting clans, steppe-pastoral tribes, and loess-agricultural states – and adding extensive and intensive dimensions, Lattimore established population pressure as the primary catalyst for state-formation. While agriculture in general emerged as uniquely capable of generating a state, irrigated agriculture was intensive enough to trigger severe demographic strain. Identifying a continuous agricultural expanse enclosed by ‘an immense mass of inhospitable terrain’ – namely, ‘the bleak highlands’ and ‘the Inner Asian barrier lands’ on one side, and the Pacific Ocean on the other – Lattimore mapped China as a circumscribed agricultural land.

Industry observers note that to cast China as the Cradle of the East and claim Inner Asia as a Chinese frontier, Lattimore framed Inner Asian pastoralism as a byproduct of agricultural expansion, attributing all historical agency to farmers. By claiming pastoralists were ‘akin by culture and probably by blood to the early Chinese’, he cast both populations as homologous. Dating steppe pastoralism to the 4th century BCE – as an offshoot of intensive Chinese agriculture – allowed Lattimore to monopolise the state-formation timeline and neutralise the invasion theory.

According to recent reports, to stall the timeline of pastoralism’s emergence, he devised a hyper-restrictive definition: dismissing categories like ‘true’, ‘strict’ or ‘normal’ as overly broad, he defined ‘pastoral nomadism’ exclusively as ‘the extreme of nomadism’ or ‘the strict or extreme phases of steppe nomadism’. This framework equates pastoralism with the advent of horseback riding and, in effect, with the rise of cavalry.

Sources indicate that to be sure, all of these claims conflicted with contemporary scholarly knowledge, including archaeology and linguistics. Back then, archaeology had shown that horse-riding nomadism and animal art emerged around 1500 BCE in the Black Sea region before spreading eastward through Mongolia to Ordos – a fact Lattimore was aware of. Similarly, linguists such as Henri Maspero had shown that the Chinese language ‘has no relation whatever, not even a distant connection with’ Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic languages. Nonetheless, Lattimore’s attribution of pastoral animal domestication to farmers and his hyper-restrictive definition of pastoralism became paradigmatic in the field. Khazanov cemented Lattimore’s thesis: he claimed that only sedentary groups with definite vegetable surpluses could domesticate animals, and characterised ‘pure pastoral nomadism’ as ‘the most extreme form’ of nomadism. In this manner, mobility and pastoralism were written out of the state-formation process.

An encampment in Inner Mongolia, 1912. Courtesy the Musée Albert-Kahn, France.

In a recent development, however, modern scholarship by Melinda Zeder shows that ‘plant and animal domestication occurred at roughly the same time, with signs of initial management … reaching back to at least 11,500 cal BP [ie, 9550 BCE], if not earlier.’ Furthermore, we now know that early animal domestication ‘only took place within a subset of the geographical distribution of the wild ancestors’, unfolding ‘often in regions distant from centres of plant domestication.’ Critically, while most herd animals were domesticated via the prey pathway rather than a commensal one, pastoralists domesticated equids – donkeys and horses – via a directed pathway. Yet, by claiming that ‘specialised pastoralism, seen as an outgrowth of agriculture’ confronts the state with a ‘problem of dispersal and mobility’, Scott continues to perpetuate Lattimore’s delayed timeline and restrictive definition – even while acknowledging that agriculture and pastoralism emerged concurrently roughly 12,000 years ago.

Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated.

By the 1970s, Lattimore’s framework had become the dominant orthodoxy. Elman Service, a leading neo-evolutionist, hailed it as ‘the pathfinding ecological theory’, while Morton Fried acknowledged that Lattimore ‘proposed a theory that stimulated my own’. Ultimately, neo-evolutionism displaced conquest theory as the mainstream paradigm. By positioning intensive agriculture as the sole economic foundation capable of sustaining the state, Fried’s social stratification scheme (egalitarian, rank, stratified, and state) and Service’s sociopolitical typology (band, tribe, chiefdom, and state) reinforced Lattimore’s irrigated agriculture thesis while anchoring evolutionary materialism. Consequently, the state – either as an instrument of the upper class or as a managerial institution – emerges fundamentally as an economic instrument and an evolutionary product.

In a recent development, by deriving the state from either social or functional differentiation, both Fried and Service rejected conquest theory. Whereas Service’s model is basically a refinement of 19th-century bourgeois materialism, Fried’s framework aligns with the Marxist model by emphasising conflict driven by internal economic differentiation. Carneiro likewise rejected conquest theory; despite his incorporating warfare and coercion, his model remains an elaboration of Fried’s framework. As one of the most influential models of neo-evolutionary thought, Carneiro’s framework was a direct product of this paradigmatic bias, and it effectively resulted in the global scaling of Lattimore’s framework. China was established as the Cradle of the East, while Inner Asia was relegated to a tribal world and ‘the barbarian “outer darkness”’. Mobility, pastoralism and tribalism were essentially conflated until Caroline Humphrey and David Sneath deconstructed the category of ‘nomadism’ and the myth of the wandering nomad in 1999, paving the way for Sneath to later debunk the tribal model as a complete misrepresentation. Meanwhile, in a corpus of historical scholarship utilising primary sources, Christopher P Atwood compellingly demonstrates that the tribal model is untenable.

However, Scott not only resurrects Lattimore’s framework in its entirety along with its long-refuted theories but also repackages it to fit his own anarchist project. Following Lattimore, Scott maintains that Inner Asian pastoralism – along with its population – was merely a byproduct of Chinese agricultural expansion. His assertion that the Great Wall was built as much to contain Chinese taxpayers as to repel external invasions likewise mirrors Lattimore’s position. Scott’s most spectacular move is his elevation of mobility into a primary form of freedom. Lattimore’s notion of free nomads – with their ‘idea of freedom, free movement, free migration’ – nicely dovetailed with Scott’s anarchist thesis, prompting him to valorise mobility as a freedom-preserving force and recast it as the fundamental state-preventing strategy.

It has been revealed that this conceptualisation clearly finds its echo in The Dawn of Everything (2021), where Graeber and Wengrow theorise ‘the freedom to move’ as one of the ‘fundamental, even primary, forms of freedom’. At the same time, Scott’s grain thesis, in particular, and agricultural paradigm, in general, powerfully guide our thinking, leading the two authors to declare in despair that ‘we got stuck’ and that ‘ours is a species that has become enslaved to its crops.’ Mobility thus emerged as a fundamentally anti-state, anti-domination and freedom-preserving force, albeit one that proved impotent against the all-powerful grain to which we, along with all our extrahuman transportation, are enslaved. This is how the Sinocentric paradigm was devised and how it erases pastoralism from state-formation. The objective of this paradigm is to eliminate mobility, and its theoretical frameworks inherently structure scholarly thinking and enquiry against pastoralism. Ultimately, this is how the Sinocentric paradigm traps us intellectually.

Recent findings suggest that with the erasure of mobility and pastoralism and the relegation of Inner Asia into tribal barbarity, the Sinocentric paradigm monopolised state-formation in China for the Chinese while establishing China as the sole empire and civilisation within the former Daiching domain. However, there were Inner Asian empires – especially the Daiching Empire – on whose identification the integrity of the regime’s claim over Inner Asia depended. This demanded their total erasure. The method – as Lattimore himself observed in 1934 while depicting the grim reality that the Open Door policy had imposed upon the Mongols, the Manchus, the Uighurs and the Tibetans – was to ‘deny their history and surrender their national and racial identities’ and, ultimately, to conquer them conceptually. Notably, this is the exact policy that the current Chinese administration pursues today.

Sources indicate that this meant the appropriation of all the empires that conquered China as inherently Chinese, and the construction of an everlasting Chinese empire. To achieve this, two problems had to be solved: the reality of conquests and the distinct identity of the conquering empires. Because these conquests were not isolated incidents but occurred in overwhelming numbers, a sophisticated framework had to be devised.

To appropriate Inner Asian empires, Lattimore devised the theory of Chinese dynastic cycles, a teleological device that powerfully legitimises Chinese nationalist claims through a veneer of deterministic, historical law. By reducing all empires to mere dynasties, this cycle creates the illusion of an enduring Chinese state where successive dynasties simply replace one another. Conquests are thus erased as mere changes in ruling houses while the empire itself remains intact. Consequently, the Chinese empire emerges as uniquely endless – an everlasting polity standing in stark contrast to the mortal trajectories of all other historical powers, including the Roman Empire.

Industry observers note that to make this everlasting empire inherently Chinese and to deny the identity of the conquering empires – in contrast to British ‘accumulative’ and Russian ‘incorporative’ models – Lattimore forged ‘the third great type’: the Chinese ‘absorptive’ empire. Unlike ‘conquest’ empires, this was a ‘defensive empire’ – one that did not conquer but was conquered, yet remained Chinese by absorbing its conquerors. Consequently, the polity emerged not as a conquering political power, but as a cultural community predicated on assimilation. Furthermore, as China was established as civilisation itself, and Inner Asia was reduced to barbarity, all Inner Asian conquests represented a barbarian advancement toward civilisation. Sinicisation was a ‘standing offer of the opportunity to become civilised, to any individual or group interested in progress’ – the civilising mission.

China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles.

It has been revealed that however, Lattimore’s highly idiosyncratic conceptualisations invert reality. Empire, by definition, is an expansionist, incorporative polity; what defines an empire is expansion, and what drives it is conquest. It is also anything but culturally homogeneous; its very nature is all-encompassing, hierarchical and heterogeneous. Thus, Lattimore’s Chinese absorptive empire is a veritable anomaly. Moreover, with hundreds of mutually unintelligible varieties divided across at least eight major language groups, even the Sinitic group – let alone China as a whole – represents immense cultural diversity.

In fact, Lattimore’s ‘absorptive’ empire was the political embodiment of the Chinese nationalist narrative of assimilative power, depicting China as a solid, homogenising mass, ‘homogeneous in race, language, and culture’, where the ‘barbarians were all absorbed by the Chinese; they became Chinese like any other Chinese.’ Hence, the Manchus were all assimilated by the Chinese and became Chinese like any other; therefore, the Manchu empire was a Chinese dynasty like any other. Had all the Mongols shared the Manchu fate, the Chinese empire would have been the largest contiguous land empire the world had ever seen; then, what June Teufel Dreyer called the ‘tianxia trope’ – the idea that a Sinocentric world is the better one – would have possessed a formidable precedent.

A 1914 map of Asia depicting China as a ‘solid, homogenising mass’. Courtesy Wikipedia.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, Lattimore’s framework immediately became hegemonic. China was reified as an everlasting empire, and its history emerged as unbroken dynastic cycles with a predictable Sinicisation pattern. Paired with the Chinese world order, the paradigm crystallised into unchallenged dogma. Lattimore emerged ‘as the intellectual godfather of all historians of China’ (as the sinologist Mark C Elliott put it), and the founder of Chinese frontier studies. Only in the 1990s did scholars like Pamela Crossley, Evelyn Rawski and Elliott finally break ranks to challenge the Sinicisation thesis, instigating what would become the Upcoming Qing History school, which demonstrates that the Daiching Empire was an Inner Asian empire and that the Manchus preserved their distinct identity until its very demise. In fact, as my recent scholarship highlights, the Daiching Empire was a Manchu-Mongolian aristocratic empire that conquered and colonised China.

Industry observers note that though the paradigm enacted a wholesale epistemic overhaul, it never succeeded in entirely suppressing critical scholarship. Instead, it produced jarring anomalies that effectively rendered the framework itself an anomaly. The greatest of these anomalies is the rise of the Eurasian steppe empires that dominated agricultural regions – including much or all of present-day China – for much of human history.

Inner Asian nomads consistently ruled over agricultural populations.

Recent findings suggest that however, as the paradigm dictates, there can be no state – let alone an empire – on the Eurasian steppe due to geographical, ecological, economic and political constraints. As Scott argues, pastoralism is the foremost state-preventing and state-evading strategy, and the Eurasian steppe is the quintessential nonstate space. Yet, from the dawn of history down to the 20th century, the Eurasian steppe has been the home of numerous empires, many of which conquered and ruled neighbouring agricultural regions. This constitutes a massive anomaly to the paradigm; indeed, because these nomadic empires – most notably the Mongol Empire – fundamentally shaped the world, human history itself becomes an anomaly within this framework. This particular anomaly fundamentally undermines the paradigm: a theory that renders human history anomalous is inherently anomalous itself, for a theory is meant to explain reality, not dismiss it.

Industry observers note that detail from Kublai Khan Hunting (1280) by Liu Guandao. Courtesy the National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Industry observers note that the paradox runs deeper, fundamentally uprooting the Sinocentric paradigm at its core. According to this framework, early regional states were founded exclusively by grain agriculturalists, and the empire was always inherently Chinese. However, the earliest states in China – the Shang and the Zhou – were not the making of Yellow River grain, but of western Inner Asian conquests. Moreover, from the rise of the Shang around 1600 BCE to the fall of the Daiching Empire in 1912, Inner Asian nomads consistently ruled over agricultural populations. China, in whole or in part, was absorbed into their empires for nearly three millennia, with nomads building the majority of the region’s states, including most of its expansive and longest-lasting empires. If grain were the primary engine of state formation, none of this should have occurred; instead, the exact opposite would have been true.

According to recent reports, indeed, modern scholarship increasingly attributes early Chinese state formation to nomadic conquest – effectively validating the conquest theory frameworks that predated Lattimore. Victor H Mair’s research demonstrates that, from the beginning in the Shang and Zhou, to the end in the Daiching – including the celebrated Tang – China was a constant creation of Inner Asian empire-builders. Even the Qin and Han carried a ‘likely Central Eurasian heritage’. Strikingly, out of 83 historical polities in the region, only 31 were of Sinitic origin. Mair concludes that these northern conquests ‘were responsible for the creation of the first states in the Yellow River Valley [and] the building of vast empires in Eurasia.’ The Eurasian steppe thus comes to light as the true cradle of state formation and civilisation.

In fact, in a striking parallel to the insights Lattimore articulated in 1934, Hugh R Clark argues that:.

Industry observers note that the more scholarship advances, the more the invasion theory is validated, and the more the Sinocentric paradigm crumbles. Scott, however, still erases the Eurasian steppe empires by reducing the Mongols, the Manchus, the Huns, the Mughals and the Ottomans to ‘barbarian “stars”’. He insists that they ‘were no different in kind from earlier and smaller nonstate peoples – hunters and gatherers, swiddeners, coastal foragers, herdsmen – who raided small states and traded with them.’.

Industry observers note that by grounding state-formation in the economy – rendering the state a mere institutional superstructure – evolutionary materialism eliminates extra-economic force and conquest from the equation altogether. Consequently, the state emerges as the exclusive preserve and just deserts of wealthy, populous, industrious societies. Its ascent is framed not just as predictable, but as automatic and inevitable – an assumption so self-evident to scholars like Scott and Mayshar et al that they do not bother to address it at all. This paradigm shift fundamentally alters our understanding of the origin and nature of political power.

In sharp contrast, Max Weber’s theory provides an idealist framework explicitly formulated to counter evolutionary materialism. In this view, history is driven by great ideas, newly introduced revelations, powerful beliefs and groundbreaking inventions – transformative forces that Weber conceptualised under a single term: charisma. ‘Charisma,’ he writes in Economy and Society (1921), ‘is the great revolutionary force’ – ‘the specifically creative revolutionary force of history’. Charisma – whether it ‘be of a religious, ethical, artistic, scientific, political, or other kind’ – sits at the root of all human institutions, organisations and arts. Consequently, the institutions of politics, religion, art and the sciences, such as the state, the church and academia, are legacies of generations of charismatic or gifted leadership. The state – a creation of military charisma and charismatic warlord conquest – is the most critical of them. As such, every technological breakthrough – from extrahuman transportation to the iPhone – is ultimately a creation of charisma.

However, it is precisely Fried and Service who erased Weber’s great revolutionary force from state-formation as well as history. They co-opted Weber’s framework of political authority but mutilated it, rendering it unrecognisable. ‘Doing some violence to Weber’s thought,’ in Origins of the State and Civilization (1975), Service mapped Weber’s charismatic authority onto ‘egalitarian-segmental societies’, his traditional authority onto ‘chiefdoms’, and his legal authority onto ‘the government of archaic civilisations’ ‘to epitomise very well the leadership’ in those societies. Thus, Service proscribed Weber’s charismatic and traditional authorities from history and civilisation. As for charisma, both Service and Fried unanimously banished it to pre-historic primitivity, to the sphere of the supernatural, or to madness – ‘a charismatic madman who just happens to be the genealogical leader of the largest kin group,’ as Fried himself put it in Evolution of Political Society (1967). In doing so, they not only effectively erased Weber’s principal agent of state-building but also made it exotic, mad, tribal and barbarian, exiling it to Inner Asia. This transformed Inner Asia into both the womb and tomb of military charisma, and Inner Asian empires into the excesses of military madmen.

Evolutionary materialists purged the patrimonial state from history, equating the state with bureaucracy.

Since they also erased traditional authority from the state and civilisation, they both posited bureaucracy – the ultimate expression of Weber’s legal authority – as the definitive form of the state, producing a theoretical scaffolding that renders all premodern political formations, such as patrimonialism, invisible. However, for Weber, bureaucracy is an impersonal rule of law where ‘what [the bureaucrat] obeys is only “the law”.’ In fact, Weber’s legal authority is an abstraction of the modern liberal constitutional state (and its German variant, the Rechtsstaat); his bureaucracy is a modern civil service; and his bureaucrat is a modern civil servant.

Though Weber noted that ‘bureaucracy has first developed in patrimonial states’, he categorically distinguished it from his legal authority and its corresponding bureaucracy. Bureaucracy under traditional authority serves the ‘master’ or the king rather than impersonal rules or the law. For this reason, Weber identifies it as ‘patrimonial officialdom’ and comprehensively contrasts it with ‘bureaucratic officialdom’. In fact, the patrimonial state, or patrimonial dynastic state, is the prime embodiment of Weber’s traditional authority and serves as the major form of all pre-constitutional states. However, by consigning Weber’s traditional authority to chiefdoms, evolutionary materialists purged the patrimonial state from history, effectively equating the state with bureaucracy.

Sources indicate that defining the state by bureaucracy – or equating it with bureaucracy – is tantamount to replacing monarchy, aristocracy and democracy with bureaucracy. The state is a sovereign rulership; hence, there is no form of rulership or political regime called bureaucracy. Bureaucracy is neither rulership nor political. No sovereign, or ruler, is made by appointment. Sovereignty and appointment are mutually exclusive. There can be no appointed sovereign: if appointed, the officeholder is a servant, not a sovereign. Likewise, there can be no bureaucracy and no bureaucrat by virtue of appropriation, election or designation; the appropriation of office and bureaucracy are mutually exclusive. If rulership excludes appointment, appropriation excludes bureaucracy. Bureaucracy follows rulership and serves it; bureaucracy is merely the administrative apparatus of the state. Ultimately, no rule is law if it is not enforced, no land is territory if it is not under sovereignty, and no authority is a bureaucracy if it is not appointed by a ruler. It is rulership that creates law, territory and bureaucracy. By equating the state with bureaucracy, the Sinocentric paradigm not only turned Weber’s theory upside down but also misled us.

Industry observers note that ironically, Weber actually conceptualises the premodern ‘centralised and highly developed administration’ as a product of conquest rule. To maintain domination, the state develops a repressive apparatus to domesticate its subjects. By necessity, it becomes ‘strongest in conquered territories, because of the continuous threat to’ the conquerors. Weber notes:.

He similarly attributes bureaucratic administration ‘in the Orient’ to ‘upcoming conquerors’ who ‘counteracted quite effectively the otherwise natural process of decentralisation and appropriation.’.

Conquerors by necessity had to monopolise power, especially military power, themselves. Yet, because of linguistic, cultural and other local barriers, they had to rely on local interlocutors. However, giving them hereditary military power amounted to creating rival power centres, as the early Manchu creation of the Three Feudatories demonstrates. The most effective means to concentrate power in their own hands, and at the same time efficiently domesticate and administer the conquered population, was to appoint easily removable civilian administrative officials.

Industry observers note that however, scholars – including Scott, Fukuyama, Graeber and Wengrow – equate the state with bureaucracy, and search for traces of bureaucracy to find the state. Thus, Scott confidently asserts that ‘it was only in such settings that the first bureaucratic states were likely to arise.’ Graeber and Wengrow go further to advance a novel conceptualisation that essentially defines the state as bureaucracy, ‘as a combination of sovereignty, bureaucracy and a competitive political field.’ Clearly, Jean Bodin’s and Thomas Hobbes’s sovereignty or Weber’s monopoly of violence is not enough to constitute the state. Indeed, Graeber and Wengrow discourse ‘on sovereignty without “the state”’ and search for ‘a great bureaucratic machine’ to find a state. Ultimately, to be a state is to be a bureaucracy. For this reason, Fukuyama in 2011 declares that ‘China alone created a modern state in the terms defined by Max Weber … in developing a centralised, uniform system of bureaucratic administration’. Consequently, by declaring: ‘I take China as a paradigm of state formation and ask why other civilisations didn’t replicate the path it followed,’ Fukuyama positions China as the norm, thereby casting the rest of the world – including Greece, Rome and Europe as a whole – as a ‘divergent’ abnormality, that is, what Lattimore called a ‘barbarian plague’. The Sinocentric paradigm thus places China at the centre and the summit of ‘All under Heaven’.

We set out to learn the origins of the state by studying its preeminent theories and the deep history of the earliest states. Yet, have we truly learned anything about the state’s origins? Or, have we instead, as Scott notes, merely learned what ‘can serve as a basis for taxation’ – namely, its ‘productive base’? Mayshar and his colleagues, who similarly argue that ‘hierarchy arose as a result of the shift to dependence on appropriable cereal grains’, also demonstrate how grain serves as a basis for taxation. This is Scott’s theory of the origin of the state, and it is – one might say – fundamentally a theory of the state’s productive base, not of its origin. Yet, this is the preeminent theory of state origins – the reigning evolutionary, materialist, population-pressure paradigm that I call the Sinocentric paradigm. Ultimately, this paradigm represents a colonial legacy that displaced conquest theory.

What, then, is conquest theory, and what does it say about the origin of the state? What exactly is the state, and how is it defined? Remarkably, both theories accept the same definition of the state. That the state is a human community that (successfully) claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory is a universally accepted definition. Weber defines the state sociologically ‘only in terms of the specific means peculiar to it, as to every political association, namely, the use of physical force,’ that is, ‘the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force’ (italics original). In short, the state is the institution that exercises a monopoly on legitimate violence. Therefore, when looking for the origin of the state, we should examine how this institution arose. That is exactly what conquest theory does.

Therefore, in looking for the origin of the state, conquest theory examines the rise of physical force – that is, the institution of violence – and the establishment of a monopoly over it. This framework locates that physical force in the warband and the monopoly in the warlord, and explores how that monopoly becomes both necessary and legitimate. Specifically, it finds the monopoly in the need for leadership and organisation within the warband, and the legitimacy in the warband’s need for security. Finally, it explores the conditions that give rise to, or necessitate, this force, and locates those conditions in a state of war.

By rendering the security of the warband paramount, war makes violence legitimate.

Recent findings suggest that making life and liberty scarce, war necessitates physical force in the form of a warband. A warband emerges as a warrior consociation – a community of common political struggle over life and death, and a warrior brotherhood – where individuals are expected to face death in the group’s interest. War also forges the warband into a rational normative community: in Weber’s words, a ‘pressing need for security against internal and foreign enemies induces a growing rationalisation of lawmaking and lawfinding.’ Thus, war creates the warband as a warrior fraternity and a rational-legal consociation.

In a recent development, demanding unity, organisation, discipline and leadership, war not only moulds a warband into a cohesive group but also fashions the warlord as its leader. In turn, the unity, organisation and discipline – which require both centralised authority and the monopolisation of power – render the warlord a monarch who commands and compels obedience. Ultimately, by rendering the security of the warband paramount, war makes violence legitimate. As Weber writes: ‘Violence acquires legitimacy only in those cases, however – at least initially – in which it is directed against members of the fraternity who have acted treasonably or who have harmed it by disobedience or cowardice.’ Therefore, a warband is a human community that successfully claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force. As such, the rise of the warband marks the beginning of the state. Thus, in the rise of the warband, conquest theory locates both the military differentiation and the military constitution – the archetype of the state. A victorious warband that has successfully established a monopoly of violence over a population in a stretch of land becomes the state.

Industry observers note that therefore, the state is fundamentally a relation of political domination – specifically, domination by virtue of authority (defined as the power to command and the duty to obey) – based ultimately upon a monopoly of violence over life and liberty. It is a domination founded on both the threat to and the protection of life and liberty; this is the fundamental reason for the monopoly of violence, which constitutes sovereignty. In short, war brings kingship as a war power in the form of a warband, and the king as a war leader in the person of a warlord. As Weber observes, ‘Everywhere the king is primarily a warlord,’ and ‘kingship is normally charismatic war leadership that has become permanent and has developed a repressive apparatus for the domestication of the unarmed subjects.’ This is entirely Weber’s theory, and this reading makes him one of the most conceptual, yet profoundly misunderstood, conquest theorists.

It is not resource surplus, scarcity or appropriability that leads to the rise of the state; instead, it is the direct and unmediated monopoly over life and liberty. This domination is not mediated by resource control, but by direct control over life and liberty. For this reason, not only does the political exist on its own terms, but political relationships are also primary and fundamental. It is the political constitution that determines and defines both the social and the economic. Consequently, private property, land scarcity, social stratification and social classes – and, indeed, society and economy – are consequences of the state rather than preconditions for it, institutions ultimately forged by conquest, subjugation, expropriation and political integration.

Sources indicate that however, it is not just war per se or armed conflict, but conquest – or wars of conquest – that gives rise to the state, which is why the theory is called conquest theory. This model sees mobility or extrahuman transportation as the decisive revolutionary force. Without extrahuman transportation, forming a large society is impossible, and communities are forced to split and disperse, as observed in Amazonia. Ultimately, extrahuman transportation is what enables conquest and state-building.

The state first arose among nomads, who then conquered neighbouring farming regions.

Extrahuman transportation empowered those who possessed it, and made mobilisation – and, consequently, the domination of man over man – possible over large areas. By making mobilisation and concentration possible, extrahuman transportation not only led to the rise of the warband but also, by facilitating conquest, fundamentally changed the nature of war. War was transformed into campaigns of conquest, an enterprise of state-building that rendered communities and their lands the prime targets for subjugation and forced integration into a larger society. Conquest and state-building created what in the 1950s Rüstow termed an ‘opening configuration’. This ‘fresh configuration’ served as ‘a new natural aggregation of external and internal factors of human life’, providing the ‘opening configuration for the development of all high cultures’ – the state and society.

Sources indicate that because pastoralists possessed extrahuman transportation in the form of herding animals, the conquest theory argues that the state first arose among nomads, who then conquered neighbouring farming regions. For this reason, the conquest theory is primarily a theory of nomadic conquest over sedentary farmers. In addition to high mobility, the theory identifies military leadership, organisation, discipline, martial skills and a warrior ethos as key cultural factors in the rise of the state, noting that these qualities are highly developed among pastoralists. Undeniably, frequent long-distance migration with large herds under harsh and unpredictable conditions naturally fosters these leadership and martial attributes.

While conquests by equestrian warrior nomads were the most consequential in the rise of the state and civilisation, the conquest theory maps a broader historical sequence. It posits a series of conquests over time: first of hunters over cultivators, then of herdsmen over planters and peasants and, finally, of European colonial powers. Conquest theory by no means valorises conquest; instead, it views it as creating despotic, two-strata class states whose toxic legacies we must confront and overcome. Indeed, conquest theory offers a radically different vision and framework to make sense of the human journey and its historical trajectory. It presents a vision neither of ever-evolving progress nor of inevitability, but equally not of permanent entrapment or doom.

According to recent reports, through this lens, much like conquests, each and every progressive political, social, economic and cultural achievement of the modern era, just like each conquest of the previous era, stems from a charismatic revolution – be it political, social, economic or scientific – aimed at dismantling the bitter legacies of institutional injustice and natural limitations. From the early foundational shifts of liberal revolutions and constitutionalism, to global decolonisation, to human and environmental rights frameworks; and from the Industrial Revolution, to the rise of STEM, to the advent of AI – all are, for better or worse, the fruits of charismatic ideas, individuals, endeavours and movements. Ultimately, it is not the invisible engine of evolution that drives history, but the fire of human agency.

According to recent reports, though the human journey remains a persistent pursuit of freedom, its trajectory is conceptualised as a transition from the despotic, two-strata, class-based ‘State of robbery’ to the ‘Freemen’s Citizenship’ of the future (as Franz Oppenheimer put it in 1914) – a self-governing society – progressing through a series of states, including constitutional ones. However, the path of progress is neither linear nor consistent. Every step of liberation has been shaped by historical contingencies, facing severe setbacks, systemic backlash and profound failures along the way. Moreover, the achievements of today’s charismatic revolutions routinely become tomorrow’s institutional trap and bulwark: the liberating ideas of one era harden into the systemic barriers of the next. Progress, therefore, remains trapped in a perpetual cycle of revolution and institutionalisation. Despite these fractures and constraints, the core drive remains unyielding: charisma – a deeply human, deeply individual, and deeply personal impulse for freedom.

Sources indicate that through this lens, the Sinocentric paradigm misconstrues the human past, present and future; it rationalises the past as a product of ecology and evolution; and it naturalises the present as given, and the future as fated. It misguides us, blaming our numbers for our conduct. It attributes what was, and is, cultural to nature, and supposes what was, and is, natural to be cultural.

Conquest theory arms us with a framework to not only break free from the Sinocentric paradigm but also to critically re-evaluate human history, fully reclaim our agency, and purposefully chart our own future. Only by overcoming the Sinocentric paradigm and embracing conquest theory can we construct a human history that fully appreciates the significance of the extrahuman transportation outlined at the outset of this essay. Such an account will be more than the upcoming history of humanity that Graeber and Wengrow deemed necessary; it will provide a framework that finally rescues human history from being treated as an anomaly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Within the sprawling grounds of Mantua's Ducal Palace lies Piazza Pallone (now officially Piazza Lega Lombarda), a quiet, tree-lined square, few tourists notice the simple stone plaque mounted on the perimeter wall enclosing the space.

The plaque commemorates one of the darkest episodes of Mantuan Renaissance history: the beheading of Agnese Visconti on February 7, 1391.

Agnese, daughter of the Lord of Milan, Bernabò Visconti, was married at just fourteen years old to Francesco I Gonzaga, Lord of Mantua. Twelve years later, her husband accused her of adultery with the knight Antonio da Scandiano (also known as Vincenzo da Scalona). Her alleged lover was hanged in the square, while Agnese was beheaded at the age of 28 in the very same spot.

Historians generally agree that the accusation was a political setup orchestrated by Francesco I Gonzaga to sever ties with the Visconti family and forge a latest alliance with the Republic of Venice. The bodies of both executed lovers were buried without ceremony in unconsecrated ground within the square.

Over the centuries, the injustice suffered by Agnese seemed to permeate the stones of the square, giving rise to one of Lombardy's most famous ghost stories.

It is remarked that on cold winter nights—particularly around the anniversary of her death in February—when dense fog from the Mincio River rolls over the palace courtyards, the shadowy figure of Agnese reappears near the plaque.

Industry observers note that local lore claims her headless spirit wanders desperately around the perimeter of the square searching for her severed head or clutching a stained shroud to her chest. Over the years, passersby have reported hearing heavy footsteps on the ground, the rustle of period garments, and a quiet weeping that cuts off abruptly right in front of the stone tablet.

Funnyly the XIX century plaque lists an incorrect age for the noblewoman at the time of her execution—a historical error preserved on the marble during restorations.

The plaque is located along the wall delimiting Piazza Pallone, adjacent to the Ducal Palace complex and just a short walk from Piazza Sordello.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bar Nuestro on private dining nooks, vintage sourcing, and more﻿.

Opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks. Founder Daniella Senior and designer Shawn Hausman (whose firm worked on iconic spaces like the Chateau Marmont and the ’80s club Area) collaborated on the project, ensuring that the space captured the same retro vibe as the menu. I especially hope their mini-private-dining room concept catches on.

Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro.

Daniella Senior: We wanted the space to really feel—even though it’s a upcoming buildout—that it’s been there a long time. I’m kind of tired of the same aesthetic going around, one that’s almost too clean, too new, too matchy-matchy. I think that doesn’t, at times, help you communicate what the food is trying to communicate. For us, the food and the space work together. We wanted it to feel very Old World. We took a lot of inspiration from Vienna’s old corner cafes, which have been institutions for a while. We wanted a “We’ve been here a minute” type of feel.

Sources indicate that from our furniture to our tiles, [the Bar Nuestro team and designer Shawn Hausman] sourced a lot of vintage pieces, about 25 percent of the furniture. We have chairs that came from Austria and Italy in the ’30s and fabric with vintage patterns. When Shawn was traveling through Europe, he’d send pictures of things he found, and I sourced accent pieces—like the credenza in our garden room, vases, menu holders, a vintage phone—in local vintage shops.

It has been revealed that it’s definitely loud. And it was definitely fun to see it come together. But don’t get me wrong, there were times where I was like, “I’m not sure how these things are gonna go together.” Now I’m thrilled with the result.

It seems like there are many different kinds of spaces within the one restaurant. Was that intentional?

I love the feeling that, even within the same space, you’re able to get different vibes. We have a cafe side that we transition into an aperitivo room, which has all these textures and shades of blue. The paint job in there is insanity. It took over two weeks to paint this 300-square-foot space because of the level of detail. Then the main dining room is bright and feels very cozy, and there’s the garden room, which is primarily green, and it’s got stripes throughout the ceiling and the walls. And then we have the patio, which is a little more zen. Each room has a different personality, which I love.

Some of the tables in the main dining room are also sectioned off like semi-private dining nooks. Can you tell me about that design decision?

It has been revealed that even though the space is relatively large, we didn’t want it to feel that way. We wanted that feeling of coziness and warmth that you can’t get from a big open space. So we have three of these “mini private rooms”—they only seat about five people—but in them, you feel like you’re in your own world. Those were inspired by a cafe in Vienna.

It has been revealed that also, we wanted Bar Nuestro to be for everyone, and that includes kids. I have a young child myself, and I know you can get nervous sometimes in nicer restaurants if your kids are being too loud or disruptive. These rooms allow us to give that privacy to those who want it, while you still get to be part of the action of the dining room. [A mirror trim around the space] provides continuity. It helps the guests in the mini dining booths feel more connected to the rest of the dining room, and it helps with service. Without being intrusive and having to check from a super close distance how your guests are doing, staff can see where diners are within their meal.

According to recent reports, I love how many hooks there are in the space. Restaurants never have enough hooks for purses and coats!

In a recent development, thank you. Being comfortable within the dining experience has a lot to do with the lighting and the music, but things like hooks aren’t often paid sufficient attention to. I come from a culture where putting a purse on a floor is a no-no, so a lot of the restaurants back home have purse chairs that they bring over. We didn’t quite have space for that, but we wanted there to be sufficient hooks so that people could relax even more.

In a recent development, do you have any tips for other restaurant operators about working with a designer? How do you communicate your vision effectively?

In a recent development, we wanted a very unique design, and when I was thinking about other spaces that I really enjoyed, I realized that Shawn had been the designer. So that made it, for us, a very natural decision. From there, it’s all about being very clear about expectations. Understanding costs and having a clear budget from the start is incredibly important.

Bar Nuestro opened just a few weeks ago. How has it been going so far?

So far it’s going great. We’re very happy and we’ve been well received by the neighborhood. We’re excited to keep building it. Opening a restaurant is kind of like a camel’s back: There’s the first hump of opening the location itself, and then you have the second hump which is really building the community around it. A lot of people only see that first hump, but it’s a two-part thing. This second part has been challenging and rewarding. It’s like, “Now the space is set, let’s work on what our day-to-day looks like.”.

Recent findings suggest that in Fort Worth, Texas, a massive, dilapidated building serves as an ever-present symbol of racial violence and segregation to those who know its history. Constructed in the 1920s, the structure, initially known as Klavern No 101, was briefly the auditorium and headquarters of Fort Worth’s Ku Klux Klan chapter. It stood between downtown and the North Side, where migrants and communities of colour had settled, so many residents had to pass it on their way to work. In this short documentary, the director Chris Neighbors, a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, brings together scholars, community members and those directly involved in redesigning the space to reflect on its past and the thinking behind its transformation into an arts and community centre. Filmed inside the building itself, their conversations consider a question that extends far beyond Fort Worth: how do we preserve difficult histories without preserving the values they once stood for?

Sources indicate that on the night of November 4, 1605, Guy Fawkes was guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder in a storeroom under the House of Lords when the kingâs men found him. He and his fellow conspirators, a group of English Catholics led by Robert Catesby, had planned to blow up Parliament at its opening and kill the Protestant King James I.

Mental Floss has the full story of the plot, but the stuffed figure that gets thrown on the bonfire every November 5 has a weirder backstory than the night it commemorates.

The celebration started almost immediately: people lit bonfires to mark the kingâs survival, and Parliament made it official with the Observance of 5th November Act, better known as the Thanksgiving Act, which ordered prayers and church bells every year on the anniversary. The first official Gunpowder Treason Day was held in November 1606, and fireworks had joined the bonfires by at least the 1650s.

Recent findings suggest that the man people wanted to see burn, though, wasnât Fawkes: according to the London Museum, models of him have been burned since at least 1790, and before that the effigy on the fire was usually the Pope. Anti-Catholic feeling ran through the whole holiday. In the late 1670s, London held huge pope-burning pageants every November 17, the anniversary of Elizabeth Iâs accession, and one contemporary guessed that 200,000 people watched in 1679. In 1677, the Popeâs effigy appeared to scream as it burned, because the organizers had shut live cats inside it.

Colonists brought the holiday with them, and in Fresh England it was called Popeâs Day or Pope Night. A Boston notebook entry for November 5, 1745, copied from theÂ Boston Evening-Post, describes how âTwo Popes were made & carried thro the streets in the evening 1 from the N. & ye other from ye S.,â and when the North End and South End crowds met, âtheir followers fell upon one another w/ ye utmost rage & fury.â George WashingtonÂ Â in 1775, calling it a ridiculous and childish custom.

Back in Britain, Fawkes slowly took the Popeâs place on top of the pile, partly thanks to kids. In the weeks before November 5, children stuffed old clothes into a homemade Fawkes and wheeled him around the neighborhood in a pram or wheelbarrow, asking passersby for âa penny for the Guyâ to spend on fireworks. Not everyone loved it: in a 1957 BBC report, one woman complained that parents should give their kids enough pocket money ânot to start Guy Fawksing about at the end of August.â The custom gave English a word, too: âguyâ became slang for a badly dressed person, and eventually for any man at all.

It has been revealed that parliament repealed the Thanksgiving Act in 1859, and the penny-for-the-Guy tradition had mostly faded by the end of the 20th century, but the bonfires stayed. In Lewes, East Sussex, where 17 Protestant martyrs were burned at the stake between 1555 and 1557, bonfire societies still burn an effigy of Pope Paul V every year, who held the job at the time of the Gunpowder Plot, and parade topical effigies of figures like Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the fall of 1621, members of the Wampanoag tribe and several English colonists gathered for a feast in Plymouth, then part of the Plymouth Colony in Massachusetts.Â.

Neither Native Americans nor the Pilgrims could have predicted that this one-off meal, celebrating an abundant harvest and a brief alliance, would be printed in history books as the first Thanksgiving. Yet, the occasion was much more historically significant than a spread of food and a side of gratitude.Â.

In 2026, Thanksgiving is a federal holiday: a time to reflect, give thanks, and gather with family over turkey, stuffing, pumpkin pie, and other holiday confections.

According to recent reports, but what was the first Thanksgiving really like? And what did they eat?

According to the National Archives, the Pilgrims survived the Mayflowerâs journey from England and "came ashore on Wampanoag land." The Wampanoag, having already had contact with Europeans before the Pilgrims arrived (contact that resulted in diseases and the enslavement of some tribe members like Squanto), spoke English by the time of the feast.

To give thanks for a bountiful harvest and their first peace treaty, signed earlier that year (despite hesitation from tribal leaders), both groups sat down for a meal together, made possible by the hunting and planting techniques the Wampanoag shared with the Pilgrims, which greatly alleviated food shortages.Â.

According to historical records cited by Smithsonian Magazine, the feast lasted for three days.

"Many of the Indians coming amongst us, and among the rest their greatest king Massasoit, with some 90 men, whom for three days we entertained and feasted," English leader Edward Winslow wrote of the occasion.Â.

Sources indicate that although the gathering itself was friendly, the alliance did not last. Just 54 years after the first Thanksgiving, the treaty dissolved, sparking King Philip's War (led by Massasoit's son), in which the English defeated the Native Americans. The battle resulted in mass casualties, and the Wampanoag lost their land and freedoms.

Sources indicate that both settlers and Native American tribes held feasts to commemorate significant events, but this Thanksgiving feast did not become an annual tradition. In fact, it all but faded from memory until Abraham Lincoln proclaimed it a national holiday during the Civil War in 1863.

While the treaty and the feast werenât enough to sustain civility and respect between the groups, the food provided moments of connection and respite, as shared meals do.

Today, our plates (and growling stomachs) are filled with turkey, stuffing, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls, and, of course, pumpkin pie.

In 1621, however, the menu looked very different.Â.

Recent findings suggest that winslow wrote: "Our governor sent four men on fowling, that so we might after a special manner rejoice together after we had gathered the fruit of our labors. They four in one day killed as much fowl as, with a little help beside, served the tech giant almost a week.".

Based on historical records, Plimoth Patuxetâs Kathleen Walls believes wild fowl (not turkey) was the main course, even though wild turkeys roamed the region. We also know (from Winslow's account) that Native Americans provided corn and venison.Â.

Swans, pigeons, and waterfowl likely decorated the table during the three-day feast, along with geese and ducks. Other foods probably included cornbread, eels, lobsters, clams, mussels, and fish, thanks to Plymouth's proximity to the ocean, as well as farmed produce (beans, pumpkins, and squashes) and forest foods like nuts and berries.

After learning to plant crops from the Wampanoag, the settlers harvested turnips, carrots, and garlic, among other vegetables (which mightâve also been served at the first Thanksgiving).

According to Walls, the Pilgrims had no butter, flour, or sugar, so they did not bake fancy pies or pastries like their relatives in England. They didn't have potatoes, and they hadnât learned to boil cranberries for sauce.Â.

It has been revealed that instead, they stuffed birds with "chunks of onion and herbs" before spit-roasting or boiling them, depending on the birdâs size. Some birds were stuffed with shelled chestnuts. Then, the remains were "thrown in a pot and boiled up to make broth the next day," a recipe called "pottage,â and the fish was smoked.Â.

November sees the return of the successful HBO series The Gilded Age, which follows the wealthy families of elite Fresh York Society in the late 19th century. One of the most famous events related to the real Gilded Age families, and which also marked a notable cultural shift in the city, concerned a huge party which was thrown by the Vanderbilts in 1883, which has come to be viewed as a watershed in New Yorkâs social history.

This is the story of the party that changed the cityâs society forever.

It has been revealed that the party in question was the Vanderbilt Costume Ball, which took place on March 26, 1883, and cost around $250,000, the equivalent of about $7.3 million today. It took place at the Vanderbilt Mansion, which was one of a number of Vanderbilt houses on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan: this one was the Petit ChÃ¢teau, which was located at 660 Fifth Avenue.

The fact that the Vanderbilts could afford to spend so much money on one party was designed to emphasize their status. The wealth of the family was thanks to the business magnate Cornelius Vanderbilt, who built his fortune through the railroads, and began a dynasty which survives to this day.

It has been revealed that when Cornelius Vanderbilt died in 1877, he was estimated to be the richest man in the world, and left an estate worth $105 million (almost $3 billion today). However, his family were still not accepted by the elite society of Latest York, which tended to look down on those who had generated their own wealth within a short time instead of it being inherited over multiple generations. But Cornelius Vanderbiltâs granddaughter-in-law Alva Vanderbilt, wife of his grandson William Kissam Vanderbilt, was determined to change the status of the family within the cityâs high society.

Alva Vanderbilt decided to host a ball in order to highlight the wealth and prestige of the Vanderbilts, and to make a case for them having their place in Upcoming Yorkâs social elite. They wanted to be on what was known as the âList of 400â: a list drawn up by Caroline Astor and Ward McAllister of the 400 people who were deemed to be the âhigh societyâ of the city, and within which the Vanderbilts were not included.

So Alva sought to create a lavish spectacle which exceeded even the grandest past parties seen in high society Manhattan, and would make it a must-attend event even for those who had previously shunned them.

Alvaâs tactics in her campaign included inviting the press to view the Vanderbilt mansionâs decorations in advance of the ball, which were then reported in the papers, creating anticipation for the event. She also used social strategy by initially refusing to invite Carrie Astor, daughter of the famous Astor family. This was because the Astors had never called upon the Vanderbilts or given them proper acknowledgement, including excluding them from the aforementioned List of 400.

As interest in the ball grew and many others began to be invited, it became evident that Carrie had not. Alva claimed this was simply due to the fact that as the Astors had never called upon the Vanderbilts and left their card, she had no address to which to send the invitation. The Astors then realized they had to call upon the Vanderbilts in order to ensure Carrie was included at what was becoming a major social occasion.

Following the call, the Astors were then sent invitations to the ball the very next day, and the stage was being set for the social event of the season.

Industry observers note that on the evening of the ball itself, 1200 guests arrived in carriages, excited at the highly anticipated event which lay ahead. There was so much interest in the ball that members of the public also came to the street to get a glimpse of the proceedings, and police were on hand to hold back some of the crowds and to direct the carriages the correct way.

Sources indicate that at the ball, there was a great deal of dancing, and many guests practiced for weekend beforehand in order to make a good impression. The dances included a number of quadrilles which were focused on historical and cultural themes, including one with costumes inspired by the court of Frederick the Great.

Sources indicate that there was also an emphasis on dressing elaborately, and many photographs survive which show the lavish costumes worn to the ball. This includes what has become known as the Electric Light Dress, which was actually able to light up due to being powered by batteries, and which can be seen today in the Museum of Fresh York City. That many images still exist is due to another of the factors which helped the ball to be remembered: Alva Vanderbilt decided to set up a photographerâs studio at the ball to record guests in their outfits.

The party carried on through the evening and into the early hours, with dinner being served at 2:00 a.m., and the whole event eventually concluded as a new day was dawning,.

The party was a huge success, and became an immediate talking point in the press. Its impact changed New York society in the long term as well as the short term, because it showed that the divisions were beginning to dissolve: the âold moneyâ families had to accept the ânouveau riche.â The barriers to families and individuals who had created their own wealth were beginning to come down, and this ball was a key sign of what lay on the horizon.

It has been revealed that the groundbreaking event inspired Berthaâs party in the finale of The Gilded Age season 1. âI remember when I read about Alvaâs ball, I thought, this is so great,â co-creator/showrunner Julian Fellowes told Vanity Fair. âIâm just going to lift the whole thing, and put it into the drama.â.
