📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you might know bits and pieces about the U.K. holiday on the 5th of November, the slightly ominous mask, and the political activist group Anonymous, but have you ever wondered how they're all connected? It all goes back to a 17th-century man named Guy Fawkes.

In a recent development, asking why Fawkes is associated with the black-and-white mask worn by rebels and activists worldwide is a bit ironic. That's because the mask is Fawkes's face, or at least a stylized version of him. A better question is: how did his face become a modern symbol for people fighting against tyranny? Fawkes might have faded into obscurity if not for the media depictions of him, and political groups took those depictions and ran with them.

It has been revealed that guy Fawkes was an English Roman Catholic who wanted the Protestant oppression of his people to stop. Though he is the most famous participant in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, the attempt to blow up Parliament, he was far from the mastermind. Of all the men who were behind the plot to kill the Protestant leaders of England to make way for a Catholic ruler, Fawkes was a bit of a last-minute addition.

The Gunpowder Plotters needed someone who wouldn't be recognized easily while rigging the gunpowder in a cellar underneath the Parliament building. Fawkes was chosen because he had been in the Netherlands as a soldier fighting for Spain. On November 5, 1605, he was caught and arrested before he could fulfill the proposal, and was tortured until he gave up the names of his co-conspirators. He died a few months later, on January 27, 1606, after jumping or falling from the execution platform he was meant to die on and breaking his neck.

Celebrating a failed assassination attempt sounds strange, but the English government decided to create a holiday out of the unsuccessful Gunpowder Plot. This was partly to warn anyone against similar aims, but also to rub it in the Catholics' faces. Catholics actually faced even more persecution after Fawkes and his crew's ill-fated attempt.

According to recent reports, to celebrate the 5th of November, Guy Fawkes Day, or Bonfire Night, the English would light bonfires and fireworks. They also made effigies of Guy Fawkes to burn in the bonfires. Fawkes became a well-known villain through the centuries of commemorating his failure, and while not as popular today, the holiday is still celebrated.

Sources indicate that the story of Guy Fawkes and the Gunpowder Plot was spread through novels, poems, and other literature, but it wasn't until the 1980s that the infamous mask came into social consciousness. That was when Alan Moore and David Lloyd created the graphic novel, V for Vendetta. The main character, V, wears a mask of Guy Fawkes's face to both maintain anonymity and link his anti-fascist mission with that of the Gunpowder Plot. He sees Fawkes as someone worthy of emulation, not being afraid to use violence to make changes to government and politics.

When the film adaptation of V for Vendetta came out in 2005, Warner Bros. gave out replica masks as part of its marketing campaign. Inspired by V in the film, people would wear the masks to protest unjust laws and corrupt governments. In 2008, the activists of Anonymous chose this mask as a disguise and a representation of their group.

Anonymous, the collective of internet hackers who use their skills to protest governments, billionaires, and corporations globally, has never specifically remarked why they chose the Guy Fawkes mask, but many tie it back to a specific scene in the V for Vendetta film where a crowd of people in the masks marches to Britain's Parliament. Whatever the reason, Anonymous is now irrefutably linked to the mask, with people associating both the mask and the group with protests, and sometimes anarchy.

Industry observers note that with Anonymous's use of the Guy Fawkes mask, it has become a symbol of anti-establishment and anti-authoritarian rule. Fawkes went from villain to anti-hero, and the mask of his face ironically became the face of those who wished to remain hidden. Because when you need to commit acts of resistance, it's better to hide behind the face of a failed rebel than to reveal your identity and risk failure yourself.

Driving down the stretch of Route 66 that passes through Albuquerque, New Mexico, I found myself swathed in the glow of countless roadside neon signs that shone even brighter than the full moon overhead.

It has been revealed that route 66 has long occupied a unique space in the American imagination. Commissioned in 1926, the road stretches from Lake Michigan to Los Angeles and winds through thousands of miles of desert plains and mesas on its way to the Pacific coast. It became a thriving artery that brought business to countless rural communities, many of which set up motels, shops, and all manner of roadside attractions to capitalize on the flow of life moving across the highway.

But how did neon so popular on this famous road in the first place?

The answer is simple: before Google Maps and digital itineraries, neon gave drivers an easy way to find food, lodging, and more in the dark. Additionally, neonâs heyday coincided with Route 66âs, making them a match made in highway heaven.

It has been revealed that the first neon was created in the early 20th century by French engineer Georges Claude, and it made its way to the U.S. in the 1920s. Los Angeles car dealership owner Earler C. Anthony is thought to be the first U.S. business owner to use neonâhe ordered two signs reading âPackard.â 1924 saw the first neon sign go up in Times Square.

It has been revealed that from the 1930s to the 1950s, neon spread around the world and became an institution on Route 66. Many of the signs that went up along the road drew from local cultures, mythologies, and aspects of the regions they illuminatedâthunderbirds, saguaro cacti, rearing cowboys, and four-pointed Zia sun symbols from local Native American tribes among them.

Neon began to decline in the 1960s as the novelty around it started to wear off, concerns about lead rose, and LED lighting offered a safer and cheaper alternative. Sources indicate that the best way to see neon might be in a lowrider, a customized American car with a lowered body that became popular after World War II, largely among Mexican-American youth. I drove in one with Jessica Roybal, who explained sheâd started her career photographing women and children in lowrider communities before investing in her own vehicle.Â.

Neon signs gleamed above us like planets as the car's custom-made hydraulics jerked us up and down. Many of the people who originally drove on Route 66 knew they might never be coming home again, Roybal explained. Route 66, with all its neon lights and tantalizing invitations to mysterious desert haunts, I thought, must have looked even more hallucinatory back then, when it was truly a point of no return.

Yet ultimately, those bright signs were more strategic than artful, designed to draw people (and their wallets) into the small towns and businesses lining the highway. In that, they embodied the same purpose as the road itself, and even of America on the whole: a promise, a dream, a siren song in th desert night.

Sources indicate that above us, the moon waited, its light mixing with the neon. People nodded and smiled at our car. The windows were down and a warm November breeze blew through. On modern-day Route 66, life hummed on.

Recent findings suggest that earlier that day, weâd stopped at the historic Hacienda Motel, which is in the process of being converted to a food hall. Local businesses, many of them Hispanic-owned, would be invited to fill the rooms. The renovations had been painstakingly carried out around a tree that the ownerâs late father used to love, she told us. The tree soared above the little adobe buildings. Behind it, a carefully restored neon sign advertised a palm reader who no longer read the future there.Â.

Recent findings suggest that the future of America can seem unclear at times. No wonder we look, over and over again, to the past and its neon promises of linear growth and endless expansion. No wonder we find ourselves drawn to nostalgia for a world that perhaps never existed, but once seemed to at least promise that it could.

Somewhere in the distance, cranes flew among the clouds, and did not look forward or backward at all.

Industry observers note that millennials might like sending emojis and gifs, there was something about using a simpler screen or a far more complicated handset back in the day. Early 2000s flip phones might have had grayscale screens, shrill ringtones, and next to no battery life, but there was something about flipping a phone open to answer it that a swipe of a touchscreen just canât match. No wonder the tech world now seems to be nostalgically re-embracing the style more than 20 years later.Â.

Speaking comforting classics that you grew up with, one thing Millennials and Gen Z can seemingly agree on is that kids TV was far better back in the day than it is today. These two cohorts watch more repeats of classic childhood movies and TV favorites than any other generation.Â.

According to recent reports, when it comes to finding something entertaining to watch, Millennials are also near single-handedly keeping the substantial summer blockbuster alive. With a worrisome one in ten cinemagoers claiming that the summer movie experience has all but died out, Millennials are bucking that trend, with almost two-fifths proudly claiming the opposite and that the summer blockbuster is alive and well. (Perhaps growing up with The Matrix, The Mummy, The Sixth Sense and the first Star Wars prequel all released in the same summer might have something to do with it.)Â.

According to recent reports, on the subject of blockbusters, the big-budget movie experience at the moment is dominated by remakes and spinoffs, or else stories set in some pre-existing universe. Sequels and IP-mining are by no means new, of course, but with almost 40 films in the endless expanded MCU and Disney currently slating more remakes and sequels than original stories, it seems the standalone blockbusters of the 80s and 90s are a thing of the Millennial past.Â.

Case in point, 16 of the Top 20 highest-grossing movies of the 1990s were either stand-alone or entirely original movies, with only four spinoffs and sequels (Star Wars: Episode 1, The Lost World: Jurassic Park, Terminator 2 and Toy Story 2) listed alongside the likes of Armageddon, Ghost, Twister, and Independence Day.Â.

So far in the 2020s, the exact opposite is true, with only four of the current Top 20 (The Odyssey, Barbie, Michael and Oppenheimer) not belonging to an existing movie universe.Â.

The live-action remakes of Disney classics might be proving significant business, but for Millennialsâwho grew up on hand-drawn and painted classics like The Little Mermaid and Beauty and the Beastâthereâs really no comparison.Â.

Sources indicate that is it fair to say Millennials grew up at the best time for movie effects? Millennials had the best of both worlds in the 90s and early 2000s, with movies like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2 seamlessly blending practical effects with cutting-edge CGI, while others, like The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter movies, built stunning practical sets and used real-world locations to bring their universes to light. Modern substantial-budget extravaganzas that increasingly rely on green screen and LED backlots just donât seem to match up, and donât have quite the same immersive quality.Â.

If youâre a Millennial who fell deeply into the emo subculture of the early 2000s, then you might have heard your parents say that it was just a phase. Not so, it seems, as Millennials are still proudly holding on to the bands, artists, and music that defined them more than two decades ago and supporting their music still today.Â.

In a recent development, on the subject of music, though, Millennials have long been the driving force behind the recent resurgence in popularity of vinyl records, too, all but single-handedly steering the decades-old format through the choppy waters of the streaming era. Having brought LPs and record players back from the brink, however, more recent research is showing that Gen Z are catching up too and are jumping on the Millennial bandwagon as the biggest buyers of vinyl records in the mid 2020s.Â Â.

Curating a Spotify playlist just isnât the same as burning a bespoke CD or recording a uniquely compiled cassette tape, is it?Â.

Itâs not just vinyl and mixtapes, either. Millennials and Gen Z alike are increasingly expressing a preference for physical media of all typesâfrom CDs and DVDs to old-school gaming consoles and cartridge games. Turns out paying for streaming platforms that donât stream the movie you want to watch when you want to watch it (and can delete it even once youâve bought it) isnât the best business model.Â.

Industry observers note that the pandemic made board games fashionable again, leading to a resurgence of interest among Gen Z, but for Millennials they never went out of favor. Two-thirds of Millennials admit to being board game fanatics, with almost 40% claiming that they enjoy regular board games as a hobby.Â.

Not that Millennials only played dice-rolling games back in the day, of course. A pocketful of loose change was all you needed to have a good time when video game arcades were everywhereâalthough these too, it seems, are starting to enjoy a renaissance as the edge continues to wear off in the digital age.

In an era when you can make a note of absolutely anything on your phone, thereâs a growing trend among Millennials and Gen Zs for re-embracing pen and paper. As well as giving the opportunity for some much-needed time away from a screen, thereâs something satisfyingly tactile in making a to-do list by hand and scratching each job off as you do it.Â.

Speaking of things that used to be simpler back in the day, it used to be the case that if you needed, say, a new program for your computer, you would buy it, install it, and it would be yours in perpetuity. Nowadays, everything is a subscription serviceâso that one-off fee has been switched to a steady and increasingly infuriating drip-feed of monthly payments and constant downloadable upgrades.

Recent findings suggest that from the âGen Z stareâ to the rumbling debate over whether or not you can take an iced coffee into a job interview, much has been noted in recent years of the different social mores of Millennials versus Gen Z and beyond. With Boomers now retired, and Gen X not far behind them, Millennials are becoming the elder statesmen and women of the workplaceâand in that capacity are steadfastly defending the professional etiquette of the past against an ever more relaxed and less demanding style of professionalism thatâs emerging among the generations behind.Â.

Recent findings suggest that use a search engine today, and chances are youâll be shown an AI-curated overview of the search results, rather than the results themselves. Scroll a social media feed, and youâll likely end up wading through a morass of AI slop. Try to order something online, and you might get an AI chatbot asking you what youâre looking for and if thereâs anything they can do to help (if it hasnât already made things worse). Things really were better, easier, and more human back in the day.Â.

It has been revealed that on the topic of the early internet, itâs easy to forget that influencer culture is a relatively recent phenomenon, and there was a time in the not-too-distant past when people did not live their every moment online, and we were all largely anonymous. Sure, there were Facebook pages and MySpace profiles, but people typically kept themselves to themselves and used them to expand on real-life, in-person friendships and relationships, rather than build latest parasocial ones with strangers.Â.

There was a time when your downtime was genuine downtimeânot time spent still scrolling feeds, watching shorts, and digesting headlines. And whatâs more, Millennials seem to be figuring that out, with studies showing more and more Millennials are switching off when they really donât need to be online.Â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are 366 possible days to have your birthday (including Leap Year), and you probably think the best of those days is your own birthday. But how many other people feel the same way about that particular day? It might depend on just how popularâor unpopularâyour birthday is.

Timing can be a significant factor when comparing the length of a typical pregnancy to birthdays while holidays are more likely to be avoided by parents, especially by those who may need to schedule a labor induction or caesarean section.

It has been revealed that so are you likely to share a birthday with a large population of other people, or have little competition for a celebration? Check out analysis based on data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), as reported by Visual Capitalist, to see where your birthday lands.

A pregnancy usually lasts nine months, and September is the ninth month of the year. Coincidence? Maybe. But there are theories about how the two coincide.

Late December is a time of merriment and time off from jobs or school for many couples, providing extra relaxation and celebration time. There are other theories that sperm is more potent in colder months than warmer months, and less sunlight can affect hormones.

Whatever the case, it's causing a baby boom in September.

The most popular birthday is September 9, followed by September 20, September 19, and September 14. Of the top 10 most popular birthdays, only two are not in September: fifth-place July 7 and sixth-place December 28.

Sources indicate that in fact, from September 8 to September 27, only one birthday doesnât make the top 30 most popular list. September 11 is ranked 98th.

The other side of the rankings are dominated by holidays, with parents likely trying to avoid having their babies born on a date when other festivities would overwhelm their children's special days.

But before the holidays is the rarest birthday, which is also the rarest day. February 29, Leap Day, is the least celebrated birthday. The data from the NCHS that looked at birthdays from 1989 to 2024 found that almost every day occurred every year in those years, except February 29. During that stretch of years, Leap Day only occurred nine times.

The rest of the top 10 of rarest birthdays, however, has a day celebrated each year, and it usually is earmarked for another celebration already. The second-least popular birthday is December 25, Christmas. It's followed by January 1, December 24, July 4, and January 2 as the least celebrated birthdays.

It has been revealed that the top 10 least popular birthdays also have three days at the end of November, with the end of that month being quite unpopular for parents. No birthday from November 22 to November 29 makes it above 300 in the ranking of popularity. While Thanksgiving in the United States doesn't have a set date, landing on the fourth Thursday of the month, it still has enough of an effect to limit the number of birthdays during that time.

Triskaidekaphobia, or fear of the number 13, also has an effect on birthday popularity.

The date is skipped by parents each month enough that a trend emerges. Several months have their lowest birthday rank on the 13th of that month, including March, June, and August.

Recent findings suggest that other months have the 13th ranked as the second-least popular birthday, and there's usually a holiday standing in its way. April 13, for example, comes in second behind April Fool's Day on April 1 as the least popular birthday that month. October 13 is beaten only by Halloween that month. May 13 is the second-least popular birthday behind May 27. The 13th barely beats out other dates at the end of May when the floating Memorial Day holiday is celebrated.

February 13 is unique as the second-least popular birthday for that month if only because of Leap Day. In non-leap years, when there is no February 29 on the calendar, it would be the least popular birthday for that month.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spring of 1860, the Democratic Party went to its national convention and came out of it as two parties.
  • Industry observers note that the presidential election that followed had four serious candidates, two of them Democrats, and it was really two separate races, one in the North and one in the South.
  • The Democrats met in Charleston, South Carolina, on April 23, 1860, and the fight was over slavery in the western territories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spring of 1860, the Democratic Party went to its national convention and came out of it as two parties.

Industry observers note that the presidential election that followed had four serious candidates, two of them Democrats, and it was really two separate races, one in the North and one in the South. Abraham Lincoln won it with 39.8 percent of the popular vote.

The Democrats met in Charleston, South Carolina, on April 23, 1860, and the fight was over slavery in the western territories. Southern delegates wanted the platform to endorse a federal slave code; Stephen Douglas, the Illinois senator who had beaten Lincoln for a Senate seat two years earlier, knew that would cost him every Northern state. When the plank failed, about 50 Southern delegates, led by Alabamaâs William L. Yancey, walked out. Nobody could reach the two-thirds majority the party required, and after 57 ballots the convention gave up and agreed to try again in Baltimore. Mental Floss has written about that floor fight before.

Baltimore went worse. In June, after another brawl over which delegates to seat, the convention nominated Douglas, and the bolters held a convention of their own and nominated the sitting vice president, John C. Breckinridge of Kentucky, on a pro-slavery platform. So the party ran two tickets.

According to recent reports, the fourth candidate came from a brand-newly introduced party. On May 9, a group of mostly former Whigs met in Baltimore, formed the Constitutional Union Party, and nominated John Bell of Tennessee, a former House speaker and war secretary, with Harvardâs onetime president Edward Everett as his running mate. They declined to write a real platform, saying they recognized no political principle other than the Constitution and the Union. Bellâs supporters rang bells at their rallies.

The campaign itself was lopsided: Lincoln stayed home in Springfield, as nominees traditionally did, Breckinridge gave one speech, and Bell noted nothing. Douglas broke with tradition and stumped across the country, Deep South included, and spent much of that time answering questions about what would happen if Lincoln won.

In a recent development, in practice, the country held two contests: Lincoln wasnât even on the ballot in 10 Southern states, where the race was Breckinridge against Bell, while in the North it was Lincoln against Douglas. Anti-Lincoln forces tried to fuse their electoral tickets in Upcoming York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and New Jersey, and it only worked in New Jersey, where Lincoln still took four of the seven electors.

It has been revealed that the final numbers were all over the place. Lincoln got 1,867,198 votes and 180 electoral votes, well past the 152 he needed. Douglas finished second in the popular vote, with 29.4 percent, and dead last in the Electoral College, with 12 electoral votes: all of Missouri plus Upcoming Jerseyâs other three. Breckinridge won 11 slave states and 72 electoral votes, and Bell took Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee for 39.

The split didnât even decide it: Lincoln won outright majorities in 15 states worth 169 electoral votes, so even if every Douglas, Breckinridge, and Bell voter had backed a single candidate, that candidate would have had about 60 percent of the popular vote and still lost the Electoral College, 169 to 134. Lincolnâs votes were concentrated in the populous North, and that was enough. South Carolina seceded on December 20, before heâd even taken office.

Breaking: What Thanksgiving Dinner Cost in the 1970s Compared to Today

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Mentalfloss

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Everybody has been feeling the effects of inflation for the last few years, but how does it impact the holiday dinner table?
  • In November 1975, turkey in retail stores averaged 77.4 cents a pound, according to BLS figures reprinted in the USDA's Poultry and Egg Situation.
  • In the Farm Bureau's 2025 survey, a 16-pound frozen turkey averaged $21.50, or $1.34 a pound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everybody has been feeling the effects of inflation for the last few years, but how does it impact the holiday dinner table? Back in the 1970s, nobody was tallying the national cost of Thanksgiving dinner: the best-known yardstick, the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual survey of a classic feast for 10 people, didn't start until 1986, so the tidy 1970s totals that turn up online are after-the-fact estimates. What the decade did leave behind is a paper trail of actual store prices, collected by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and reprinted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and it says the centerpiece of the meal was a serious expense.

In November 1975, turkey in retail stores averaged 77.4 cents a pound, according to BLS figures reprinted in the USDA's Poultry and Egg Situation. A 16-pound bird, the size the Farm Bureau uses, came to about $12.38, which, adjusted for inflation with the Consumer Price Index, is roughly $72.58 in November 2025 dollars. Two years earlier, after grocery prices jumped about 21% in a single year, turkey averaged 89.6 cents a pound, which puts a 16-pounder at about $101 today.

In the Farm Bureau's 2025 survey, a 16-pound frozen turkey averaged $21.50, or $1.34 a pound. The two figures aren't collected the same way: the Farm Bureau's volunteer shoppers spend the first week of November hunting for the best price they can find without coupons, while the BLS averaged what stores actually charged.

Industry observers note that work time tells the same story. In November 1975, production and nonsupervisory workers averaged $4.86 an hour, so that $12.38 turkey cost about two and a half hours of pay. In November 2025, the same workers averaged $31.85 an hour, and the Farm Bureau's $21.50 bird took about 40 minutes.

In a recent development, the Farm Bureau's menu also calls for a gallon of whole milk, and that was pricier, too. Retail fluid milk averaged 78.5 cents per half-gallon in 1975, according to the USDA's Dairy Situation, or about $1.57 a gallon. In today's dollars, thatâs around $9.46, against the $3.73 the Farm Bureau found for a gallon of whole milk in 2025.

Groceries in general got relatively cheaper over those 50 years: between November 1975 and November 2025, the Consumer Price Index for all items rose about 5.9 times, while the index for food eaten at home rose about five times.

Industry observers note that when the Farm Bureau finally priced the full meal in 1986, it came to $28.74 for 10 people, which works out to about $84 in November 2025 dollars. The 2025 version cost $55.18, or about $5.52 a person, down 5% from 2024 and well below the record $64.05 of 2022. The turkey alone was 39% of that bill, and it was still a better deal than the one your parents got.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are more females than males in the United States, but it's close.

In a recent development, an estimated 168 million males and 174 million females lived in the U.S. in 2025, according to estimates from the United States Census Bureau. That makes around 49% of the population male, with the additional 51% identifying as female.

Recent findings suggest that but that balance varies by state, with more men living in some states while women dominate others. So which states top the list for men and which ones have more women?

According to recent reports, bundle up if you want to live in a state with more men, starting all the way north in Alaska. The state easily leads the nation with a ratio of 110.6 men for every 100 women, according to U.S. Census Bureau data. The ratio is a little more even in Alaskan urban areas like Anchorage or Juneau, with the western part of the state skewing results. Western Alaska is home to male-dominated industries, including fishing and oil, that push the ratio so high for men.

In fact, second-place North Dakota has a ratio of 105.1 males per 100 females. Like Alaska, a local oil boom drew more men to the state to work in the male-dominated field, shifting its overall gender ratio.

Industry observers note that if you're looking for areas where women outnumber men, look to the South, starting with the District of Columbia, which has a ratio of just 90.6 males for every 100 females. Census Bureau data suggests this gap is partly driven by college-educated women moving to D.C. in higher numbers than college-educated men.

It has been revealed that this female-heavy imbalance isn't limited to D.C., though. In fact, it's found in several East Coast states. Delaware, for example, takes second place in the U.S. with a ratio of 93.9 males to 100 females. Maryland also makes the list in fifth place with 94.8.

According to recent reports, another place with an imbalance is the South. Third-place Mississippi has a ratio of 94.2 males to females, while fourth-place Alabama has a ratio of 94.4 males to 100 females. Women tend to live longer than men, with an average life expectancy of 84.1 years compared to 80.3 years for men, according to data from the Yale School of Public Health. That gap is wider in some Southern states, such as Mississippi, which could contribute to the lower ratio of males to females in those states. In Mississippi, for example, life expectancy for women is 76.6 years compared to 71.8 years for men.

The five states that have the highest ratio of females to males, according to data from the U.S. Census Bureau, include:.

While some states have a larger ratio of males or females, not every state has that type of imbalance.

The Midwest has two states, Minnesota and Wisconsin, that barely have more males than females. Minnesota has 100.4 males per 100 females, while Wisconsin has 100.3 males per 100 females, making them the two states closest to parity with a slight male edge.

It has been revealed that on the flip side, West Virginia and California have near-parity with slightly larger female populations. Both have 99.8 males for every 100 women, making them just barely more female than male.

#165. Why Is Diwali Celebrated on Different Dates Every Year?

Why Is Diwali Celebrated on Different Dates Every Year?

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mentalfloss

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friday, November 6 marks the first day of this yearâs five-day celebration of Diwali, with the most important day taking place on Sunday, November 8 2026.
  • It has been revealed that while this yearâs festival takes place in November, the date is not fixed and is sometimes in October.
  • Industry observers note that the name of Diwali originates from the Sanskrit word dipavali, which means a row of lights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friday, November 6 marks the first day of this yearâs five-day celebration of Diwali, with the most important day taking place on Sunday, November 8 2026. Diwali is known as the festival of lights, which involves the decoration of buildings with lamps and other forms of lighting, including candles in addition to more modern forms of illumination like fairy lights. It is an important celebration in Hinduism, as well as for the Sikh and Jain communities, and is sometimes described as a pan-Indian festival to signify its importance to people from multiple faiths.

It has been revealed that while this yearâs festival takes place in November, the date is not fixed and is sometimes in October. Here is a look at why the celebration of Diwali takes place on different dates each year.Â.

Industry observers note that the name of Diwali originates from the Sanskrit word dipavali, which means a row of lights. Diwali is one of a number of festivals notable to Hinduism which take place during this part of the year, including Durga Puja, Karwa Chauth, and Dussehra. It is symbolic for Hindus of the return of Lord Ram to his home after years in exile; for Sikhs, it marks the day in 1619 when the sixth Sikh Guru Hargobind Sahib gained his freedom; and for Jains, it celebrates the last Jain Tirthankara, Lord Mahavira, reaching the state of nirvana.

The date of Diwali changes because it follows the Hindu calendar, not the Gregorian western calendar. The Hindu calendar is known as the Panchanga and is an example of a lunisolar calendar. It is one of the most complex calendars, which integrates both solar and lunar time, in contrast to western calendars which are focused on solar days and years.

The most important day of Diwali is also known as Kartik Amavasya, which is a sacred day in the Hindu month of Kartik, the eight month of its calendar and one of the most sacred months.

As Diwali is intertwined with the movement of the lunar calendar, it naturally fluctuates on the Gregorian calendar used in the west.

Diwali also represents the ideals of good triumphing over evil, and knowledge over ignorance, symbolized by the lights which stand for the illumination brought by knowledge. The lamps guide the way through the darkness, both literally and figuratively. Diwali celebrations include dressing up and using face decorations including the ceremonial mark of tika on the forehead between the eyes. Fireworks are also a vivid element of the festivities.

The majority of the celebrations take place on the third day of Diwali, the darkest day of the month, and therefore the day when the lights will contrast most strongly with the darkness of the night sky.

As well as marking a major cultural event important to multiple religions, the way in which this festival takes place on different dates from year to year therefore also highlights the richness of the differing ways in which time is measured around the world.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The vampire got his name before the book did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In May 1897, London booksellers got their first copies of a yellow-covered novel by Bram Stoker, the business manager of the actor Henry Irving, and the title on the front was Dracula. For most of the seven years Stoker spent on it, the book had been called something else.

Mental Floss has noted before that the book was nearly The Un-Dead, and the documents Stoker left behind show just how close it came.

The vampire got his name before the book did. Stokerâs working notes, now at the Rosenbach in Philadelphia, originally call the villain âCount Wampyr.â In the summer of 1890, Stoker borrowed William Wilkinsonâs survey of Wallachia and Moldavia from the library in Whitby and copied out a footnote about the word âDracula,â and at some point he went back through his notes and crossed out âWampyrâ in favor of the new name. Mental Floss has the full Whitby story.

The bookâs title held out much longer. The Un-Dead appears in Stokerâs own handwriting in those notes, and itâs the handwritten title on his 529-page typescript, a heavily marked-up working copy that turned up in the United States around 1980. A collector who bought it in 1984 put it up at Christieâs in New York in April 2002, where it was expected to bring about Â£1 million and failed to meet its reserve.

The oddest document in the pile is Stokerâs publishing contract with Archibald Constable and Manufacturer. Stoker drafted it himself, and the final version is dated May 20, 1897, with his initials on pages dated as late as May 25. Its opening clause still describes him as the author of a work called The Un-Dead.

By then, though, his publisher was already selling Dracula. According to newspaper research by the scholar John Edgar Browning, Constable advertised the book under that name in The Athenaeum on May 8, 1897, and began running front-page ads in the Booksellersâ Review on May 13. So the title changed at least 12 days before Stoker signed a contract that didnât mention it, for a first edition of 3,000 copies at six shillings apiece.

Stoker hedged on the stage. On May 18, eight days before the novelâs scheduled release, he staged a rushed reading of his own adaptation at the Lyceum Theatre to protect the dramatic rights, and he billed it as Dracula: or The Un-Dead. Mental Floss has the story of that performance, which drew almost no audience.

It has been revealed that thatâs the part nobody can answer. Some accounts say an editor changed it, but a 2012 study that lined up the contract, the typescript, and the ads concluded there is no way to tell exactly when the title changed, or whether Stoker was the one who changed it.

Industry observers note that the old title didnât go anywhere, either. The word âUn-Deadâ turns up more than 30 times in the finished novel, and in 2009, Stokerâs great-grandnephew Dacre Stoker and the Dracula historian Ian Holt published a sequel and called it Dracula: The Un-Dead.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Created by Oscar-winning Downton Abbey writer Julian Fellowes, HBOâs lavish historical drama series The Gilded Age brings high-society living in late 19th-century Fresh York vividly to life. The show chiefly focuses on the tension and interplay between two colorful New York familiesâthe well-established old money of the van Rhijn family, and the ambitious, up-and-coming new money of the Russell familyâas they strive to make it to the top of Manhattanâs social ladder. In a time of considerable social and technological change, the battle between the stately and dignified old money of the van Rhijns and the flashier, rougher-around-the-edges new money of the Russells becomes all the more apparent.Â.

According to recent reports, the two families at the center of all the drama are fictional, but have real-life parallels in genuine Fresh York dynasties the Vanderbilts (whose immense railroad empire made them one of the wealthiest nouveaux riches in 19th century America) and any one of the cityâs Dutch-descended old-money elite, including the Schuylers (the family of New York senator Philip Schuyler, father-in-law of Alexander Hamilton). Around them, however, the series includes a cast of genuine turn-of-the-last-centuries socialites, businessmen, politicians and other public figures.Â.

Mrs. Caroline Webster Schermerhorn Astor, known as the âMrs. Astor,â was very much the queen and self-styled arbiter of old-money high-society Newly introduced York in the late 1800s. The wife of businessman and sporting impresario William Backhouse Astor, Jr., Mrs. Astor led the so-called âFour Hundredââan exclusive and tightly controlled group of high-society elites (supposedly so named because that was the capacity of her ballroom). She oversaw the group as a means of defending the established society scene in New York against the monied arrivistes and industrialists who had recently made their wealth in the rapidly changing landscape of the time. She is played by actress and Broadway legend Donna Murphy in The Gilded Age.Â.

The youngest and arguably best known of Mrs. Astorâs four daughters, Carrie Astor went on to follow in her motherâs footsteps, and became one of the late 19th centuryâs most noted socialites and party hostesses. Labeled by the press as âthe beauty of the house of Astor,â Carrie caused controversy when she fell for Tennessee-born banker Marshall Orme Wilson, whose family her mother deemed to be nouveau riche. Nonetheless, the marriage went ahead, and the couple later lived in a lavish mansion on East 64th Street. She is played by Canadian actress Amy Forsyth.Â.

Clara Barton was the Civil War nurse whose wartime experiences led to her founding the American Red Cross in 1881. Barton appeared in an early episode of the first season of The Gilded Age, played by Linda Emond, when the van Rhijns take an interest in supporting her newly founded charity.Â.

In The Gilded Age, the 5th Duke of Buckingham, Hector Vere (played by Ben Lamb), is a handsome and charming young British aristocrat who arrives in Latest York hoping to secure a marriage to improve his familyâs increasingly fraught financial situation. Although his title is certainly a genuine one in the British aristocracy, Hector Vere himself, however, is fictional. In reality, the actual Duke of Buckingham at the time of The Gilded Age was the lavishly named Richard Plantagenet Campbell Temple-Nugent-Brydges-Chandos-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham, who was a sixty-something statesman, politician, and former soldier.Â.

Pioneering businesswoman Mary H. Dickerson appears in Season 3 of The Gilded Age, played by Christiana Clark. Dickerson was the first Black woman to open a shop on Newport, Rhode Islandâs famous Bellevue Avenue. Her dress-making establishment catered to many of the high-society women who summered in Newport.Â.

Played by acclaimed character actress Ashlie Atkinson in The Gilded Age, Mamie Fish was the quick-witted and sharp-tongued good-time-girl of nouveau riche New York. The wife of railroad tycoon Stuyvesant Fish, she was known for doing or saying anything for fun, no matter how cutting or risquÃ©, and very much became the antidote to the stuffy and stately balls of old-money Manhattan when she arrived on the society party scene in the 1890s.Â.

Industry observers note that the son of slave parents, T. Thomas Fortune arrived in Newly introduced York in the early 1880s having already made a name for himself as a journalist writing for a groundbreaking Black newspaper in Washington, DC. He continued his work in New York, eventually serving as managing editor of the New York Age for 20 years, during which time he was a major voice in advancing African American causes in post-Civil War America. He is played by Sullivan Jones in The Gilded Age.

It has been revealed that american lawyer and socialite Ward McAllister, played by Nathan Lane in The Gilded Age, was the close friend of Mrs. Astor who aided in her compilation and management of New Yorkâs glittering âFour Hundredâ list. In fact, according to some versions of the tale at least, it was McAllister who came up with the listâs name when he explained in an 1888 interview with the New York Tribune that, âThere are only about four hundred people in fashionable New York Society â¦ If you go outside that number, you strike people who are either not at ease in a ballroom or else make other people not at ease.â The Four Hundred list went on to be published in public for the first time in The New York Times in 1892.Â.

Played by actor Bobby Steggert, the artist John Singer Sargent pops up in season 3 of The Gilded Age, when Russell family matriarch Bertha commissions him to paint a portrait of her daughter, Gladys. Although born in Florence, Sargent was the son of an American surgeon and divided his time between America and Europe. Having made his debut exhibition in Paris in the 1870s, he soon became one of the most sought-after portrait artists of the day on both sides of the Atlantic.Â.

Booker T. Washington, played by actor Michael Braugher, escaped crippling poverty to get himself an education in Virginia in the 1870s, before dedicating his life to educating and expanding the opportunities of Black children in post-Civil War America. He is introduced in Season 2 of The Gilded Age, when Peggy, Agnes van Rhijnâs secretary, stays with him in Tuskegee, Alabama, where he established a renowned institute for Black higher education.

In a recent development, even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

It has been revealed that cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Recent findings suggest that cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Industry observers note that gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Experts say there’s a mix of factors at play as for their rise in popularity: little treats and micro indulgences in an expensive world, the idea of “saving significant” on high-value bundles, and the sensory satisfaction of unboxing 25(ish) little boxes leading up to Christmas.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Souped-up Advent calendars are here to stay this holiday season, with just about every big player in food and beverage getting in on the trend.

Experts say there’s a mix of factors at play as for their rise in popularity: little treats and micro indulgences in an expensive world, the idea of “saving significant” on high-value bundles, and the sensory satisfaction of unboxing 25(ish) little boxes leading up to Christmas.

Sources indicate that “There’s something so special about having a small treat to look forward to each day,” Sockerbit Scandinavian candy founders Florence Baras and Stefan Ernberg remarked in a statement. Sockerbit is one of several newbies to the food Advent calendar space this year (and one of our new faves).

Sources indicate that advent Center, a hub for data and reviews for thousands of Advent calendars globally, says there are around 250 food and drink calendars on the market this year. The category makes up about a third of the 2026 calendars it lists.

Max Zeshut, Advent Center’s founder, remarked food and drink calendars work well because they’re a cheaper, noncommittal entry point into the ritual, compared to, for instance, a beauty box. And for all the upcoming and zany iterations out there, chocolate calendars remain an anchor.

Broadly, the global Advent calendar market is anticipated to grow from $1.32 billion in 2024 to $2.47 billion by 2033, according to research compiled by Accio, a B2B platform. Food and drink calendars hold a huge share of that, with the help of mainstays like Bonne Maman, whose annual calendars have inspired “Jamvent” fan groups for a decade, alongside newcomers that announced inaugural calendars this season.

Sources indicate that “As a small team, we try to be very conscious of the operational demands of every product launch,” Fishwife CEO and co-founder Becca Millstein told Bon Appétit. “Still, the demand [for calendars] grew too loud to ignore, so we decided to go for it.”.

Millstein cited Fishwife’s success in the online gifting space as motivation to launch a calendar this year. Fishwife’s includes 12 doors of tinned fish and extras, retailing for $150. The manufacturer noted the calendar’s “elements of surprise and delight” drives chatter and user-generated content on social media.

“In the end, we simply had to do it,” Millstein stated.

According to recent reports, when the Sichuan condiment company Fly By Jing’s Advent calendar introduced in 2024, it sold out in about a month. That’s when founder Jing Gao knew the brand was onto something.

Gao mentioned that 65% of its Advent calendars were purchased by newly introduced customers this year and that historically, 20% of customers who purchase a calendar go on to make another Fly By Jing purchase by the end of the year.

“To me, that really speaks to the power of discovery and giving people a chance to explore our flavors in a fun, unexpected way,” Gao noted. “We never want that sense of discovery to go away, even for people who have been with us from the beginning. It's become such a fun creative outlet for our team. I think that joy really comes through in the experience.”.

The stewards at Onyx Coffee Lab in Arkansas describe a similar phenomenon. “There's so much storytelling, education, and human connection surrounding coffee, and Advent gives us a unique opportunity to explore those things in ways that might not make sense within our everyday offerings,” Onyx’s co-founder Andrea Allen mentioned. Their box features 24 different coffees, each a 56-gram package of whole beans that are roasted on a schedule for peak brewing by their respective reveal day.

Sources indicate that at Bonne Maman, Advent calendar planning starts two years in advance. The development team pays close attention to seasonal ingredients and market trends to produce 24 limited-edition jams and spreads made just for the calendar. The result sells out every year, with production growing by 400% since 2017, according to a spokesperson. This year will mark 10 years of the Bonne Maman Advent calendar.

It has been revealed that “We’re grateful to the fans who have made it part of their holidays,” a company spokesperson mentioned. “On social media, we see everything from matcha pairings and coffee creations to new takes on toast, along with plenty of flavor-by-flavor reviews. Many fans also write to us to tell us which flavor they loved most. It helps us decide which flavors should return or come in larger sizes.”.

Industry observers note that have we stretched Advent calendar hype to its absolute limits? Advent Center’s Zeshut indicates no.

According to recent reports, “The clearest sign of demand is that people search for calendars that don't exist,” he said. “There's no official Monster Energy calendar this year, and 'monster Advent calendar' is still one of the most searched terms that brings people to our site,” he said. “I don't think we've reached peak calendar, but we may have reached peak chocolate.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Diwali occurs over five days during the Hindu month of Kartik, which means it typically falls around late October or early November.Â The main day of the festival always takes place on the upcoming moon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that november 6, 2026 marks the start of Diwali, one of the largest festivals in Hinduism. The holidayâs name comes from the Sanskrit term dipavali, which is also sometimes spelled deepavali, and which translates to ârow of lights.â Though it is celebrated differently across various regions, the festival generally centers around the theme of lightâs triumph over darkness.

Diwali occurs over five days during the Hindu month of Kartik, which means it typically falls around late October or early November.Â The main day of the festival always takes place on the upcoming moon.

Diwali is observed differently in different places. One of the most common traditions is the lighting of earthenware lamps called diyas on the new moon in order to invoke Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of abundance and wealth. In Northern India, the festival honors the homecoming of the god Rama, his consort Sita, Ramaâs younger half-brother, Lakshmana, and the deity Hanuman after their defeat of the demon Ravana. In Southern India, the festival celebrates the god Krishnaâs vanquishing of the demon Narakasura.Â.

Diwali is also sometimes viewed as a celebration of Lakshmiâs marriage to Vishnu, or of Lakshmi's birthday. Bengal honors the goddess Kali, who is associated with time, darkness, and destruction. Meanwhile, in Jainism, Diwali is seen as a celebration of the moment Mahavira, the founder of Jainism, reached nirvana, or liberation. In Sikhism, it celebrates the day that Guru Hargobind Ji, the Sixth Sikh Guru, was released from imprisonment.Â.

This festival is typically celebrated over the course of five days. On the first day, known as Dhanteras, people often clean their houses and purchase gold items. The second day, Naraka Chaturdashi or Choti Diwali, honors Krishnaâs defeat of Narakasura, and people often decorate their houses with diyas, use colored powders to create designs known as rangoli on the floors, and pray to their ancestors.Â.

The third day, Lakshmi Puja, is the primary day of the festival, which people often celebrate by lighting candles and fireworks and visiting temples. The fourth day, Govardhan Puja, Balipratipada, or Annakut, is the first day of the Hindu New Year in some regions, and often involves visiting friends and delivering gifts. The fifth day, Bhai Dooj, Bhai Tika, or Bhai Bij, celebrates the relationship between brothers and sisters, and brothers often visit the homes of their married sisters on this day.

People frequently wear new clothes, give food to the poor, and celebrate with games and other festivities. While the holiday is celebrated differently depending on location, it always revolves around one theme: the victory of good over evil, knowledge over ignorance, and light over dark.

In a recent development, as previously mentioned, Diwali takes its name from the Sanskrit term deepavali or dipavali, which means ârow of lights.â The festival existed prior to its adoption of this name, which references the practice of lighting oil lamps, or diyas, known as deepas in Sanskrit. Avali, the second half of the Sanskrit term, means row. âDiwaliâ is merely a shortened, informal version of the Sanskrit term.

Recent findings suggest that the festival is believed to have originated over 2,500 years ago, and is thought to have started out as a way to honor the yearâs final harvest. The earliest written references to the festival that use the name Deepavali have been traced to texts from the 7th century.Â.

Industry observers note that in some places, especially those that speak regional languages, among older generations, and in formal contexts, Diwali is still called Deepavali. It is often also called by this name across Southeast Asia.

It has been revealed that you hear a joke (a really funny one), and your first instinct is to laugh. But why?

Like many of our reactions, your brain needs time to process the joke before you respond. That simple joke travels through three parts of your brain before you find it funny enough to laugh at.Â.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While she might not have lived happily ever after, Amonute, better known as Pocahontas, played a nonetheless indispensable, pivotal role in shaping early relations between Native Americans and English colonists.

It has been revealed that daughter of Wahunsenacah, leader of the Powhatan Confederacy in Virginiaâs Tidewater region, Pocahontas was given two names at birth: Amonute, her formal name, and Matoaka, her âsacredâ birth name known only to her parents. âPocahontasâ was simply a nickname meaning âplayful one,â given to her in childhood.

Later, when she was captured and held for ransom by English colonists in 1613, she was âencouragedâ by her captors to convert to Christianity and was given the name âRebeccaâ following her baptism.

According to recent reports, in late 1607, English explorer and colonist John Smith was captured by Wahunsenacahâs men while exploring the Chickahominy River. Smith later claimed that just before he was to be executed by his Powhatan captors, the chiefâs young daughter, Pocahontas, threw herself atop Smith and begged her father to spare his life.

Despite the dramatic episode later becoming a central tenet of Pocahontasâs historic legacy, experts have speculated the ordeal was either fabricated by Smith, or at the very least heavily embellished.

Alongside the unlikelihood that the interference of a young girl could stop a Powhatan leaderâs ordered execution, Smith himself never publicly recounted the ordeal until years later, by which time Pocahontas had already become internationally famous through her trip to England with her husband, John Rolfe, in 1616.

In a recent development, during the First Anglo-Powhatan War, Pocahontas was captured and held for ransom by the Jamestown settlers. Throughout her near year of captivity, Pocahontas was held at Henricus, an English settlement in what is now Chesterfield County, Virginia, where she was taught English language and customs, baptised, and introduced to her future husband, tobacco farmer John Rolfe.

It has been revealed that rolfe married Pocahontas on April 5, 1614, ushering in a fresh era of peace between the Native Americans and English settlers. Just a year after they wed, the couple welcomed their first and only child, Thomas Rolfe, in January 1615.

While returning home from a lengthy trip to England with her husband and son in 1617, Pocahontas grew gravely ill. Just about 21 years old at the time of her passing, Pocahontasâs exact cause of death remains a mystery, though many historians have speculated smallpox, pneumonia, or tuberculosis to be the cause.

Recent findings suggest that shortly afterward, she was buried at St Georgeâs Church in Gravesend, Kent. After the church was destroyed in a fire in the late 1720s, Pocahontasâs exact gravesite, thought to reside somewhere beneath the church, was lost. In the mid-20th century, a statue was erected in the churchyard to commemorate Pocahontasâs memory.

Thomas, like his mother, had grown seriously ill on the journey back to Virginia. Fearing his young, ailing son could not survive the journey back to America, John Rolfe asked Sir Lewis Stukley, vice-admiral of Devon, to serve as his sonâs guardian while he remained in England.

Thomas was later raised by his fatherâs brother, Henry, but never reunited with his father, who passed away from an unknown illness in 1622, about five years after his wife.

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.).

In a recent development, helloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

Sources indicate that this kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

In a recent development, the pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

In a recent development, this dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Sources indicate that anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

Recent findings suggest that the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. One of the working titles for the novel was The Un-Dead, and Stoker signed the contract for the book under this title, before ultimately deciding on the name of the central character as the final title.Â.

Recent findings suggest that dracula was published in the UK on 26 May 1897 by the British organization Archibald Constable, at a cost of 6 shillings. It would not lead to financial success for Stoker, whose contract with the publisher stipulated that he could not receive any royalties until half of the initial print run was sold, while every copy sold after the first 1000 would earn him one shilling and sixpence from the overall cost of the book. The initial print run was 3000 copies. To help promote the book, 500 copies were sent out from the initial UK print run to friends, family, and journalists who would be in a position to let people know about the novel.Â.

Sources indicate that those who liked it included the Bristol Times and Mirror, which stated, âThe story is cleverly constructed and brilliantly told, and we do not think we can add further praise to the manner in which Mr. Bram Stoker sets forth the mysterious and the awfulâ and British Weekly, which declared: âIt is certain that no other writer of our day could have produced so marvellous a book.â Another notable fan in the world of literature was Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, with Doyle writing a personal letter to Stoker expressing his enthusiasm for the book: âI think it is the very best story of diablerie which I have read for many years. Those who were mixed on the novel included the Athenaeum, which stated, ââDraculaâ is highly sensational, but it is wanting in the constructive art as well as in the higher literary sense. It reads at times like a mere series of grotesquely incredible eventsâ and the Spectator, which said: âIts strength lies in the invention of incident, for the sentimental element is decidedly mawkish. Mr. Stoker has shown considerable ability in the use that he has made of all the available traditions of vampirology, but we think his story would have been all the more effective if he had chosen an earlier period.â.

Another feature in some contemporary reviews were warnings on the potentially frightening story, including The Times cautioning readers: âWe would not, however, recommend it to nervous persons for evening reading.â.

Ultimately, readers tended to side with the critics who liked the book, and it sold well, although it was not the bestselling novel of its year, being outdone by other works including Richard Marshâs novel The Beetle. Likewise, for several decades after the novel was published, little was written by scholars before academics began to take it seriously.

In a recent development, yet we can see from some of these early reviews that those who did foresee it ultimately having a lasting impact would eventually be proven right. It is ironic that one of the less well-known papers to have reviewed the novel, the Derby Mercury, would turn out to have some of the longest foresight when it said that Dracula âwill hold its own with the few really powerful stories of its kind which have lived in literary history.â.

According to recent reports, if you've ever been frustrated by the early hour your grandparents serve dinner, then you understand how people visiting the U.S. feel. The culture shock is substantial when people from other countries try to shift their circadian rhythms and digestion to match their American hosts.

But why is the time we eat dinner such a stark difference from the rest of the world?

It has been revealed that the United States is unique in many ways, like culture and work/life balance, which affect when and how we eat our meals. Even social media has had an influence on American dinnertime, making earlier evening meals trendy among younger generations.

Even though many other countries eat dinner much later than the 5:00-6:00 pm of Americans, it doesn't seem like the U.S. will be changing its schedules anytime soon.

In a recent development, despite the saying that breakfast is the most crucial meal of the day, America tends to prioritize dinner as the heartiest meal. Many Americans only eat light breakfasts and lunches, saving their biggest meal for dinnertime. Because of the light meals, Americans are understandably hungry earlier in the evening, and ready to eat a massive meal sooner.

In a recent development, other countries make lunch the biggest meal of the day. Mexico, Spain, and many South American countries have longer breaks for lunch, so they are able to eat a filling meal before going back to work. They just aren't hungry until later in the evening, because they already ate their biggest meal.

Their dinners are light and simple.

It has been revealed that another reason that lunch in other countries is bigger than dinner is because of the different work schedules. Americans work from 9 to 5, with a quick break for lunch. Our time revolves around the workday, leaving little time to focus on meals until after work ends.

Other countries break up their work hours with a longer midday break, allowing them time to enjoy a massive meal without rushing to get back to work.

In a recent development, in some instances, like in Spain, their time zone makes it so that the sun sets as late as 9 or 10 pm, so their daily schedules are adapted to keep working during daylight hours. Getting home later than Americans do, they would obviously need to have dinner later. Countries like the U.K. and Australia plan an afternoon snack called tea time, making it easier to push their evening meal later as well.

Americans tend to eat around work, while other countries work around mealtimes.

Work isn't the only thing countries schedule their meal times around.

Sources indicate that in France, primetime TV series don't start until nearly 9 pm to make sure dinner doesn't have to be rushed. Italians, known for their love of food, make dinner an entire experience. They spend hours socializing and sharing quality time while eating. Americans tend to see dinner as just another item on the to-do list.

It has been revealed that social media has affected American culture so much, and influencers are proclaiming early dinners to be healthier. Health and wellness TikToks have cited studies that say eating dinner early is better for your body's digestion and sleep. Those studies say that eating three hours before bedtime is best, and Gen Z influencers swear by "dinner by 8, in bed by 9.".

There are merits to both early and late dinners, but the American lifestyle fits better with earlier meals.

The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it.
  • In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.
  • Sources indicate that my friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Plan.

Sources indicate that my friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

Sources indicate that this habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

With the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food proposal,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

The USDA established the Thrifty Food Strategy in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over New York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”.

Industry observers note that however, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Recent findings suggest that note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

Fruit cart vendors, common in New York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

Industry observers note that what if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

In a recent development, whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

In a recent development, note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

The TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Sources indicate that patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

According to recent reports, last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

Shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

It has been revealed that so I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:.

According to recent reports, does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

Sources indicate that um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Sources indicate that thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

It has been revealed that C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.
