📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to a creepy makeup trend on TikTok, the phrase âuncanny valleyâ has fallen into wider use in recent years (and became even more of a talking point when that same makeup technique was used to unsettling effect in the horror blockbuster Obsession earlier this year).

But far from being simply a synonym for creepy or unsettling, the phrase âuncanny valleyâ itself has a rather more specific meaning and origin story behind it.Â.

Industry observers note that strictly speaking, âuncanny valleyâ refers to the feeling of unease a person experiences on seeing or encountering something that is designed to appear lifelike but ultimately falls short, making it seem eerily almost-but-not-quite human. Humanoid robots, AI-generated faces or voices, synthetic dolls, toys, puppets, waxworks, and computer-generated characters might all fall under this definition, creating an ever-greater feeling of creepiness the more lifelike something tries to become.Â.

Both the term uncanny valley and the theory behind it were the work of noted Japanese roboticist, Masahiro Mori. A professor at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, he spent more than 40 years working in the field of robotics (Hondaâs famous ASIMO robot was developed by one of his proteges), and in the 1970s developed a pioneering bipedal humanoid robot, utilising a upcoming kind of knee joint to walk upright on two legs. Alongside this, however, Mori became increasingly interested in human attitudes toward increasingly humanoid robots, and theorized that the more human-like a robot becomes, the more peopleâs attitude toward it changesâand not always for the good.Â.

Industry observers note that simple, bare, functional robots, such as those that work on industrial assembly lines, Mori theorized, elicit next to no response from people at all. The more human-like a robot becomes, however, the more people begin to feel an affinity with it. An upright-walking toy robot with a face, for instance, instantly feels more recognizably human-like than a whirring and clanking metal arm assembling parts in a car factory, and so it naturally resonates with us more readily. But as robots continue to become more lifelike, there eventually comes a tipping point, where things become almost too close to the real thing. Eventually, our natural affinity or empathy with these almost-but-not-quite robots and humanoids disappears, and collapses into eeriness.Â.

Mori plotted this trajectory on a line graph, showing with a rising line that as a robot becomes more humanlike, our affinity with it increases; but as it approaches a 100% human likeness, our affinity not only drops away, but plunges into revulsion and negativity, creating a noticeable dip on the graph that extends far below the x-axis. And this noticeable negative dip is what Mori named the âuncanny valley.âÂ.

According to recent reports, admittedly, Moriâs original theory was initially based more on his own intuition than any empirical studies, and so was intended more as a commentary on robot design than anything else. âPointing out the existence of the uncanny valley was more of a piece of advice from me to people who design robots rather than a scientific statement,â he later explained, making it clear that he saw the valley not as a problem to be overcome, but rather a phenomenon that robotics designers should be aware of. Humanoid robots, he ultimately believed, should be intentionally made less lifelike, rather than risk alienating or unnerving the people who encounter them.Â.

But what causes the uncanny valley in the first place? Well, not even Mori himself could answer thatâalthough science is busy trying to find an explanation.Â.

In 2019, a team of neuroscientists at Aachen University in Germany found that interacting with humanoid robots sets two parts of the brain in action: the medial prefrontal cortex, which responds with a kind of âhuman detectionâ signal, and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which converts this first response into a âlikeability valuation.â This package of information is then dealt with by the amygdala, which creates an emotional response.Â.

It has been revealed that their research not only proved that the uncanny valley exists, just as Mori had theorized, but found that not everyone responds in the same way, with some having a far more negative reaction than others. As a result, it seems the valley is unavoidable, and there is no single robot design that pleases (or terrifies) everyone. The solution in the future, ultimately, might not be to aim for ever greater human-like features in an effort to âsolveâ the uncanny valley, but to follow Moriâs advice and intentionally make robots appear less human to avoid any kind of reaction at all.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If "you are what you eat," then you might want to rethink "eating the rich." From our history books to the HBO series The Gilded Age, records and recreations show that the wealthiest Americans often ate foods that would make a poor man's plate look a lot more appealing.

The Gilded Age reveals that not everything that glitters is gold. This flashy period between the 1870s and 1900 was fueled by new money at the hands of tycoons like Vanderbilt and Carnegieâfortunes that embossed New York's Fifth Avenue and Newport, Rhode Island, in glitz and gold leaf. The era was a snapshot of America's elite that included clifftop "cottages," lavish balls, andâ¦ tureens of turtle soup?

That's just one of the delicacies that graced Gilded Age tables. While the servants and working classâlike the show's Mrs. Bauer and Jack Trotterâate far simpler fare and leftovers, the upper crust's menu was a lot more eclectic.

From oysters on the half shell to meat jelly, here are five foods families really ate during the Gilded Age that you may or may not see on season 4 of HBO's namesake show.

Recent findings suggest that today, we see celery as nothing more than the free side given with chicken wings. But back in the Gilded Age, this crunchy, watery vegetable was the centerpiece of the mealâliterally. 19th-century aristocrats even had decorative glass "celery vases" made to hold the hard-to-grow stalks, displaying the unlikely status symbols upright for all to see. As celery production increased and its price decreased, Gilded Age chefs began experimenting with the vegetable in the kitchenâbraising it, dressing it in mayo, and more.

In a recent development, no trip to Newport is complete without stopping by Midtown Oyster Bar for a dozen on the half shell, and back in the Gilded Age, high society was just as obsessed. Much like lobster, oysters had a humble beginning as a working-class staple across 19th-century coastal cities. They were shucked and slurped down by maritimers on the streets of New York long before becoming an elegant appetizer on Gilded Age menus. From raw oysters on sparkling beds of crushed ice to decadent baked preparations like Oysters Rockefeller, the modest mollusk underwent one of the greatest glow-ups in culinary history.

On The Gilded Age, most meals start with the clink of silver spoons against porcelain bowls. Menus from Gilded Age establishments like Delmonico's and period etiquette magazines back up this soup starter standard. An excerpt from Godey's Lady's Book on how to throw a proper dinner party goes as follows: "Commence dinner with raw oysters, then a choice of one or two soups.".

The soup du jour wasn't always lobster bisque or cream of celery, though. A luxury at the timeâand a dish rarely seen today due to strict conservation protectionsâturtle soup was all the rage in the Gilded Age. Chefs favored the diamondback terrapin, a turtle found from Cape Cod down the Gulf Coast. Whether eating out at a fine dining establishment in the city or hosting an intimate dinner party, these turtles were boiled, chopped, and finished with a swish of sherry before landing on high-society tables in the 1880s and '90s. That is, until overhunting almost wiped the creature out by the 1910s, sending prices soaring and pushing the dish off most menus.

Before 1950s housewives discovered Jell-O molds, Gilded Age kitchens were constructing towering aspics that served as equal parts savory centerpiece and sign of a master chef. These edible gelatinous sculpturesâwhich migrated from Europe and were made from boiled animal bones before powdered gelatin was popularized in the late 1800sâcontained meat, fish, produce, and eggs suspended in translucent broth like an edible display case. Served midway through formal multi-course banquets, colorful aspic creations were more of an art form than the cold course they were presented as.

In a recent development, you might recognize the name from the popular 2000s women's clothing store, but unlike the store, this sweet, berry-topped cake wasn't always made for the masses. Concocted by French chefs in the late 18th century and said to be named in honor of Queen Charlotte, Charlotte Russe cakeâa tower of ladyfingers surrounding cold Bavarian cream or custard and berriesâwas the creme de la creme of Gilded Age dessert spreads.

According to recent reports, while the nouveau riche enjoyed decadent riffs, sometimes even decked out with a decorative ribbon, the treat eventually evolved past wedding breakfasts and banquets of the elite. Decades later in the 20th century, the spongy sweet shifted from the white tablecloths of Delmonico's to the streets of Brooklyn, where pushcart vendors served simplified versions out of cardboard cups to working-class Fresh Yorkers.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender quickly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to initiative what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

It has been revealed that “We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke says. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”.

In a recent development, being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Sources indicate that tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

In a recent development, although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”.

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

Sources indicate that “Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

According to recent reports, puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

According to recent reports, huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

According to recent reports, the best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I quickly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

It has been revealed that although Huyke auditions fresh Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

Next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in New York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in New York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

According to recent reports, then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

Many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also reveals me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

“I believe every cuisine evolves,” she claims. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sesame Street has been a much-loved part of American popular culture for 57 years, first making its debut on November 10, 1969. One of its most enduring characters is a muppet known as Oscar the Grouch, who has been a part of the show since that inaugural season, and is visually defined by his vivid green fur.

It has been revealed that however, this isnât the color he originally wore when he first appeared on TV screens. Here is the story of why one of the distinguishing features of this character changed over time.

Oscar the Grouch is characterized by a number of things: he is as grumpy as his name suggests, lives in a trash can on the titular Sesame Street, and even has his own signature song, âI Love Trash.â Like other Sesame Street characters, he has also been used for educational purposes, including to encourage childrenâs interest in science.

He also has an emotional purpose: Oscar was intended to teach children that it was okay to feel sad or unhappy at times and to want to be left alone for whatever reason, to help children understand negative emotions and why itâs not always possible to feel upbeat, and to understand that this was a normal aspect of life.

Like a number of Sesame Street characters, he was intended to have a colorful appearance, but that color altered over time.

Industry observers note that oscar was first intended to have magenta-colored hair, and illustrations of this have survived, but this hue was never used in the show itself because it became clear that this shade wouldnât show up well on TV, given the limitations of color television at the time. It was therefore decided that he would be orange instead, and there are surviving images of him in his original shade in the first season. However, after the first season, things changed, and viewers who tuned into season 2 were met with a different sight.

Oscar was redesigned in green because it was felt that this more muted color was better suited to his personality than the brightness of orange, and that green also had more of a connection with the idea of trash. The in-universe explanation for this was that Oscar had gone on vacation to Swamp Mushy Muddy, and had become covered with slime which had changed him from orange to the green of the swamp.

According to recent reports, the change to green has also had other benefits. In recent years, given Oscarâs close connection with trash, he has also been used to raise awareness of being green in an environmentally friendly sense, including participating in campaigns on the importance of taking out litter and recycling.

In an âinterviewâ with the Radio Times, Oscar also drew a connection between his current green color and green in the environmentally conscious sense of the word: âAre you good at recycling? - Do you know who you are talking to? I am GREEN for a reason. I love recycling and composting.â.

With the need to protect the environment all the more important, the choice to switch Oscar from orange to green seems like an even more astute choice than it did when it was first made.

According to recent reports, veterans can face unique challenges, yet the U.S. offers plenty of resources and benefits for those who have served the nation. Yet not every location in America offers these opportunities equally.Â.

They measured 19 factors, including the number of available jobs that align with military skill sets, access to VA health facilities, and more.Â.

The unemployment rate for veterans is 3.6%, yet roughly 32,000 veterans are still experiencing homelessness, and seven out of 100 veterans experience PTSD, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Austin, Texas came in first as the best city for veterans in the U.S. The city boasted the best array of colleges for veterans, as well as the seventh-best job-growth rate in the U.S. and the ninth-highest annual median income for this demographic. It also offered plenty of opportunities for veterans to connect and enjoy life: it had the fourth-smallest projected decrease in veterans between 2024 and 2053, and some of the highest concentrations of restaurants and arts and entertainment venues offering military discounts in the country.Â.

Recent findings suggest that madison, Wisconsin came in second, largely because of the economic growth opportunities available to veterans there. Madison-based veteransâ median income increases 8% each year, the sixth-largest average annual increase anywhere in the country. Homelessness among veterans is also low there, with just two homeless veterans for every 1,000 veteran residents.Â.

In a recent development, up next was Scottsdale, Arizona, where veterans have a median income of $68,000 annually, the sixth-highest in the nation. The city also has the third-fewest homeless veterans and ranks highly among the best places to retire and to raise a family, among other factors.Â.

Fremont, California ranked first in terms of the highest percentage of military skill-related jobs, followed by Madison, Wisconsin; Durham, North Carolina; Boston, Massachusetts; and San Jose, California.Â.

Meanwhile, Lincoln, Nebraska had the lowest percentage of unemployed veterans, followed by Chesapeake, Virginia; St. Petersburg, Florida; Irving, Texas; and Fremont, California.Â.

When it came to veteransâ income growth, Miami, Florida came in first, followed by Garland, Texas; San Bernardino, California; Gilbert, Arizona, and Boston, Massachusetts. Gilbert, Arizona also had the lowest percentage of veterans in poverty, followed by Virginia Beach, Virginia; Chula Vista, California; Fremont, California; and Charlotte, North Carolina.Â.

Virginia Beach, Virginia had the lowest percentage of homeless veterans per veteran population. Also among the five lowest were Raleigh, North Carolina; Colorado Springs, Colorado, Buffalo, Fresh York; and Jacksonville, Florida.

Additionally, Virginia Beach, Virginia; Chesapeake, Virginia; Colorado Springs, Colorado; and Norfolk, Virginia were tied for the highest population of veterans in the country, followed by Anchorage, Alaska.

In a recent development, at the bottom end of the rankings was Detroit, Michigan, which ranked poorly due to a high unemployment rank and low quality of life scores. Newark, Upcoming Jersey ranked second-lowest, followed by Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Memphis, Tennessee; and Toledo, Ohio.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The '80s were tubular; each year made a bold, colorful statement in music, movies, style, and slang.

It's hard to believe the decade of cult-classic blockbusters, massive hair, MTV, and shoulder pads began almost 47 years ago, though some trends have made a comeback in the 2010s and 2020s, like high-waisted jeans and neon-colored clothing.

The '80s are remembered for next-generation technology: the Sony Walkman, VHS tapes, boomboxes (cue John Cusack), CDs, camcorders, and the Nintendo Entertainment System.

It has been revealed that hair was always teased, and hairspray was a non-negotiable for men and women. Music videos took over pop culture; Michael Jackson had us dancing with Billie Jean, and Madonna invited material girls to live in a material world.

Movies that remain beloved, including Ferris Bueller's Day Off, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Back to the Future, Top Gun, The Breakfast Club (or really anything with Molly Ringwald), Ghostbusters, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Return of the Jedi, lit up theater marquees in the '80s.

Industry observers note that beyond fashion, media, and tech, the '80s also gave us several slang terms. Some faded as soon as they arrived, while others stuck around.Â.

According to Your Dictionary, here are nine â80s slang words we still use today.Â.

It has been revealed that âCruisingâ in the 1980s meant enjoying a long drive with nowhere specific to go. If someone invited you to "cruise" or remarked they were out "cruising," you knew they were driving around aimlessly.

In 2026, "cruising" still describes a leisurely drive without a destination, just for fun.Â.

It has been revealed that the word "harsh" has always sounded, well, unpleasant, so itâs no surprise its meaning took on the same tone. Since the '80s, people have used harsh to describe something uncomfortable or intense.

In 2026, we use it the same way, whether weâre talking about someoneâs actions, a tough experience, or something extremely unappealing, like a bright light shining right in your face.

Awesome is one of those words that has never lost relevance. The '80s popularized it as the go-to way to describe something amazing or exceedingly cool.

In 2026, people of all ages still use "awesome" to express excitement about something (or someone) extraordinary.

The slang "for sure" is another classic that has stuck around, and hopefully always will. In both the 1980s and 2026, itâs an easy way to say "of course," often to reassure someone or dispel uncertainty. Sometimes a casual "for sure" is just what someone needs to hear in an anxious moment.

Outrageous is a fun, expressive word that spices up any conversation. In the '80s, it described something so bold or abnormal that it was actually cool. In 2026, we use it less as a compliment and more to denote something shocking, but the basic meaning remains.Â.

In a recent development, "Burn out" is so common today that we forget people used it to describe the same feeling in the '80s. Someone who was burnt out was totally exhausted and just over it.

It has been revealed that in 2026, we use "burn out" to describe how we feel after a long workday, or maybe a trying year thatâs absolutely depleted our motivation. Anything that leaves someone feeling overly drained (work, a conversation, or a hobby) is an example of burnout.Â.

It has been revealed that whoa, like many words on this list, has definitions that couldnât be more different. Centuries ago, people riding horseback or steering carriages used "whoa" to slow or stop the horses.Â.

Industry observers note that in the 1980s, "whoa" became an exclamation of surprise or intense reaction, both pleasant and unpleasant. In 2026, we say "whoa" to express excitement, surprise, or concern, depending on the instance.

"Chill" has lots of meanings, both formal and informal. In the '80s, it broke away from its "cold" definition and became slang for someone or something calm, laid-back, or relaxing.

In 2026, we still use "chill" to describe someone whoâs low-key, or to relay when we want to unwind.

According to Merriam-Webster, "excellent" may not have been invented in the '80s, but the decade surely made it a household word. Back then, people used "excellent" to describe something very good.

In 2026, we use "excellent" when "good" or "great" doesnât fully explain how we feel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though Cincinnati is best known for breweries, another effervescent beverage has a long history in the Queen City: the nectar soda.

It has been revealed that home to the oldest pharmacy college in the U.S. west of the Alleghenies, the Eclectic Medical Institute (1845-1952), and Lloyd Brothers Pharmacists, Cincinnati was long on the forefront of the pharmaceutical industry. The city had a number of apothecaries with soda fountains, as well as confectioners serving countless carbonated concoctions—some claiming to cure a variety of ailments, and others simply providing customers with something sweet and refreshing to drink.

Enter the nectar soda. The flavor is a combination of vanilla and bitter almond, and the drink is pastel pink in color—a nod to the hue of almond flowers, according to Dann Woellert, a Cincinnati food historian, etymologist, and the author of Cincinnati Candy: A Sweet History. Nicknamed the “drink of the gods,” the bitter almond flavor of nectar soda balances out what would otherwise be overly sweet vanilla, creating an addictive taste that grows on you with each sip.

Nectar sodas have been served in Cincinnati since at least the late 1870s, though, like many iconic foods and beverages, its precise origins are murky. The only other U.S. city to embrace nectar sodas was Upcoming Orleans, but unlike Cincinnati, the tradition fizzled out in the Big Easy in the mid-20th century. Plus, Woellert says that the Queen City popularized them first. “They were served in Cincinnati nearly a decade before New Orleans,” he says.

While the Cincinnati nectar soda has multiple origin stories, each crediting a different pharmacist or confectioner, Woellert has concluded that John Mullane created the flavor after traveling to Quebec City to learn the art of confectionery from a prominent Canadian candymaker. He began serving nectar sodas in his confectionery shop in downtown Cincinnati in the late 1870s.

Recent findings suggest that so, why did the nectar soda end up in Cincinnati and Fresh Orleans, of all places? Wollert suspects that the bitter almond and vanilla flavor was used by the French Acadians who settled in both Quebec City and New Orleans.

Industry observers note that though nectar sodas aren’t as common as they were in the early 20th century, when they could be found at countless confectioneries and pharmacy soda fountains across Cincinnati, they’re still served at establishments throughout the city and the surrounding area. Nectar sodas have been on the menu at ice cream and chocolate shop Aglamesis Brothers since it opened in Cincinnati in 1908, if not shortly thereafter. That’s according to company president and CEO Randy Young, who is also a third-generation family member.

It’s unclear when nectar sodas were added to the menu at Graeter’s, a Cincinnati ice cream and chocolate shop that opened in 1870 and now has locations throughout the city and the Midwest, but Chip Graeter, chief of retail operations and a fourth-generation family member, indicates that they were especially popular throughout the 1940s, 1950s and 1960s.

In a January 28, 1947 article in the Cincinnati Enquirer, Tom Moore, the head of the soda department at Dow Drug Store—which operated 32 soda fountains throughout the metropolitan area at that time—stated that “nectar is one of the most popular flavors in all of their stores, and has been for many years.” Five years prior, Dow ran an ad in the same newspaper which read: “Be glad you live in Cincinnati, the only place in the country where you can enjoy a Dow double-dip nectar soda.”.

Industry observers note that originally, nectar syrup was made by combining half-and-half or milk with water, bitter almond extract, vanilla extract and red food coloring. While Aglamesis eventually switched to a dairy-free shelf-stable syrup, Graeter’s recipe has never changed—it still contains milk and needs to be refrigerated.

Both Aglamesis and Graeter’s make nectar soda by mixing nectar syrup with a dollop of whipped cream, adding a scoop or two of vanilla ice cream, then topping it off with some soda water and more whipped cream.

Industry observers note that though Young says that nectar sodas are most popular with older adults, they’re also a hit with members of younger generations who try them. “People who grew up with them still love them today,” Graeter says. “We still make them in all of our stores, but they’re not nearly as popular today as they once were, simply because milkshakes and smoothies have taken over.”.

Industry observers note that according to Young, there is a commercially available descendant of the nectar soda. “Commercial soda companies like Barqs and others came out with their version of cream soda—a bright pink soda—which got its flavoring from nectar soda,” he explains.

In a recent development, located a roughly 15 minute drive from downtown Cincinnati in the historic Oakley neighborhood, this ice cream parlor has been serving customers since 1913, five years after the confection company was founded. Nectar sodas come in old-fashioned fountain glasses with metal handle holders, and their frothy, light pink color matches the chairs and striped indoor awning. While you’re there, be sure to check out the pair of Tiffany stained glass lamps on the counter.

Recent findings suggest that there are 18 Graeter’s locations throughout Cincinnati, as well as outposts in Cleveland, Columbus, Chicago, Indianapolis, Pittsburgh, Louisville, Lexington, and other locations in southwestern Ohio and northern Kentucky. The Graeter's in Cincinnati's historic Hyde Park neighborhood is one of the chain's oldest locations.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Gene’s has been an institution in the South Cumminsville neighborhood of Cincinnati since it opened in 1962. While they’re best known for their cheese coneys (a chili dog covered in shredded cheddar cheese, served with onions and mustard), they also make a mean nectar soda and nectar soda milkshake—the perfect accompaniment to one of their famous hot dogs. The hot dog stand is open from mid-February through the beginning of October, and is always closed on Sundays.

According to recent reports, yes, UDF is a chain, but it started in Cincinnati in 1940. And because there are locations all over the city, you’re never far from a nectar soda. Expect a no-frills experience, but a delicious nectar soda in a (plastic) soda fountain glass.

Industry observers note that glossy and pourable, about the consistency of warm maple syrup—not thick like caramel. Recent findings suggest that they have a noticeable kick, but they’re more tangy-sweet than fiery. The honey and butter temper the chile flakes. If you’re sensitive to spice, use less than the suggested ¾ tsp. or leave the flakes out entirely.

Recent findings suggest that place a rimmed baking sheet on bottom rack of oven; preheat to 450°. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, and ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large bowl; sprinkle with ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and season with freshly ground black pepper.

Carefully remove baking sheet from oven. Using tongs, arrange brussels sprouts cut-side down on hot baking sheet. Roast brussels on bottom rack until softened and deeply browned, 15–25 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring ¼ cup honey to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring often, until honey is a deep amber color but not burnt (it will be foamy, that’s okay), 3–4 minutes.

It has been revealed that remove from heat and add ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar (it will bubble up quite aggressively) and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes; whisk until sauce is smooth. Return saucepan to medium heat and add 3 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, whisking constantly, until glaze is glossy, bubbling, and slightly thickened, 3–4 minutes.

Transfer roasted brussels sprouts to a large bowl. Add half the hot honey glaze and scallions and toss to combine. Taste and add more glaze if desired. Transfer to a platter and top with lemon zest. Serve remaining glaze alongside.

Do ahead: Glaze can be made 5 days ahead; refrigerate after cooling.

Why Veterans Day Was Originally Called Armistice Day

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that november 11 is Veterans Day, the national holiday commemorating those who have served in the military.
  • To celebrate the end of World War I, the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, on November 11, 1918, World War I effectively came to an end as the Allies and the Germans agreed to an armistice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that november 11 is Veterans Day, the national holiday commemorating those who have served in the military. It is often confused with Memorial Day, which honors those troops who were killed or died from injuries caused by the wars they fought in, but Veterans Day is more about showing gratitude to the living troops who served. But the holiday didn't originally include veterans of all wars.

To celebrate the end of World War I, the U.S. implemented a newly introduced holiday called Armistice Day. It wouldn't become Veterans Day for a couple of decades, after more wars had taken place and more soldiers were coming home needing support. It became important not just to commemorate those who fought to end one war, but those who fought in other wars and those who served outside of wartime, working to maintain peace.

According to recent reports, on November 11, 1918, World War I effectively came to an end as the Allies and the Germans agreed to an armistice. The word armistice comes from the Latin "arma," meaning weapons, and "sistere," meaning to halt or bring to a standstill. So, while World War I is officially recorded as ending in June 1919 with the Treaty of Versailles, the actual combat ceased in the previous November.

Armistice Day was first celebrated in November 1919, just months after the Treaty of Versailles. In 1926, Congress passed a resolution to officially name November 11 Armistice Day, and in 1938 it was made a national holiday. Britain also made November 11 a holiday, opting to name theirs "Remembrance Day," to honor soldiers of all wars, not just World War I. America didn't know it yet, but our country would adopt that same idea after participating in other major wars.

According to recent reports, after World War II (1939-1945) and the Korean War (1950-1953), the United States wanted to honor the soldiers who fought in these wars as well as World War I. In 1954, instead of creating separate holidays for each war, Congress voted to strike the word "Armistice" from the official legislation and replace it with "Veterans." President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the resolution, legally changing the name to Veterans Day.

Since then, the U.S. has fought several more wars, including the current Iran War. Each November 11, any man or woman who served in the United States military, in wartime or peacetime, is to be honored for their hard work and dedication to our country. This does not include active-duty members, and many of them will ask that you not give them special attention that should go to those who previously served. You can thank active-duty members on Armed Forces Day, the third Saturday in May, or any other day of the year.

Recent findings suggest that as culture and politics have evolved in the U.S., veterans began to be treated terribly. The Vietnam War, which had many critics, saw soldiers returning home to be mocked, harassed, and threatened. The following wars also saw a lack of respect for those who fought to protect the country. Leaders and governments that should have taken accountability for wartime errors have often been quiet as veterans became scapegoats.

Sources indicate that thanking veterans for their service on Veterans Day is a good start, since there are troops who come home and never receive gratitude. But it's not the only thing we can do to support these men and women. Donating to organizations like the Wounded Warrior Project, DAV, or the Gary Sinise Foundation helps veterans get medical care, housing, and other needs met. Honoring those who served is best done by taking care of them when it's time for them to rest.

If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork.

What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing?

Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Made In 9-x-13-inch Baking Dish.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

In a recent development, meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind.

Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

According to recent reports, whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes.

Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking.

According to recent reports, within weeks of its Christmas Day 2020 premiere, Bridgerton quickly rose in the ratings to become Netflix's biggest hit ever. The lavish period drama, which is set in Regency-era England, is based on Julia Quinn's eight-book series. The debut season followed the events of The Duke and I, the first book in the series, in which the eldest Bridgerton daughter, Daphne (Phoebe Dynevor), sets out to find a husband in 1813.

Bridgerton has now released four seasonsâwith a fifth on the wayâalong with a spinoff series titled Queen Charlotte. Here are some things you might not know about the historical romance-drama thatâs had the world besotted for years now.

Shonda Rhimes and her production company Shondaland signed a nine-figure deal with Netflix back in 2017. Bridgerton was the production company's first project under this deal, and it reunited Rhimes with Chris Van DusenâBridgerton's creator and showrunner for seasons 1 and 2, who also served as a producer on Shondaland demonstrates like Grey's Anatomy and Scandal.

In addition to Bridgerton, Shondaland has released Inventing Anna (2022) and The Residence (2025) on Netflix.

In a recent development, netflix publicly predicted that approximately 63 million homes would have watched Bridgerton in its first month of release when the series first debuted. On January 27, 2021, Deadline declared that Bridgerton had already been viewed by 82 million households, making it Netflix's biggest original hit ever. And while other seasons have been successful for Netflix, its first is still the most-watched.

At the time of this writing, Bridgerton has fallen in the rankings of most popular Netflix originals, with its first season sitting at No. 8 on the list of most-watched series globally. The third season is presently at 10th place. Wednesday season 1 owns the top spot.

In a recent development, in an interview with Radio Times, the season 2 lead recounted the advice Phoebe Dynevor, who took the lead as Daphne Bridgerton in season 1, gave him so that he could prepare for taking over the helm of this fan-favorite show. âPhoebe was great at [counseling] me, because itâs not something you can explain to your friends and family, who you donât see for weeks on end,â Bailey mentioned.

It has been revealed that dynevorâs first piece of advice was to be physically ready, meaning: Eat healthy, exercise, and sleep as much as you can, as shooting days can sometimes last up to 14 or 15 hours. Because each season focuses on a different Bridgerton siblingâs love story, Bailey created a notebook he hopes to pass on. âItâs a Bridgerton guide for the next sibling who plays the lead,â he stated.

Fans of Jane Austen and William Shakespeare will spot plenty of Easter eggs in season 2 that reference the works of these prolific writers, as well as adaptations of their stories.Â Most notably: The second season of Bridgerton uses the classic enemies-to-lovers trope for Kate and Anthony that mimics Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy's romance in Pride and Prejudice.

Recent findings suggest that during the first episode, Kate is seen eavesdropping on Anthony talking about the women at the party being insufficient, just as Elizabeth does with Mr. Darcy when he makes very similar complaints. And fans of the 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice will notice a not-so-subtle nod to Colin Firthâs iconic wet shirt moment in episode 5, when Anthony falls into a lake.Â.

In another nod to Austen, the Sharma sistersâ tight-knit relationship resembles that of the Dashwood sisters from Sense and Sensibility. Both families have lost their fathers and the elder sisters are determined to find a match for their younger sisters while denying themselves the potential for love. In episode 7 of season 2, Kate falls off her horse and suffers a concussion, similar to Louisa Musgrove in Persuasion. (Though in Bridgerton the fall makes Anthony realize how much he loves Kate, while Louisaâs accident makes Captain Frederick Wentworth reexamine his feelings for Anne Elliot.)Â Â.

Shakespeare fans will see the parallels between Kate and Edwinaâs sisterhood and that of The Taming of the Shrewâs Katherina, also called Kate, and Bianca. In both stories, to gain an audience with the younger sister, suitors must first go through the elder sister and âtame the shrewâ or, as Lady Whistledown states âtame the rather prickly spinster of a beast.âÂ.

In addition, the Bard's Much Ado About Nothing is also an enemies-to-lovers story featuring a failed wedding much like Anthony and Edwinaâs would-be nuptials. Bridgerton even features a scene that bears a striking resemblance to Kenneth Branaughâs 1993 adaptation of the play, in which enemy characters Beatrice (Emma Thompson) and Benedick (Branagh) finally admit their feelings for one another and kiss in a church after the failed wedding, just as Kate and Anthony do.

According to recent reports, ashley told Glamour UK that because she was one of the leads in season 2, she wanted to make sure she was fully hydrated and well-fed before shooting her first scene. So she ate a âmassive portion of salmon,â but because she was wearing a corset, she then felt sick. âI [realized] when you wear the corset, you just donât eat. It changes your body,â Ashley noted.

According to recent reports, georgina Musgrave serves as Bridgertonâs sustainability coordinator, which means she was finding latest ways to be environmentally conscious and overseeing steps to minimize the showâs carbon footprint. In addition, Lisa Heathcote, the showâs head food economist, used fake food so it wouldnât spoil while shooting. Meal scenes had real food but used lighter ingredients and raw vegetables so that the actors could eat over multiple takes.

Sources indicate that most of Bridgerton's first season was filmed in Bath, England, where the Royal Crescentâan architectural landmark comprised of 30 Georgian terrace housesâis prominently featured (it played a role in 2008's The Duchess, starring Keira Knightley, as well). Hatfield House, Wilton House, Castle Howard, and Lancaster House all make appearances alongside some notable gardens, including Painshill Park in Surrey.

When it came time for season 2, several episodes take place at the Bridgertonsâs ancestral home, known as Aubrey Hall. To create this country estate, the production team utilized Wrotham Park, which was also featured in Vanity Fair (2004) and Jane Eyre (2011). The Palladian-style manor in Hertfordshire is located about 17 miles from central London. The Aubrey Hall gardens and orangerie were shot at Wrest Park in Bedfordshire.

Bridgerton isn't the only project that has filmed in these historic homes: Netflix's The Crown, Joe Wright's Pride and Prejudice (2005), and Autumn de Wilde's Emma (2020) all filmed scenes at Wilton House; Hatfield House appeared in Enola Holmes (2020) and Yorgos Lanthimos's The Favourite (2018). Lancaster House, which is located next door to Buckingham Palace, has played the role of its more famous neighbor in both The Crown and Downton Abbey.

Sources indicate that speaking of Buckingham Palace: Chris Van Dusen revealed in a tweet that production had a very tight window to film a pivotal season 1 scene at Lancaster House, because Queen Elizabeth II needed to use the space. Today, Lancaster House is used for formal events and dinners, though it was originally constructed as a private residence for Prince Frederick, Duke of York and Albany (the second son of King George III). Over the years, it has been the site of many historical occasions, including an 1848 recital by Chopin, with Queen Victoria in attendance.

In a recent development, ellen Mirojnick, head costume designer for Bridgerton, and her team of nearly 250 artists are behind the show's (often ostentatious) fashion sense. In a 2020 interview with Vogue, Mirojnick said they created approximately 7500 pieces for season 1 alone, and ended up using about 5000 of them. Dynevor wore 104 different costumes during the eight-episode season, and in a behind-the-scenes video released by Netflix, actress Nicola Coughlan, who plays Penelope Featherington, mentions how many of the details on each costume, like flowers and other accessories, were handmade by the team.

According to recent reports, for season 2, the costume department didnât back down on the opulence. Netflix revealed that the dress Penelopeâs sister, Phillipa Featherington (played by Harriet Cains) wears to Queen Charlotteâs Diamond Ball in episode 2 required more than 14,000 crystals in four shades of gold.

It has been revealed that since Bridgerton revolves around the upper crust during the 19th century, it was essential for there to be plenty of show-stopping jewelry on display. According to Harper's BAZAAR, jewelry for the show was sourced, in part, from Upcoming York City, Italy, and England. And the tiaras worn by the series' main cast members came from Swarovski's crystal archives.

In an interview with BuzzFeed about season 2, Van Dusen shared that, due to COVID, "We had to edit everything virtually, so a lot of the show was put together in my basement and not a fancy studio like most people would think.".

Along with music from composer Kris Bowers, producers also enlisted the Vitamin String Quartetâwho are known for their classical covers of famous songsâto perform their unique renditions of modern pop songs. Throughout the seasons, there have been several covers of hit â70s, â80s, and â90s tunes, including Madonnaâs âMaterial Girl,â Alanis Morissetteâs âYou Oughta Know,â âJust What I Neededâ by The Cars, and Nirvanaâs âStay Away.âÂ.

In addition, there have been other modern songs featured like âDiamondsâ by Rihanna, âDancing on My Ownâ by Robyn, âEnchantedâ by Taylor Swift, and âBad Idea Right?â by Olivia Rodrigo.

In a recent development, van Dusen tweeted that Princess Diana's childhood home, Althorp, was the main inspiration in designing the Bridgerton family home. Though Diana was considered a commoner by some, she still lived in an elegant and refined estate in Northamptonshire.

Industry observers note that you know those portraits on the walls of the grand homes in Bridgerton? If you look closely, you'll notice that many of the figures are based on the show's stars. When matriarch Violet Bridgerton (Ruth Gemmell) is invited to Buckingham Palace to have tea with Queen Charlotte (Golda Rosheuvel), you can see that the portraits of the Queen and King George III (James Fleet) on the walls are all based on the actors themselves, rather than their real-life counterparts. Even Bridgerton House has portraits of the cast for some added authenticity.

While Daphne and Simon got their happily ever after in season 1 of Bridgerton, it was announced in 2021 that RegÃ©-Jean Pageâthe series' breakout starâwould not be returning for a second season. Initially, Page told Variety that the role was always meant to be a short-time gig, which was part of its appeal.

In a recent development, â[I]t felt like a limited series. I get to come in, I get to contribute my bit and then the Bridgerton family rolls on," he remarked. Though other reports have suggested that creative differences might have played a part in Page's decision not to return, those rumors have not been confirmed.

Industry observers note that while Dynevor returned for the second season in a supporting role, she did not appear in seasons 3 or 4, telling Variety in 2023: âIâve done what I wanted to do with that character and she had a great arc. If they ask me back in the future, who knows?â Other cast members who have exited include Ruby Barker as Marina Thompson, Charithra Chandran as Edwina Sharma, and Ruby Stokes as Francesca Bridgerton (who was replaced by Hannah Dodd).

Recent findings suggest that in a shock announcement back in 2021, Bridgerton fans learned that showrunner Chris Van Dusen would be exiting after two seasons, and Jess Brownell would be replacing him. Brownell had worked in multiple Shondaland shows, including Greyâs Anatomy and Scandal, before taking on the fresh gig.

Though the reason for the behind-the-scenes shakeup was never revealed, Van Dusenâs statement at the time was nothing but appreciative of his time on the show.

Recent findings suggest that âWith Bridgerton, I set out to make the period show I always wanted to see,â he said in 2021. âI never could've anticipated how much the rest of the world also wanted to see it. Iâm deeply proud of this remarkable cast and incredible crew, and Iâm so grateful for the enduring support of Shonda, who Iâve worked alongside for 17 years. Shondaland is where I learned how to make TV, craft incredibly complex characters and how to tell stories. Though the first two seasons of Bridgerton followed the first two books in Julia Quinnâs series, the third and fourth seasons flip-flopped, with season 3 skipping ahead to Romancing Mister Bridgerton, which follows Penelope and Colin's love story, and season 4 going back to An Offer from a Gentleman, following Benedict and Sophie.

It has been revealed that for the forthcoming fifth season, the show will adapt the sixth book, When He Was Wicked, with a few major changes. (More on that to come.).

Penelope undergoes a glow-up for the third season, and the scene in which everyone realizes it was influenced by a classic 1990s movie.Â.

The moment where she walks down the stairs at the Four Seasons Ball, catching everyoneâs attention, came from 1999âs Sheâs All That. Showrunner Jess Brownell was inspired by the memorable scene in which Laney walks down the stairs to âKiss Meâ to show off her makeover, according to Shondaland.

Recent findings suggest that bridgerton season 5 is due out sometime in 2027, and itâll mark a first for the Netflix series, featuring a queer couple as the leads. Following Francescaâs story this time around, the show has gender-swapped book character Michael Stirling, with the Bridgerton sibling ending up with Michaela Stirling. âAs Johnâs cousin, Michaela is the only other person who fully understands what Francesca might feel like,â actress Hannah Dodd teased. âThat just connects them on another level.â.
